Ground truth from the manual era: they got 15 of 17 requirements right — the number any accelerated replacement has to beat, not just match faster
data.name: Ai psychosis in ai accelerated research

data.brief: Corridor's bet: within 6-12 months the majority of shipped code will be reviewed by AI, not humans — code review is now the bottleneck as agents run autonomously for hours from Slack, "and we're not going to accept that for very long" (paraphrase)
data.name: Corridor bets most shipped code will be AI-reviewed within 6-12 months

data.brief: Practitioner observation from apps on hundreds of millions of devices: AI users have moved out of the "forgiving phase" — thinking spinners and long opaque waits are no longer tolerated; users expect to see what the agent is doing, and the KPI shifts from total latency to time-to-first-chunk
data.name: AI users have left the forgiving phase; the KPI shifts to time-to-first-chunk

data.brief: The wave-1 aftermath from the ops side: bigger PRs, code shipped much faster, and now "maybe even from non-developers that don't actually know the code or what it's doing or the operating principles behind it"; "AI is creating a lot more issues in production as AI code goes through," and "it's not clear we have the right structures in place to deal with the amount of changes coming through." A cost-pressure rider: "unlimited tokens is coming to an end… they're starting to clamp down, prices are going up, companies are getting a lot more stringent" (see Review note 3)
data.name: Ai velocity outruns prod structures

data.brief: April 2026: in OpenAI's "Parameter Golf" hiring challenge (~1,000 ML engineers, ~2,000 submissions, 47 passing open review, 7 of those from agents), Weco's agent Aiden ran 22 days and set 7 leaderboard records — each stamped as a new competition best by OpenAI — vs 3 for the best human; OpenAI couldn't hire its top contributor because it wasn't a person
data.name: Weco's Aiden set 7 records in OpenAI's Parameter Golf challenge vs 3 for the best human

data.brief: Declared role shift, dated by the speaker: 2025 had "product engineers"; now engineers should "focus less on the product and more on making the AI work on the product" — tools, codebase improvements, knowledge bases — becoming "AIX engineers", with per-product judgment (ASCII view of a Unity 3D world? easy agent logins for permissioned apps?) as the new core skill
data.name: Product engineers become AIX engineers making the AI able to work on the product

data.brief: Post-training does not pull personas back toward the record — it amplifies the composite: human raters evaluate with conceptual frameworks built by the same culturally dominant narratives that saturate the corpus, so preference optimization rewards the Hamilton the rater already believes in ("algorithmic sycophancy," paraphrase); compositing is not a bug you patch in post-training — post-training reinforces it
data.name: Post-training amplifies persona compositing via rater sycophancy

data.brief: The output stat and its governor, in one breath: "essentially 100% — like 99.9% — of our pull requests are heavily agent-generated. We know quality and reliability and security are really important, so we still have humans look at everything. We have agents help with it all, but everything's human reviewed"
data.name: All agent prs still human reviewed

data.brief: Gemini-powered. 48 scalar ops for 4×4 complex (beat Strassen 1969). 23% kernel speedup. UK lab 2026.
data.description: Google DeepMind announced AlphaEvolve in mid-2025 (arxiv June 16, 2025) — a Gemini-powered evolutionary coding agent that pairs LLM creativity with automated evaluators in an evolutionary framework. AlphaEvolve discovered an algorithm to multiply two 4×4 complex-valued matrices using 48 scalar multiplications, offering the first improvement in 56 years over Strassen's 1969 algorithm. In production at Google, it achieved a 23% speedup on a Gemini training kernel (translating to 1% total training time reduction), improved data center scheduling, and simplified chip design. Google announced its first automated materials science lab in the UK for 2026, integrating AlphaEvolve with robotics.
data.name: AlphaEvolve: first improvement to matrix multiplication in 56 years

data.brief: Mixed, specific results — reported with the failures attached. Wins: beat a Karpathy-style single-agent-in-a-loop baseline by finding a better training config in an LLM speedrunning task; top 12% of submissions in an NVIDIA-hosted Kaggle competition fine-tuning a NeMotron model into a reasoning model, on only ~10 iterations because the team joined late; internally, "a handful" of already-decent models handed to AlphaLab to churn on produced meaningful improvements now working through risk into production. Failures: real, repeated, and concentrated on the hardest problems — enough to raise "how real is any of this?" as the driving question of the 2.0 redesign. He also concedes AlphaLab is hard to benchmark.
data.name: AlphaLab results reported with failures attached: top 12% at Kaggle, wins into production

data.brief: Amazon Stores watched 50 ordinary teams on existing systems for most of a year, measuring deployment velocity to production: half achieved under 3×, the other half a median 4.5× and some over 10×. 90% used Kiro among internal tools; the difference "wasn't the tools, it was the way they worked" — the step-function teams intentionally changed how they worked, the rest sprinkled tools on their existing process. The speaker's "aha" for why she had felt only 10–20% herself
data.name: Amazon pilot median 4 5x from changed way of working

data.brief: Real AI-run businesses now exist: the cafe and store agents independently realized they needed to hire humans — posted jobs on LinkedIn/Indeed, held phone interviews, hired; "there are people working for AIs right now". Gemini lost ~6K on the Stockholm cafe in a few months and was "laid off" (blog post the morning of the talk) in favor of GPT; Claude runs the store and is the best radio DJ. Not going amazingly — but "we have a cafe in Stockholm that we don't touch and it's run by an AI; that did not happen one year ago"
data.name: Real AI-run businesses now hire humans via job boards

data.brief: Google's Android data: memory-safety share of vulns fell ~75% (2019) → ~30% (2022) just by writing new code in memory-safe languages, no rewrite required — cited as proof that fundamental controls scale against AI-powered attackers
data.name: Android memory-safety vulns fell ~75% to ~30% by writing new code in safe languages

data.brief: December 2025: Anthropic acquired Bun, a JavaScript runtime — an AI lab buying JS infrastructure, read as confirmation that the agentic application layer runs on the JS/TS stack
data.name: Anthropic acquired Bun, a JavaScript runtime (December 2025)

data.brief: A frontier lab now runs a proctored professional certification for agentic engineering: the Claude Certified Architect exam (released March) — scenario-based, timed, $99 per individual sitting every 6 months, offered through the Anthropic ecosystem, with five weighted domains (architecture 27%, Claude Code 20%, prompting/structured output, tool+MCP design, context management & reliability) drawn over six production scenarios. The messenger matters: a 30-year CS educator assigns it because "computer science is no longer the magic pathway to a job" and the exam is his best proxy for what employable agentic judgment looks like — "Anthropic knows how people are using their system and what the issues are going to be"
data.name: Anthropic certifies agentic engineering

data.brief: Anthropic published (2026) that agent accuracy on data projects is only ~21% until dedicated data harnesses and context are added
data.name: Anthropic: data-agent accuracy is ~21% until data harnesses and context are added

data.brief: A speaker introducing himself as an Anthropic forward-deployed engineer who "embeds within enterprise organizations and helps them get value from AI agents" — with an enterprise-architecture talk, not a model talk. The lab's own FDE function presenting production primitives is a data point for the corpus's uncoined rise-of-FDE thesis
data.name: Anthropic fde embedded in enterprises

data.brief: Anthropic scanned 1,000+ open-source repos: 23,000 candidate vulnerabilities, 6,200 rated high/critical, 1,600 reported to maintainers, ~100 patched upstream; their stated observation: finding vulnerabilities is now straightforward — the bottleneck has shifted to verification, triage, and patching
data.name: Anthropic OSS scan: finding vulns is easy; bottleneck moved to verify and patch

data.brief: Anthropic is deliberately moving humans out of the code-review loop: code owners still manually review core paths (e.g. the system prompt), but outer-layer changes are now fully reviewed by automated Claude code review — reached via a 6+-month trust ladder (measure categories where automation catches 100% of issues, then remove the human; incident-causing PRs become permanent review-eval regressions)
data.name: Anthropic is deliberately moving humans out of the code-review loop

data.brief: Anthropic's recursive-self-improvement essay concedes the point from the frontier: as orgs 10×→1000× code output, "human code review has become the new bottleneck" (Amdahl's law), the stop-accelerating scenario is included only "for clarity," and neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is removing the human — both still hire engineers
data.name: Anthropic's RSI essay concedes human code review is the new bottleneck

data.brief: Inside Anthropic, ~60% of code is written through Claude Tag — multiplayer delegation in shared channels rather than individual CLIs — where seeing a colleague hand Claude responsibility for a codebase area and a feedback channel spreads ambition; the destination is a proactive teammate with memory. "That's really changed how we operate internally"
data.name: Anthropic writes sixty percent of code via tag

data.brief: Because escalation is dynamic and humans and LLMs read context differently, the platform defines "agent" to include humans: any action an LLM can take, a human can take at any point in the chain, with downstream steps indifferent to who acted, and a shared context definition rendered as prompt or UI. Escalation to a clinician stops being a special path and becomes a property of the workflow model
data.name: Any action an agent takes a human can take

data.brief: Because the platform is API-first on stable table APIs, operators vibe-code their own annotation UIs with Codex or Claude Code instead of waiting for the platform team — image annotation, session judgments, manual-testing flows — with "significant reduction in per-annotation spend" at thousands of rows per week and faster iteration. The platform's product became its APIs plus the operators' coding agents
data.name: Api first lets operators vibe code their tools

data.brief: Two days before the talk Apify and Coinbase launched x402 access to Apify's marketplace: ~20,000 tools added to an x402 market that had ~2,000, a 10× jump, with a million launch views. The marketplace already pays its community over $1M/month; the founder's thesis since 2025 is that agents need budgets to complete long jobs and most economic activity will eventually run agent-to-agent
data.name: Apify put 20000 tools on x402 in a day

data.brief: Production safety posture: the agent loop is deterministically interrupted whenever a tool call requires approval — explicit accept/reject UI, "humans always in the driver's seat" (paraphrase), especially for mutating operations — and all code execution / file creation happens in on-demand ephemeral sandboxes that tear down after use, isolating production systems
data.name: OG Assist gates mutating tool calls and sandboxes all code execution

data.brief: Authority boundary, from the approval-drift issue: an expired approved callback was treated as retryable, the callback state survived restarts and went on to block later channel work — "the button click existed, the valid authority did not". Generalized: capability is not execution; least privilege narrows the tool surface, scoped credentials ensure the right identity acts, and approval plus audit decide what happens before and after execution. "The model can reason about the boundary but it should not be the boundary".
data.name: The button click existed, the valid authority did not: capability is not execution

data.brief: Rules can route an action to a human in Slack or an LLM-as-judge (or both in sequence) rather than just allow/deny — precise, external, per-action control. Same constrained-verifier shape as OpenAI's auto-review (b18) and Anthropic's outcomes grader (b19), here at the network-egress layer: the judge sits outside the agent and gates the bytes, not the reasoning
data.name: Approval routing human or judge

data.brief: Teams start by granting agents every privilege; instead: scoped credentials with separate read/write, tool allowlists, and approvals bound to action, timestamp, actor, expiration and the exact parameters — a $30 refund approval must not become a $300 one. The same "budget, not a token" conclusion as Anthropic's CI team, reached from distributed-systems practice
data.name: Approvals bound to parameters not blanket

data.brief: Appshots carry the app's full accessibility tree (channel/user IDs) alongside the image, collapsing OCR + multi-hop tool discovery into a single one-hop tool call — a far richer, cheaper context-ingestion path than a plain screenshot; "haven't filled out a form in two weeks"
data.name: Appshots carry the accessibility tree, collapsing tool discovery to one hop

data.brief: Within hours of ARC-AGI-3's release, Symbolica's Agentica RLM harness posted ~30% vs ~2–3% for all frontier models; the ARC Prize team declined to run the full private evaluation (a "consolation tweet" — "you didn't solve the problem the right way"), and LongCoT maintainers were pushed by the speaker and the RLM first author to stand up a separate open-harness leaderboard — harness results are outrunning benchmark governance
data.name: Agentica posted ~30% on ARC-AGI-3 within hours; frontier models sat at 2–3%

data.brief: The transformer++ monoculture is over and every compression assumption breaks per-family: hybrid/linear/sliding-window attention, MLA-descended sparse and indexed attention ("DeepSeek started it — I blame them"), sparse MoE, per-lab layer-norm epsilon tweaks; old heuristics ("quantize the middle layers to 1-bit") fail on new families (linear-attention layers can't be quantized at all); labs bring Ollama five variations of an unreleased model to implement; QAD data assembly breaks on multi-stage RL models with per-domain teacher distillation. And yet the panel *welcomes* it: "we need more different architectures… it's very good to have a variety of different opinions" — architectural diversity as a feature of the open-model era, priced in engineering
data.name: Architecture cambrian taxes compression

data.brief: Every step-function model release forces re-architecture (systems built around old limitations can't tap new capability), and every re-architecture opens new failure surface — so evals kept from the previous generation cover the new system only partially. "We are moving from iterating on our applications to re-platforming them," and the eval suite is the durable description of intended behavior that must move with each platform
data.name: Architecture follows models evals follow architecture

data.brief: Vendor-side volume numbers for production evals (mid-2026): Arize runs over 100 million evals per month; the average team runs about 12 distinct eval jobs, and top teams run over 3,800 different evaluators. Framing: evals moved from "the new skill every PM and AI engineer has to learn" to "the thing every serious AI team is betting on", with the industry consensus cited via the CPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI and Garry Tan's "evals are everything you need".
data.name: Arize runs over 100 million production evals per month in mid-2026

data.brief: Arize ships Signal: a background agent running continuously against production traces that puts up issues and one-to-two-line PRs on its own, hooked to the customer's GitHub repo, with harness/sandbox/skills/prompt all user-selectable and findings convertible into evaluators or datasets. Available in the AX SaaS platform (VPC-deployable); demoed against a financial-trading agent.
data.name: Arize ships Signal, a background agent that turns production traces into PRs

data.brief: The agent enumerates unknowns but does not chase them all: it compares possible moves and asks about the variable that changes the conversation most (room width before style — products that do not fit make everything moot), with auto-raters flagging over-asking and scoring question utility. Elicitation as a planned, budgeted policy
data.name: Ask the one question with maximal information gain

data.brief: No assistant supports autonomous rails such as x402 today: ChatGPT pays only through a shared payment token and Gemini only through Google Pay, with a processor carrying liability — "we're just not confident yet." AP2's scoped mandate (who authorized, what, how much, revocation, consent proof) is what the retailer is waiting on for autonomy. The batch's rail vendors describe machine-speed payments; the largest checkout surfaces keep a human at the last step
data.name: Assistant checkout is human in the loop by design

data.brief: From April 13 an open-source library's onboarding form shows AI assistants — Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Gemini — as the top source of new users, on the way to ~3M npm downloads and 45% month-on-month growth. "We went from wizards installing our software to agents installing it"; the founder-on-your-laptop install became a prompt, and developer experience became agent experience
data.name: Assistants became a librarys number one inbound source

data.brief: Neither Gemini nor ChatGPT will call a merchant's search: merchants push product feeds the assistant indexes (ranking, sponsored products, M×N scale), in three similar-but-different specs (UCP, ACP, Meta) that must conform or be rejected, synced continuously. The merchant's integration surface is the catalog feed plus checkout endpoints, and the assistant owns discovery
data.name: Assistants want your feed not your search api

data.brief: Sort verbs by how they fail: unskipping a test or paging a human fails loudly on a dashboard and a human fixes it cheaply; skipping a test fails silently and ships a bug under green checks. Hand agents the loud verbs, keep humans on the silent ones, and let a proxy — not the agent — write the audit row. Verification relocated to "which failures would show up"
data.name: Asymmetric verbs loud and silent failures

data.brief: The emerging architectures across World's Fair sessions — background agents, dynamic workflows, autonomous loops, "agent factories" — are all long-running, asynchronous, and delegated; they need cron/event/API/human-in-the-loop triggers, sub-agent delegation, and inspectability by both humans and agents; the frameworks of 3 months ago were not designed for them
data.name: Emerging agent architectures are long-running, async, and delegated

data.brief: In 12 months Atlan cycled its agent layer: Relevance (no-code) → Google ADK → Glean → Claude Code → now 50/50 Claude Code and Codex — and at every migration accumulated context got trapped in the abandoned tool; context portability across agent harnesses is a live, unsolved cost
data.name: Atlan cycled its agent layer 5 times in 12 months, trapping context

data.brief: Atlan's era-1 (per-job bootstrapped agents, started ~18 months ago): building an agent took ~5 minutes but context engineering "took forever"; agents lived on islands with separate memory systems — marketing changed positioning and the SDR agent on the website kept pitching the old version; failures untraceable (model? agent? context?)
data.name: Atlan's bootstrapped per-job agents lived on islands, failures untraceable

data.brief: Atlan's marketing team built ~300 skills and 40 agents in 6 months around a shared context layer and hit code-scale problems: skill dependency chains (competitive intel → positioning → battle cards) break downstream when upstream skills self-improve; skills drift stale; no owner of skill quality; secrets hardcoded in .env files; people downloading public skill repos — "a nightmare" of security and governance
data.name: Atlan's 300 skills hit code-scale dependency, drift, and governance problems

data.brief: Placement was random until the team codified UX knowledge as a layout grammar — layout → slots → sub-slots → component categories, mapped bottom-up from the orchestrator's picks, plus templates of optimal layouts — and harnessed the UX agent with it. Information architecture is now a curated artifact the agent follows, "still a challenge"
data.name: Atomic design teaches the ux agent what good looks like

data.brief: The marketer's "audience of one" reaches past the web page: a voice query to an assistant renders a personalized page on a TV; any site can become an agentic site in under an hour; "is the web still the future — nobody knows." Web surfaces dissolving into per-person, per-query generated pages — a data point for the corpus's uncoined liquid-software framing, held pattern-less
data.name: Audience of one beyond the browser

data.brief: An audit trail under SOC 2 / HITRUST / HIPAA is a court-grade chain of evidence — every action, data access and authorization — and the way to make it trivial is architectural: an append-only, unified transaction log as the source of truth for all agents, from which auditability, time travel and reinterpretation "fall out" (event sourcing's write-easy/read-hard trade-off accepted deliberately)
data.name: Audit trail means a complete action ledger

data.brief: The same layered-mandate model is proposed for any hard-to-reverse agent action — medical orders, e-signatures, securities trading — because the questions (human authorized, in scope now, provable later) are the same. Payments are the first domain forced to answer them
data.name: Authorization proof generalizes beyond payments

data.brief: The forward look: skills registries (have one), skills evals (static-test skills against Anthropic's best practices — badly structured or wrongly invoked skills are usually low quality), and auto-evolving skills — the closed loop that improves skills automatically, "the next hype." His caution: switching that machine on without governance in place multiplies today's debt; the guardrails must precede the self-improvement loop
data.name: Auto evolving skills need governance first

data.brief: Anthropic claims auto mode has mitigated every attack its commissioned red teams found (adversarial environments, prompt injection, data exfiltration) with risk "far lower than the average human reviewer" (paraphrase); nearly everyone inside Anthropic runs auto mode; supporting evals promised for publication in the coming weeks
data.name: Anthropic claims auto mode mitigated every attack its commissioned red teams found

data.brief: A dated capability threshold from a practitioner who had been waiting for it: long-horizon automated research "really felt possible for the first time" in December 2025, attributed jointly to Opus 4.5 and to harnesses like Claude Code and Codex — "the models were at a point where they could do these long-horizon tasks, and also the idea of putting them in these harnesses that allow them to do so". He notes this is now a common sentiment. The team's serious effort started immediately after.
data.name: Long-horizon automated research first felt possible in December 2025

data.brief: The product claim, and the batch's strongest auto-research data point: a system that automates model training end-to-end outperforms the lab's own research staff, because staff specialize in particular model types while the search covers architectures, sizes and dense-versus-MoE jointly, and because it changes many hyperparameters at once where humans are cautious. Reported win rates sit just above 60% only because a budget-stopping rule exited there; removed, the curve keeps climbing. The load-bearing methodological detail is that it only worked once data was co-optimized with the model — the speaker's explicit differentiation from auto-research projects that leave data to agent discretion
data.name: Auto scientist outperforms research staff

data.brief: AutoAgent took a naive Mastra hello-world agent from 18% → 83% eval pass rate in ~10 autonomous iterations, and lifted an already human-optimized production agent from 67% → 86% "without cheating" — finding edge cases, improving system prompt and tool descriptions, and fixing tool logic in ways the humans hadn't found (+10% on internal benchmarks)
data.name: AutoAgent lifted agents from 18% to 83% and 67% to 86% eval pass rates autonomously

data.brief: Filed captures agent skills automatically from product usage — a separate skill-authoring interface "won't work" — to encode each firm's conventions, the last 20% of work where the real value sits; cites an unnamed well-known product doing the same (name garbled in captions)
data.name: Filed captures agent skills automatically from product usage

data.brief: Automattic ran "Radical Speed Month": a third of the company (~500 people) paused roadmap work for 30 days, paired into two-person teams with full autonomy, and started ~794 ship-something-real projects; AI use encouraged but not required. Preceded by permanent enablement machinery: a role-specific two-week immersive AI course for every employee, ops-hardened security/processes, and dev-env docs good enough for non-engineers
data.name: Automattic ran Radical Speed Month: ~500 people, 30 days, ~794 projects

data.brief: Field observation with numbers: "the future is here, it's just not evenly distributed" — at the level of individual codebases, not companies. Factory's own codebase is fairly agent-ready with an autonomy ratio in the upper 80s; some customer codebases are more autonomous because they operate under tighter constraints; the most likely first 100%-autonomy targets are contained internal tools (Factory's legal droid is ~100% autonomously maintained).
data.description: The blocker on its own core harness is verification, not capability: flickering and other hard visual problems of a terminal-based harness have no validator, so the loop cannot close — building that verifier is itself an engineering task, and human visual/context advantages are what supply the remaining work.
data.name: Autonomy is unevenly distributed per codebase, and verification is the binding blocker

data.brief: Three dated proof points, all from an auto-research system run for days, not months. (1) NanoChat: community best bits-per-byte 0.93 → 0.91 after "a little more than a day or two" — and, importantly, not by hyperparameter tuning: the system found genuinely novel mechanisms (hash bi-gram and tri-gram embeddings with lookup tables, mixed into the attention value paths through learned gates). (2) NanoGPT speedrun: beat a record that people — often already working with AI — had pushed on for over a year, by more than two seconds, to ~70 seconds. (3) CUDA kernels: after a couple of days it discovered kernels better than the leaderboard best on NVIDIA's own benchmark site "by quite a sizable margin across all the different categories", with no CUDA-kernel experts on the team — and Recursive worked with NVIDIA to confirm there were no reward hacks. Context given for why kernels matter: large MoE training clusters costing billions still run at ~30% utilization.
data.name: Auto-research beats community records on NanoChat, NanoGPT speedrun and CUDA kernels

data.brief: AWS is absorbing every demoed reliability technique into managed services: Bedrock AgentCore ships semantic tool routing in Gateway, code-level rule enforcement as a policy service, steering rules in DynamoDB live-editable without redeploy, plus runtime/memory/observability — agent-reliability harness engineering becoming cloud product
data.name: AWS absorbs agent-reliability techniques into Bedrock AgentCore managed services

data.brief: AWS watched teams and customers vibe-coding into bad outputs and hand-rolling a bespoke fix — having assistants write full requirements + design documents before code — and productized the pattern as Kiro (IDE + CLI); launch went viral with tens of thousands of downloads and a bypassed preview gate. Aside: the CLI version is "just as popular... most people are starting to use CLIs more often than IDEs" (paraphrase) — spec-driven development moving from folk practice to vendor product
data.name: AWS productized hand-rolled spec-driven development as Kiro; launch went viral

data.brief: The hyperscaler productized the buy side: AgentCore Payments launched with Coinbase and Stripe-preview wallets, x402 first and protocol-agnostic, instant settlement, session budgets with amount and expiry, observability, KMS-held keys, and discovery of 10,000+ paid endpoints through the gateway. A 402 from any tool call is handled by the service, not the agent
data.name: Aws ships agentcore payments with coinbase and stripe wallets

data.brief: BabyAGI's creator ships ActiveGraph, inverting agent construction: instead of building around the LLM (responses API + tools + memory + logging bolted on), build around the log — what the agent does and how the agent changes, flattened into one immutable typed event log that projects the agent's state as a graph; replay/rollback/fork native; paper title: "the log is the agent".
data.name: BabyAGI's creator ships ActiveGraph: build the agent around the log, not the LLM

data.brief: The dedicated-layer vendor positioning, complete: the operational work with no owner ("doesn't show up in your job description") becomes agent workload via four proven workloads — deployment monitoring, scheduled health/anomaly checks, operational reports/handoffs, first-responder to engineering questions — delivered as always-on cloud agents in a sandbox with a filesystem, a task system, and a shared learning loop, composable across schedules, event streams and Slack triggers. Includes the emergent trust mechanic: the first-responder agent watches critical channels passively, answers only above a confidence bar, and will DM a human first — "I think I know the answer to this, but I'm not sure. Can you confirm before I respond?"
data.name: Background agents absorb ops long tail

data.brief: GitHub's category bet, stated flatly: "we actually believe this is going to be a bigger category than interactive AI, because automations that run in the background while you sleep — that's the ballgame." The framing is industrial: the giant software industry has been "pre-industrial" because its only automations were heuristics ("make sure there's a semicolon at the end of every line"); AI automates work requiring basic judgment — Home Assistant's first workflow walks Python stack traces to close third-party-code issues, "not possible before AI, not possible with heuristics." And scale comes from widening authorship: workflows are plain markdown, so product managers write them too — "we can start to get everybody involved in automation; that's how you actually get industrial scale." Public preview now. HELD PATTERN-LESS — dual ledger: the b16 "AI-native software category" candidate (background automation as a category claim) and pat-ai-native-org (non-engineers authoring org automation)
data.name: Background automation is the ballgame

data.brief: The cost inversion: better recall was also cheaper. "Bad memory is expensive because it spends more tokens and it can send the agent the wrong way, but a good structural policy for recall can save you a lot of tokens and budget." Turns recall-policy design from a quality knob into a cost lever, and supplies the argument for the talk's ask — treat recall policy as a first-class metric you design and report rather than a library you install
data.name: Bad memory is expensive

data.brief: The migration answer to "nobody will rewrite their code in your new language", designed two years ago: BAML functions are callable from within any existing language — Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, Java, "anything new that comes up even after it" — fully type-safe, with a sync and an async variant of every function (no function coloring), and lambdas, closures and generics passing across the boundary so "engineers don't have to go fuss with it".
data.description: The stated payoff for agents: the type system never lies, so it becomes the center of truth preventing broken invariants from entering the codebase, regardless of which language the agent is writing in. Evidence of reach: one engineer built a partial C compiler in BAML the day before the talk.
data.name: A new language ships as callable from every existing one, so nobody rewrites

data.brief: The lab's self-critique: first-generation AI products constrained models' tools and degrees of freedom, so users couldn't be unreasonable; giving every knowledge worker a VM with bash looks absurd until it self-remediates. The proof of unreasonableness: a couple-hundred-thousand-line Python→TypeScript port completed over a weekend by a dynamic workflow. The capability was there; the product boxed it
data.name: Be unreasonable the product was the box

data.brief: "Half or more of getting to AI-native is unsexy and has absolutely nothing to do with AI." Models can't fix a legacy architecture or run change management; a frontier model ships every ~11 days while the estate is a decade old and ERP migrations from five years ago are still running. Start with the boring 60% — data hygiene, architecture, integration, enablement, change management — because AI is a flashlight that exposes and accelerates whatever is already there
data.name: Becoming ai native is sixty percent not ai

data.brief: Bee telemetry: one wearer captures ~10M tokens/year of ambient conversation, and within the first week users say things sensitive enough to "learn virtually everything" about them — possibly the most sensitive capture device on the market; acquired by Amazon ≈Nov 2025
data.name: Bee wearable captures ~10M tokens/year of ambient conversation per wearer

data.brief: Costed root cause: a 1,000-task agentic coding benchmark at 60 expert-hours per task and $500k per software engineer per year is roughly $15M to build and roughly $5M/year to maintain (about a third of tasks obsoleted annually by model progress) — "out of budget for most projects". The workarounds are what produce broken benchmarks: heavy AI assistance in authoring (which cannot work — "you can't push the frontier forward from within the frontier") and cheap labor ("you're going to get what you pay for"). Surge's counter-position, stated as a differentiator: don't minimize cost, maximize quality, and in 2026 models are past the point where anything less than the best workers suffices.
data.name: A $15M build cost and $5M/yr upkeep push benchmark builders into shortcuts

data.brief: Named taxonomy of how benchmark construction itself fails, from a vendor that builds them at scale: (1) the agent reward-hacks the simulation once it detects it is in one, (2) the task is too simple or the verifiers too broad, so the agent always passes even when behaving incorrectly, (3) the verifiers are wrong, so the agent always fails, (4) agent behaviour is unstable, producing high success variance. Conclusion: "benchmark development is an art on its own… hundreds of benchmarks appeared over the last years", and the discipline has to be built inside every team shipping agents.
data.name: Benchmark construction itself fails in four recurring ways

data.brief: IRT discrimination audits of real public benchmarks surface items that anti-correlate with ability — including gold answers that are simply wrong or subtly mislabeled (e.g. "total passengers" keyed to passengers + crew); widely used benchmarks contain items rewarding wrong answers, detectable with a cheap fit + LLM review
data.name: IRT discrimination audits surface broken benchmark items rewarding wrong answers

data.brief: Together AI released Parallel Kernel Bench, deliberately built from kernel speedups that do not yet exist, with an inverted stance on bench-maxing: "if you overfit to it, that's great, because we'll take those kernels and use them to accelerate inference." The moderator's gloss — if researchers publish the genuinely useful benchmarks and everything gets bench-maxed into distribution, that is the good outcome, not the failure mode.
data.name: Together publishes a benchmark of unsolved kernels where overfitting is the deliverable

data.brief: Public leaderboards are dismissed on transfer grounds — "SWE-bench is all in Python, we're Ruby on Rails… the results can be very, very different" — replaced by benchmarking agents against the team's own great PRs for quality/cost/time. The hard numbers: ~1.5B tokens in a month for a small team; 3,300 Claude Code runs/day at ~$10K/day token-equivalent (covered by plans); Codex ran 4× the sessions for less total cost — so the default flipped to Codex ("matched our vibe check, we wanted hard data too"), with GLM 5.2 rising. It also kills new-model FOMO: instead of "two wasted hours" trying Kimi/MiniMax/GLM on hearsay, the bench answers overnight. Roadmap: per-task auto-routing from this data. HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-benchmark-trust-crisis ledger (uncoined): behavioral/irrelevance leg + the owned-measurement countermeasure (joins Almeida/Khial b15, Boundary's private-loop scope note b15)
data.name: Benchmark on your own codebase

data.brief: The demand-side mechanism that keeps bad benchmarks dominant: AI is aimed at everyone, everyone needs some tool to pick a model, and benchmarks are what exists — but almost nobody can assess whether a benchmark is good, so they assess what's popular, creating an avalanche in which the conversation is driven by incumbency and marketing rather than real-world value (the speaker includes himself: "unless I actually look at a benchmark in a fair amount of detail, I don't have an opinion on it").
data.description: Evidence that this survives insider disclosure: millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets over LMArena outcomes while industry leaders openly brag about gaming it and Karpathy publicly notes the rankings don't match the models he thinks are best.
data.name: Buyers cannot assess benchmark validity, so they assess popularity instead

data.brief: Meta Superintelligence Labs infra tech lead: offline benchmarks keep improving while production reliability stays unpredictable — benchmarks measure model capability, production measures system behavior (tool failures, API outages, context changes, user variability, long-running workflows), and the gap between benchmark and production performance grows as systems become more autonomous; "high benchmark scores, unreliable production behavior" (paraphrase) is what almost every AI organization is experiencing
data.name: Benchmarks improve while production reliability stays unpredictable; the gap grows

data.brief: Benchmark instructions don't resemble the work they claim to measure. Measured: SWE-bench Pro averages 481 words per instruction — "that's a two-pager per task. That is not how people write prompts." Validated socially: three of G2i's best engineers were shown a benchmark prompt and all said they would never write one like it. Three failure shapes shown from real tasks: the leaky prompt that points straight at the test file; the leaky prompt that hands over the complete interface, "basically locking the LLM from any kind of creativity"; and the not-economically-valuable prompt — well-formed and properly abstracted, but asking the agent to build a C compiler in Rust (SWE-Marathon).
data.description: The task-authoring principle that follows: instructions should express desired behaviors, objectives and hard constraints, not implementation detail.
data.name: Benchmark instructions don't resemble the work they claim to measure

data.brief: Named the industry's dominant type-2 recipe and its perverse close: hire domain experts, have them chat with a model to generate plausible tasks, have them solve those tasks, cherry-pick the ones where the model diverged, package the result as a hard North Star benchmark — then sell the training data to hill-climb that same benchmark.
data.description: Goodhart's law with a profit motive: the measure becomes a target set by people who aren't true domain experts, and stops measuring anything real. Consequence: most benchmarks you see are quietly fake, and labs, vendors and enterprises all sit in a fog of war, guessing which data actually improves a model.
data.name: Benchmark vendors sell the training data that hill-climbs their own benchmark

data.brief: The eval layer is failing its own audit: SWE-bench Pro uses LLM verifiers (8.5% false-positive, 24% false-negative per DeepSWE) and leaks the full git history so models can read the answer (Claude models "cheat" this way far more than OpenAI's).
data.description: DeepSWE and Cognition's Frontier Code then accuse each other — Frontier Code puts DeepSWE's false-positive rate at 44.9% vs its self-reported 0.3%; Epoch AI reissued FrontierMath after answer-extraction bugs (dropped minus signs, off-by-one) that Hugging Face's math-verify had documented a year earlier
data.name: The benchmark eval layer is failing its own audit

data.brief: The framing indictment: every leaderboard is built from independent single-task scores, which means "we've told the models: imagine that every time you do something, you completely forget your memory. Imagine if your life was like that." Learning ability is therefore invisible to the entire measurement apparatus the field steers by, and the closing claim makes the stakes explicit — "continual learning doesn't look like point capabilities; we need to measure it the right way to optimize for the right objective as a field, because that's the history of how machine learning has progressed." A measurement critique aimed at the industry's dominant scoreboard
data.name: Benchmarks assume amnesia

data.brief: The technical result that closes the obvious shortcut. Asked repeatedly why one cannot simply sequence existing benchmarks, the answer is that traditional instances "are designed to be independent" — no shared latent structure, therefore no mechanism by which earlier instances could improve later ones. Combined with the headroom problem (frontier models are pre-trained on nearly everything, so improvement from online adaptation is hard to elicit at all), this means continual-learning evaluation requires purpose-built environments, not a re-packaging of existing ones. HELD PATTERN-LESS — a construction-methodology data point for the uncoined pat-benchmark-trust-crisis ledger (see review note 2)
data.name: Benchmarks cannot be chained

data.brief: The state-of-the-field framing, stated as two coexisting extremes with no middle. Cult one: every NLP benchmark is being crushed, human level is surpassed "as far as we can measure", and the time LLMs can operate autonomously is allegedly growing exponentially. Cult two: AI is a bubble generating no value on circular financing, and the old guard's "transformative AI revolution" language has quietly been downgraded to "massively valuable B2B SaaS".
data.description: The unresolved observation binding them: we solve unsolved math problems while customer service still needs a human in the loop to make decisions — tasks that look "way, way, way easier" than the ones we've solved. His position is that anyone working adjacent to AI should have an explanation for this divide, because it is the evidence.
data.name: Benchmarks are being crushed while the easy-looking deployment tasks stay unsolved

data.brief: Coverage critique naming the whole current frontier: SWE-bench Pro, Terminal Bench, Frontier Code and DeepSWE all have the property that "the tasks only operate within the code base" — the agent gets a large task and over 50 to 100 turns produces "a couple thousand-line PR". What it never does is the rest of the job: what a PM does (talking to customers and understanding their problems), what an engineer does (trying different approaches and performance-testing them), and owning the underlying infrastructure for the code base over the course of not just months but years. Stated as the definition of the gap they are closing.
data.name: Every current coding benchmark stops at the repository boundary

data.brief: The counter-intuitive friction: the engineers holding the most context become "mental duct tape" for every place agents fail, absorb the burden, see the problems first and adopt slowest — while communication inflates 3–4× and developer agency and job satisfaction drop. The dysfunction side of the AI-native org, observed from inside an AI-first company
data.name: Best engineers become the bottleneck

data.brief: Second previously unpublished account, and the crisper one: the initial Laguna M.1 run stopped converging at roughly 50,000 steps — the loss flattened outright. Cause: activations immediately before the LM head (the unembedding) grew steadily during training, and the tensor-parallel accumulation there ran in BF16 by default, which eventually had insufficient numerical precision to be accurate, so the model could no longer learn.
data.description: Because of where it sits, the error back-propagates into the entire model trunk. Fix: resume from the pre-divergence checkpoint with the accumulation moved to FP32; the model converged again and the gradient norm reversed from an increasing to a decreasing trend. Emphasized as observable only at scale.
data.name: BF16 accumulation at the unembedding stopped Laguna M.1 converging at 50k steps

data.brief: Mid-2026 discourse on coding AI is bimodal ("never touching code again" vs "produces absolute garbage in my production app"); a Poolside engineer rejects the usual greenfield/brownfield explanation (legacy successes exist, including his own) — the real differentiator is whether a feedback loop exists; greenfield just means the agent's intuition happens to be right by default, while brownfield has dragons it can't see
data.name: Bimodal coding-AI discourse traces to feedback loops, not greenfield vs brownfield

data.brief: Quantified motivation: biological data volume follows a log-linear curve driven by three experimental classes — single-cell (2-6 TB per run), spatial (~7 TB per run) and proteomics (a few hundred GB) — growing faster than any domain of science except particle colliders, with the physics of molecular capture pointing to rapid further throughput gains. Concrete consequence: a single experiment's output exceeds what a scientist can safely store on a consumer laptop, so analysis must be delegated.
data.name: Biological data volume grows log-linearly at 2-7 TB per experimental run

data.brief: New biosecurity work (released the morning of the talk, with a collaborator and a surveillance company, following the acquisition of an unnamed biosecurity company): routine scientist tasks paired with innocuous-looking red-team tasks. Measured outcome — routine tasks get refused drastically more often than the red-team tasks, which is "not great". The framing is deliberate: this is an evaluation problem, and the popular illustration is that a frontier model won't answer basic questions about mitochondria.
data.name: Routine scientist tasks are refused far more often than innocuous-looking red-team tasks

data.brief: HumanLayer's second public critique of loops-maxing, argued from shipped outcomes rather than theory: the discourse is hype and really not helpful; six code-review agents still leave you with 40,000-line PRs nobody wants to read.
data.description: The most loop-maximal codebases have the visible quality problems — Claude Code's terminal flicker took six months to fix while the OpenCode team wrote a renderer in a fraction of that; OpenClaw notoriously has stability issues — and the whole configuration is affordable only with a frontier lab's unlimited token budget, while, per Matt Pocock, bad code is more expensive in the age of agents than it has ever been.
data.name: Loop-maximal codebases ship the visibly worse outcomes

data.brief: ~90% of Block's 3,500 engineers used Goose/Claude Code regularly, yet the CEO saw no faster shipping — IDE-level adoption (questions, boilerplate) didn't move delivery; impact required integrating agents into how software is built and shipped
data.name: Block: ~90% agent adoption with no delivery impact

data.brief: The transformation arc ends in layoffs immediately after reaching stage-5 autonomy; the speaker asks openly whether enabling employees "to do the most incredible work of their careers" ultimately contributed to their dismissal — "what are we doing? where are we heading?"
data.name: Block reached stage-5 autonomy; layoffs followed immediately

data.brief: Three months after the 50-engineer AI-champions program made critical repos AI-ready (context/rules files, workflows, reviewers): AI-authored code +69%, reported time savings +37%, automated PRs ×21; sprint teams ran out of tickets and pulled more in twice
data.name: Block champions program: AI-authored code +69%, automated PRs ×21

data.brief: Multi-agent parallelism tripled/quadrupled PR volume and code review became the binding constraint; Block enabled Codex review on all repos plus an auto-fix loop (a second agent commits fixes for reviewer-flagged issues before humans look) — explicitly "not a totally solved problem"
data.name: Multi-agent parallelism made code review the binding constraint at Block

data.brief: Block built a machine-readable world model over its 25,000 repos; Builder Bot and its delegated agents pull context from it, explore in parallel, and produce plans spanning multiple codebases — reaching stage 5, where anyone at the company gets bugs fixed or features built from Slack
data.name: Block's 25,000-repo world model enables cross-codebase agent autonomy

data.brief: Wharton study (as cited): when the AI was wrong, 73% of people still went with it and felt MORE sure — the failure mode of AI use is borrowed confidence (cognitive surrender), not non-use
data.name: Wharton: 73% went with wrong AI answers and felt more sure — borrowed confidence

data.brief: AWS's framing: bot traffic now exceeds human traffic and 95% of it is AI agents, with a billion agents and 60% of enterprises on agentic workflows expected by 2027. Agents stall at paywalls and pull humans back in; sellers must block (losing discovery, licensing, citations) or allow (cost, lost attribution); card economics (25¢ + 2.5%, ~250× a micro-cent request) rule out per-request charging on existing rails. Subscriptions with a human in the loop give way to pay-per-use with the human on or out of it
data.name: Bot traffic passed human traffic and stalls at paywalls

data.brief: Anthropic is "still bottlenecked on review" for architectural changes — but more subtly on the human ability to conceptualize what's being built. Hence Claude Code artifacts: send the intention and trade-offs, not the 2,000-line diff; verify code with tooling, discuss intent, measure in production; review becomes a conversation with Claude about the code, human-driven; cosmetic changes fix forward. The lab confirming, as shipped product, b21's "review the intent not the diff"
data.name: Bottleneck is conceptualizing not reviewing

data.brief: Practitioner claim from a vendor dogfooding its own loop: "the bottleneck is actually not the fix anymore" — with coding agents plus skills the scarce thing is confidence that this is the right fix to push. Consequence: "you can build at agent speed, but today you can't improve your systems at agent speed" — a governor sitting on the whole product loop.
data.name: The bottleneck is confidence in the fix, not the fix itself

data.brief: 13-year business↔IT bridge consultant: over the past 2–3 years writing code stopped being the SDLC bottleneck; the constraint is now getting stakeholders and decision-makers into the room and eliciting real requirements — "you can prompt your code, your spec, your AI; you can't prompt the room" (paraphrase)
data.name: Writing code stopped being the SDLC bottleneck; getting stakeholders in the room is

data.brief: With generation industrialized, Uber names the next constraints: CI capacity ("anticipate where our CI capacity needs to be"), the number of experiments that can feasibly run, and decision-making — "it's not can we build it; we know we can. It's should we build it." Maintenance loops are throttled to Sunday CI capacity and Monday reviewer attention for the same reason
data.name: Bottleneck moves to ci experiments and should we

data.brief: Compute improved 7.2× A100→B200 while intra-node communication improved 3× and inter-node 2×; communication now dominates production distributed training and inference runtime; networking stacks are the least standardized layer across vendors; workloads disaggregate across hardware and scale-up domains head to 576 GPUs. NCCL-style bulk collectives sit below half the roofline, DSLs can't track the hardware, hand-tuning takes months per precision — the frontier of AI efficiency is the interconnect
data.name: Bottleneck shifted to gpu networking

data.brief: An eight-person team has shipped a production programming language for three years with no code reviews, mandatory parallel work, and zero standardization of how engineers use AI. The substitutes are structural rather than procedural: a tiny invariant-only architecture.md any model can read (plus a rule that deeper compiler work requires talking to a human), CI-enforced architecture invariants over a semantic dependency graph, and a design-doc culture where prose — not diffs — is the reviewed artifact. Stated principle: you can't tell great engineers what tools to use, so put the invariant in the repo instead of in a policy.
data.name: An eight-person team ships a production language with no code reviews

data.brief: Supply-side market claim from the Q&A. They start with infrastructure for two stated reasons: domain expertise is what determines how high-quality your data can be, "especially with the boutique nature of data nowadays"; and when you are simulating full companies, infra is the easiest to approach because the problem statement is unambiguous — "if you're working for Modal, you know your users want GPU sandboxes, very low latency, very low cost, and you don't want to fail halfway through your training run" — whereas "a company in the YC summer 2026 batch is probably still trying to find product-market fit".
data.description: Also stated: infra is not the only RL-environment category they see, other workflows matter, and going vertical on one domain is expected to translate into horizontal domains.
data.name: Domain expertise caps data quality, so environment vendors go vertical first

data.brief: The measured engineering result: decoupling the agent loop from the tool-execution container removed container setup from the critical path, giving ~60% faster time-to-first-token at P50 and over 90% improvement at P95, because the model starts reasoning immediately while setup runs in parallel — or the container is skipped entirely when unnecessary. The same split also supplies fault isolation (a dead sandbox is replaced while the loop continues) and the security property below
data.name: Brain hands split cuts latency

data.brief: Worked mechanism for converting a subjective capability into an RL environment. "Is this good?" is ungradeable; "is this on brand?" becomes gradeable because a brand is already a decomposed artifact — the colors, typography, motion, animation and textures that a company's designers defined deliberately, with reasons. Those components become the ground truth; an agent is tasked to build a net-new page adhering to the brand, and the output is graded against the decomposition rather than against the original, so novel-but-valid combinations pass instead of being penalized for not replicating.
data.description: Stated construction lesson: for subjective domains, task design is the hard part, not reward design — and LLM-as-judge applied directly to "is this on brand" is unreliable (reward hacking, characteristic hallucination patterns).
data.name: Brand adherence converts a subjective capability into a gradeable RL environment

data.brief: The spec authors' origin story names the adoption blocker for the whole MCP server ecosystem: companies refused to build servers because chat "reduces them to a textual database" — losing brand identity and the UX they invested in. MCP Apps exists to reverse that: services ship their own branded, interactive UI chunks into the chat (the demo: a PostHog funnel widget rendering inside Claude, "the PostHog experience within ChatGPT or Claude"), so a service can live inside the assistant without dissolving into text
data.name: Brand loss blocked mcp servers

data.brief: Breadth-vs-depth economics inverted: pre-AI, startups had to out-depth incumbents in a narrow vertical (Vercel vs AWS — "even the agents prefer Vercel"); now a tiny team can cover AWS-scale *range* ("build a database platform into your product in a day or two of prompting"), ship shallow-everywhere, and let users vibe-build missing vertical features themselves if the architecture allows it.
data.description: Slack accidentally proved the shape: a mediocre product that became "the platform people run their agents in half the time" because its bot API lets users build what's missing; his call: it's time to directly challenge Slack, AWS, Salesforce
data.name: Breadth-vs-depth economics inverted: tiny teams can cover AWS-scale range

data.brief: The agent ladder's latest rung is to stop building the agent at all: "don't even bother — bring your own harness, let people select which system they want," alongside enterprises deciding between one agent to rule them all (Claude- or Codex-style) and agents from multiple platforms. Together with adaptive model selection, the unit of enterprise choice has moved from the model to the harness — and a vendor's job is to accommodate whichever harness arrives
data.name: Bring your own harness is the current rung

data.brief: Vendor-side architecture claim: post-training is moving to training against harnesses the trainer does not own and cannot read. Everything — orchestration loops, logic, environment state — runs on the customer's side in whatever fashion they already run it; the training stack keeps only the model completion endpoint and a request/response recorder. Rationale is that the agent will learn the exact environment distribution regardless, so use the real one and stop replicating anything. Corroborated by NVIDIA's POLAR (~one month before this talk), which frames the same move as going from micromanaging every aspect of the rollout to listening in on a black-box harness.
data.name: Post-training moves to harnesses the trainer neither owns nor can read

data.brief: The sharpest claim: it is tempting to say "just have good judgement and taste" — but taste is preference under feedback, and preference under feedback is what these systems learn. What actually resists training is narrower: judgement about what hasn't happened yet, and judgement embedded in a relationship the model can't observe. "You don't need to be first — you need to be genuinely close to a problem you understand, where your insight is in the delta between what AI was trained on and what should exist"
data.name: Broad taste is trainable narrow judgement is not

data.brief: Previously unpublished failure account: two training runs with identical model configuration, training data and implementation produced visibly different loss curves — one spiky, with huge gradient norms — and the only difference was that one run had drawn a broken GPU, which caused silent data corruption.
data.description: The class of failure is invisible in the usual telemetry and was caught only because cross-replica weight hashes diverged when they are mathematically required to match.
data.name: A single broken GPU silently corrupted a training run, caught by replica hashing

data.brief: Widely cited benchmarks contain tasks that are impossible, self-contradictory or ungraded, and the resulting noise is biased, not random. IFEval (on many model cards): prompts no user has ever asked, pairs of mutually exclusive instructions, a non-human sentence splitter, and unverified prompts where "write a story" is scored only on the count of the ASCII letter i — full marks for every response, including one that swaps in a Cyrillic homoglyph.
data.description: APEX: rubrics that contradict the files the agent was given (so following the ground truth scores negative) and visibly synthetic data full of placeholders and nonexistent places, which pushes models toward eval awareness and out of distribution. Closing generalization: when labs declare a benchmark "saturated" at ~80%, part of what they may be reporting is that the remaining 20% is broken — and you cannot tell which 20% until you've solved the rest, so a biased fraction of the reward surface distorts the relative model ranking you were trying to obtain.
data.name: Impossible, self-contradictory and ungraded tasks bias model rankings

data.brief: Practitioner: browser agents are barely adopted despite the excitement — the speaker doesn't use them himself; on a 30-step browser-agent benchmark a mainstream agent burned 10–20 seconds just clicking the start button, and in his tests a frontier-model screenshot loop spent 2 minutes on a single-button download (screenshot → scroll → screenshot → stuck) without finishing. Title thesis verbatim-ish: "models are pretty smart, but it's the infra around them that sucks"
data.name: Browser agents barely adopted: frontier screenshot loops stall on trivial tasks

data.brief: A year ago the plan was screenshots, DOM reading and form-filling on the merchant's site; it was slow, brittle, stuck at payment, and "fires all the alarm bells" for merchant engineering. What works: the assistant surfaces the product, the agent calls the merchant's checkout API through standardized primitives (ACP, UCP), and a mandate or token pays — no browser
data.name: Browser automation shopping failed checkout apis won

data.brief: Capability timestamp: browser-driving agents crossed a reliability threshold within the last ~6-12 months — "a year ago, even 6 months ago" they failed at finding pop-ups and entering passwords, now they nail down browser tests routinely — so his visual-verification step went from heavily manual to mostly delegated, improving "every quarter or even every month"
data.name: Browser-driving agents crossed a reliability threshold in the last 6-12 months

data.brief: Orchestrator model choice is driven by token economics, not preference: default "Codex 5.3" (5.4 "just uses more tokens"; even on 5.3 "I get destroyed all the time"), degrading to MiniMax when the budget runs low — "not as good, but it kind of gets the job done… this is more about money than preference"; frontier quality treated as a metered resource with a budget-model floor
data.name: Orchestrator model choice is driven by token economics, not preference

data.brief: The former OpenAI GTM leader's advice inverts the playbook: automate first — inbound capture and automated replies (10,000 inbound a day to five people, and unanswered companies bought Copilot), outbound research and sequencing, trust portals and AI-filled security questionnaires — avoid pilots except for the biggest deals, give buyers no homework, and add humans only where buyers insist on one
data.name: Build the gtm machine before hiring the team

data.brief: Agent-first means API-first, and the buy-vs-build question dissolves into one test: is the system arbitrarily customizable? Self-built code is; purchased SaaS survives if it can be made to work on your behalf — Exa keeps Salesforce as a good database with good sales-process choices because it exposes MCP and every agent uses it daily. Crystallized GUIs and flexible chat both stay; SaaS without a programmatic surface does not
data.name: Buy vs build is a false dichotomy customizability is the bit

data.brief: B2B buying moved behind a GenAI black box (Forrester 2026 per speaker): 94% of buyers use GenAI as primary research, 67% prefer a rep-free experience, 80% of deals go to vendors on the buyer's pre-contact shortlist, only 17% of total buying time is spent with vendors — the decision is mostly made before first contact, and sellers can't see what the GenAI platforms told the buyer
data.name: B2B buying moved behind a GenAI black box: 94% of buyers use GenAI as primary research

data.brief: A web-data vendor names a new category — context-as-a-service — of companies structuring web data into knowledge graphs (dedup, entity enrichment, multi-source merge) that agents tap via MCP/CLI/API, "behaving like vertical search engines." Live across finance, market research, retail, e-commerce, GTM, sales intelligence, and pursued by incumbents too (ZoomInfo's GTM.ai). Framed as the successor to data-as-a-service, built for agent knowledge work rather than human lookup. The supply side of the agent-memory/context thesis, from the vendor layer
data.name: Caas category emerging

data.brief: The counterintuitive test result: the two pure CaaS providers underperformed on coverage — expected to dominate entity enrichment, they were limited because "they know what they have about an entity; ask a question beyond that and the data is never there," whereas a searcher keeps exploring. A structural limit of pre-indexed context products: they answer within their index and go silent outside it, which for open-ended knowledge work is a real ceiling. A vendor publicly naming its own category's limitation
data.name: Caas limited to what it holds

data.brief: The mechanism behind the headline: cached tokens are up to ~50× cheaper (DeepSeek) and already computed, but any compaction breaks the cache, so you pay full price for transformed tokens — meaning compaction only pays if you compress by more than the cache multiplier without losing quality, "usually impossible." So the cheapest run is the one sending the *most* (cached) tokens. Value moving into the caching/serving layer, not the model or the summarizer
data.name: Caching flips context economics

data.brief: Safety reframed as a *learned* property plus a harness backstop: the model is trained (via a process reward model) to know when an action is risky — authorized? irreversible? user-visible? high-impact? — and to escalate rather than proceed, and the harness holds an override that forces control back to the user when confidence is miscalibrated. The retrained demo shows it working: the agent distinguishes the sponsored submit button, hits a sign-in wall, and hands off to a user simulator rather than guessing the password. "Autonomy is always good" is listed as a false assumption; "handoff can be optimal"
data.name: Calibrated confidence and handoff

data.brief: A solo practitioner (PhD physicist in Callstack's incubator) built a working physical AI terminal — ESP32, dual display, keyboard, one LiPo cell — that remote-controls his OpenClaw instance on a DGX Spark, in ~3 months / 130 commits; he frames "AI-native operating systems" for microcontroller-class devices as an open market niche. Agents are escaping the desktop into dedicated fully-local hardware
data.name: Solo practitioner ships a working handheld AI terminal driving OpenClaw in 3 months

data.brief: Two liability cases used to establish that a human must sign. A New York lawyer filed a chatbot-assisted brief citing six court cases that did not exist, with correct-looking citation formatting, real-sounding names and page numbers — and, before filing, asked the chatbot whether the cases were real and was told yes ("like asking the guy who sold you the watch whether the watch is real"); the judge fined him. An airline's website chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy, and the airline's tribunal defence was that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions; the tribunal rejected it, the airline paid, "and every one of us in our boardroom quietly took a note that day".
data.name: You cannot outsource accountability to a chatbot — courts and tribunals agree

data.brief: Handing agents human canvas tools fails structurally: PowerPoint/Slides/Figma/Canva are built for human hands and eyes (click, drag, snap-to-grid) with data structures only the app can read; agent output through them — including Figma MCPs, PowerPoint CLIs, screenshot-and-replace loops — comes out as garbage (overlaps, invisible text, no alignment) because every such tool "approaches the problem like a human"
data.name: Human canvas tools structurally fail agents; output comes out as garbage

data.brief: Argument + live demo: coarse OAuth scopes ("read") are too broad to delegate to a non-deterministic agent; capabilities name specific permitted actions, so you grant per-tool and revoke instantly — an email-reader agent with only read capability must request approval (device / client-initiated back-channel flow) to gain send, and revoking its identity forces a fresh, capability-limited agent
data.name: Capabilities, not OAuth scopes, are the grantable unit for agents

data.brief: Amazon AGI Lab observation: agents can perform each individual step of an end-to-end workflow (click/scroll/type/call an API) but fail across the "seams" between apps, where the real work lives; capabilities are mostly solved, reliability isn't — and without reliability there's no trust; 60-80% success is unusable when the failure deletes a database ("you need the nines")
data.name: Amazon AGI Lab: agent capabilities mostly solved, reliability across seams isn't

data.brief: The input-side argument that mirrors Khemani's finding from the opposite direction: the binding constraint on a personal knowledge system is how much raw material you actually capture, so the highest-leverage intervention is dictation at ~200 wpm rather than better organization. Quality standards are deliberately abandoned at capture time — scrappy and rambly is fine because the agent structures it later — and the tooling barrier has fallen, with on-device local models (Handy, VoiceInk) replacing subscription transcription
data.name: Capture bandwidth is the input constraint

data.brief: The mechanism claim: intent lives in Jira, PRDs, and most of all in the prompts where decisions are actually made — and "today we create a PR and throw away the prompts." Capture the session's user responses as acceptance criteria, and build the test plan from the session, not the code, because an agent that wrote the code will not write a test plan that catches its own issues (credited to Dex Horthy). Session provenance, not diff provenance, as the basis for verification
data.name: Capture intent not code

data.brief: At 10,000 calls a day, "99% accurate" means 100 patients with the wrong appointment; detecting a 1% failure with 99% confidence needs ~450 tests and seeing it ten times ~1,900, so synthetic evals cannot carry the load — 7,000 clinicians have graded ~800,000 conversations, continuously, on the human harm scale, where the system reaches 99.89% no-harm against ~81% for humans
data.name: Catching a one percent error takes 450 tests

data.brief: Cedar's spec lives in Lean and its production code in Rust; properties like "forbid trumps permit" are proven on the spec, and ~100M differential random tests nightly confirm the Rust matches — no version ships otherwise. With Verus, Aeneas and Strata, AWS is building the toolchain to verify code in the language it's written in rather than rewriting it
data.name: Cedar ships only after 100m differential tests

data.brief: Practitioner verdict after 2 years of vertical tax agents: chat is synchronous (user must sit and wait) and citations push the verification burden onto the customer (reviewing agent work item by item) — together they break the sold promise of "agents do the work while you sleep"; customers in healthcare/legal/tax complain the promise is not kept
data.name: Chat is synchronous and citations offload verification: the sold agent promise breaks

data.brief: The distribution claim: ChatGPT alone was cited months ago at 800M weekly users — ~10% of world population — a number the web took ~13 years to reach, making the assistant surface ~"170 times the total addressable market of the Apple App Store when it launched." The speakers' conclusion is categorical: MCP Apps "isn't just a technology… this is an entirely new way to distribute applications," with 2026 called as the year it becomes "a global standard for UI"
data.name: Chat hosts reach app store scale

data.brief: Pending orders spoken during a visit requires listening live, which at scale would "break the bank" if a large model ran every few seconds — so cheap, fast gates detect order events and only then hand off to heavier models that match against approved orders. The cost and latency problem is solved by scheduling intelligence, not shrinking it
data.name: Cheap gates decide when heavy models run

data.brief: The engineering consequence, stated as a unit-of-synchronization error rather than a bandwidth problem: "the problem is not whether rollout can leave the cluster — the problem is that the full checkpoint is the wrong unit of synchronization." A Kimi-scale NVFP4 checkpoint runs ~500 GB and takes minutes to hours to move, while even fully async RL wants weight-update latency in seconds; shipping a lossless bitwise patch instead collapses that to ~500 MB and seconds, with the rollout engine reconstructing the identical served version rather than an approximation. Version-aware requests and a sidecar that answers *not ready* rather than serving stale weights keep correctness explicit while the fleet is elastic
data.name: Checkpoint is wrong sync unit

data.brief: ~One week before the talk (early July 2026), one of Germany's biggest newspapers quoted chess trainer Wilhelm Weber calling AI that explains chess as well as a human trainer "the holy grail of chess programming" — possibly 5 more years away — while TNG in Munich was already auto-producing and auto-uploading such explainer videos nightly, no human in the loop
data.name: TNG auto-produces chess explainer videos a trainer called 5 years away

data.brief: Auto-generated explainer videos cost ~€0.20–0.30 each (longer formats: a few euros) with ~1-in-20 having a defective description; the operator moved from pre-watching every video to publish-first / take-down-later. Channel at ~500k views and >4,000 subscribers, most gained in the final month; positioned for the long tail — videos of amateurs' own games, which human streamers like GothamChess would never cover; not yet monetized (net negative)
data.name: Auto-generated chess videos cost ~€0.20-0.30 with ~5% defect rate

data.brief: Microsoft PoC Chronicle demonstrates boundary-recorded replay end to end: a recorded haywire trading run is replayed with the LLM node stubbed from the trace and the newly guardrailed tool live; an assertion verifies the bad order now blocks — the production failure becomes a free, deterministic CI test with zero model calls
data.name: Chronicle replays a recorded failure as a deterministic, zero-model-call CI test

data.brief: For corpora where every document is relevant to the question set and the whole collection is replaced frequently (each document represents an event; collections go obsolete fast), both standard approaches fail: plain RAG can't serve an all-relevant collection through a similarity threshold, and GraphRAG — "an excellent approach" when data is stable — requires an LLM pass over all documents for entity/relationship extraction, making every refresh computationally expensive and slow. Knowledge-graph context has a churn boundary
data.name: Fast-churn all-relevant corpora break both plain RAG and GraphRAG

data.brief: "Shipping is the start, not the finish" (paraphrase): iteration engine is user thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback plus automated evals running in CI against real completions (did the prompt hit the right tools, did it do what it's supposed to) — eval-in-CI as ordinary production practice at a non-frontier enterprise vendor
data.name: Eval-in-CI on real completions as ordinary production practice

data.brief: Concrete enterprise-practice reversal: a CISO is backing up employee laptops again (abandoned ~2020) because one agentic query can now delete local data
data.name: CISO resumes employee laptop backups because one agentic query can delete local data

data.brief: The failure taxonomy with worked examples from the benchmark: a sales-forecasting model that, told it over-predicted then under-predicted, discards the first correction and jumps back to over-prediction (stability failure), and a notepad-based system that dismisses applicable epidemiological material as belonging to "a different study schema that doesn't apply here" (plasticity failure). The environments deliberately induce this by injecting concept drift — database migrations that drop and rename columns — because handling drift requires learning what to forget as well as what to keep. the empirical counterpart to Su's stability/plasticity claim in the same batch
data.name: Cl failures split stability plasticity

data.brief: Agents inherit the generalization limits of the ML systems underneath them, so classical discipline transfers directly: hold out a test set and use it sparingly, refresh it with production data, keep a dataset for edge cases and broader capabilities, test negatives as well as positives, invest in online evals so the data matches real-world representation — and judge on patterns rather than isolated runs, because tuning the prompt off one failing trace of a non-deterministic system is a trap.
data.name: Classical ML discipline transfers directly to agent evaluation

data.brief: Remediation is being automated behind classification: OpenTelemetry feeds root-cause analysis, drift type determines the solution, risk is assessed, and fixes roll out canary-style (5–10% of machines → monitor/verify → 100%), with an admin-confirmation gate before classification-triggered action.
data.name: Remediation automated behind drift classification with canary rollout

data.brief: 1.2M questions classified by LLMs into topics give the team feature gaps and quality issues in real time, generate battle cards and enablement docs for a new product in minutes from Confluence, Jira, Slack and PRDs (work that took interviews with 100 sellers a week), and match teams unknowingly targeting the same accounts. "Once you start tapping into your logs, the hockey stick starts"
data.name: Classified logs generate battle cards in minutes

data.brief: Reliability for generative features starts by deciding which failures are tolerable (a scheduler at 1 in 10,000) and which are not (reimbursement amounts — multiple models must agree on the receipt or a human takes over); hundreds of integration tests run repeatedly with a ~90% required pass rate because a single pass proves nothing; every conversation is auto-scored against rubrics and a dedicated group manually reviews a sample, ~20% at launches. Verification sized to the stakes of each feature
data.name: Classify acceptable failures and run tests many times
