data.brief: Claude Code's dynamic workflows made the most-used coding agent capable of recursive, model-chosen decomposition; RLM co-author Omar Khattab publicly conceded Claude Code is "finally an RLM" — frontier harnesses are converging on recursion as a first-class primitive
data.name: Claude Code's dynamic workflows made it capable of model-chosen recursion

data.brief: Why Claude Code went from nothing to $4B (now ~$9B) revenue in under a year despite prior CLI agents (Aider, Codebuff) having identical tools: first time a lab RL-trained the model against the harness it ships in; OpenAI team's own November talk: a harness builder who doesn't own the model weights is always at a disadvantage vs. someone who owns both
data.name: Claude Code's moat is RL-training the model in its own harness

data.brief: "If you're not a graph expert, guess what — Claude is": Claude writes Cypher better than the DevRel lead, builds entity extractors, and does everything needed to stand up graph memory once you know the basic model you want — graph expertise is no longer the adoption barrier to graph-backed agent memory.
data.name: Claude collapses the graph-expertise barrier to graph-backed agent memory

data.brief: Claude is today the only client that, given a task with no matching tool, searches the MCP registry and selects the best store-listed connector dynamically; ChatGPT expected to follow soon. With 1B+ active users expressing intent in chat, model-mediated connector selection becomes an organic, high-intent acquisition channel
data.name: Claude dynamically discovers store-listed connectors from the MCP registry

data.brief: Claude announced generally available in Microsoft Foundry the day before the talk (~2026-07-16) — Anthropic's models distributed inside Microsoft's unified enterprise agent platform ("best of both worlds")
data.name: Claude announced generally available in Microsoft Foundry

data.brief: Failure-mode finding that cuts against Claude's reputation for thoroughness: on multi-part prompts it silently completes one half and drops the other — asked to support both synchronous and async versions of calling a hook, it implements the sync path and omits the async one. Observed in roughly two out of three Claude rollouts across all trials.
data.description: Counterpoint from the same analysis: GPT was the least likely model to miss requirements (GPT 5.5 best, GPT 5.4 second), reading prompts and repository contracts literally and honouring existing conventions and signatures; both traits converged across rollouts rather than appearing as lucky runs.
data.name: Claude silently drops half of multi-part requirements in ~2 of 3 rollouts

data.brief: Anthropic's internal Claude Tag lands 65% of the product engineering team's PRs; work splits into Claude Code for complex interactive tasks vs Tag for proactive background work; a large share of sessions are multiplayer (PM tags in Claude, then design, then eng to take it to prod)
data.name: Claude Tag lands 65% of Anthropic's product engineering PRs

data.brief: Prediction: a claw shakeout in the later 2020s, on the 2010s mobile-platform template — every app category (rides, payments, food, video) collapsed to one or two logos because people hold only a few products in mind; survivors are either very economically valuable (Airbnb) or very frequent (Uber/DoorDash), and everything else (Thumbtack) is forgotten like a college friend who moved cities. With rate of change up 3–4×, agents lacking capabilities users need get dropped fast — and another shakeout wave follows even for hill-toppers
data.name: Prediction: a claw shakeout in the later 2020s on the mobile-app template

data.brief: Failure anatomy (illustrative broker-API scenario): user asks to sell $1,000 of stock; the agent drops the raw 1,000 into the quantity field and sells 1,000 shares at ~$190 — a ~$190K wrong action that returns a clean 200 OK in 30 ms. Zero exceptions, zero alerts, dashboards perfectly green: semantically wrong agent actions are invisible to conventional monitoring
data.name: A ~$190K wrong agent action returns a clean 200 OK: semantic failure is invisible

data.brief: Sonar research (as cited): clean and messy repos show roughly the same agent pass rates, but clean code uses fewer tokens and causes fewer revisits — code maintainability has become a line item in agent operating cost
data.name: Sonar: clean repos match messy pass rates but cost fewer tokens and revisits

data.brief: Distribution-shift claim from an AI-storytelling practitioner: 15 years ago a great product might be found organically; in the crowded 2026 AI market the clearest-story products are the ones getting funded, bought, and talked about — "great tech that nobody understands dies quietly" (paraphrase)
data.name: In the crowded 2026 AI market the clearest-story products get funded and bought

data.brief: The tooling argument with numbers: an Arize AI study finds CLI and MCP roughly tied on capability (~83% success) but the CLI winning decisively on reuse, speed (7 turns/<1min vs 71 round-trips/8min), and cost (Anthropic: up to 75× cheaper in tokens), because a CLI sequence is programmed once and replayed without a model in the loop while MCP invokes the model every turn. A concrete data point in the corpus's CLI-vs-MCP / code-mode thread, from the browser-control domain
data.name: Cli beats mcp for browser control

data.brief: A 20-year editor-native Microsoft engineer now starts the workday in the CLI — six-plus terminals of parallel agent runs ("build me an app", "fix this issue") while sipping coffee — and opens the editor only for fine adjustments, recast as a control board listening to CLI/repo streams
data.name: A 20-year editor-native engineer now starts the workday in the CLI

data.brief: The methodology as a reliability principle: sense–act–verify (verifying through a *different* channel than the action), and climb the human-likeness ladder only to the lowest rung that works — synthetic click, then trusted CDP click, then real mouse paths with jitter and vision — then persist the working path as code or a skill. "You figure it out once and you do it forever." A disciplined-engineering account of durable web automation, explicitly not a model-capability story
data.name: Climb only as high as forced

data.brief: The learning loop, stated as a design principle: our system isn't deciding what correct is in a clinical edge case — a licensed professional is. Conversations are traced; flagged edge cases go to a clinician's annotation queue with a small rubric (expected result, expected observation, turn index, category, note).
data.description: An extraction script both triages flagged traces into a report for discussion and normalizes the annotations into typed evals in the team's eval schema; committed, a clinician's judgment is living in CI and every prompt, model and guardrail change is scored against it. The scenarios themselves come from the clinician's real patient experience — she knows the type of people our system is going to meet before we meet them — and the payoff is categorical: not one sentence fixed, the entire self-harm category lifted.
data.name: A licensed clinician, not the system, defines correct in clinical edge cases

data.brief: Uber's agents re-tune themselves in production without a human in the loop: cadence-sampled production data goes to labelers under the golden-set guidelines, mismatches go to a diagnoser that localizes the failing component, a reflect/synthesize prompt-optimizer rewrites that agent's config, the rewrite is benchmarked against the golden set, and on pass it is registered in an agent store the next production run picks up. Stated rationale: an offline-tuned static model provably will not hold in the real system, so "every component in our system is able to tune itself for any drift online" — with observability on guardrails and quick rollback as the safety net.
data.name: Uber's production agents re-tune themselves with no human in the loop

data.brief: The platform's shape follows user preference for harnesses: "who here prefers Claude Code locally? Codex? something else? — so much diversity in the room." Oz supports Warp's own harness, Claude Code, Codex and custom ones, but flexibility "crammed in" fragments the experience, so the platform imposes structure around every harness (state rehydration, uniform artifacts). Same conclusion as Box's "bring your own harness" rung, arrived at from the vendor side: the harness is the user's choice, the platform's job is to hold it
data.name: Cloud agent platform must be harness agnostic

data.brief: The vendor's answer to unknown unknowns: cluster all production traffic to surface new categories of failure with no guardrail and no eval, and turn them into eval cases — so the flywheel discovers failure types rather than only collecting examples of known ones. Continuous learning applied to the eval suite itself
data.name: Cluster production to find unknown failures

data.brief: The first-principles production lesson, presented as something the speaker has not heard discussed: clustering traces is useful for one-off analysis and does not scale, because clusters cannot be tracked reliably over time and their boundaries are not yours to set — "wrong price quoted" and "wrong refund calculated" merge into a useless "price issues" cluster despite unrelated root causes. What an issue must instead carry is when it started and what percentage of users it affects, on the telemetry analogy that nobody clusters ordinary logs. Framed by the premise that "agents will have an infinite number of problems," so the job is triage
data.name: Clusters are not issues

data.brief: The CMU GitHub study, in more detail than the batch-2 keynote: projects sorted by metadata into traditional-tooling vs AI-tool (Cursor) cohorts show a temporary productivity spike lasting ~3 months, then reverting — while a persistent increase in static-analysis warnings and code complexity (measured with SonarQube) continues well past the 3-month mark. The debt is what reverts the spike: the accumulated issues "end up actually slowing developers down even more". ⚠ near-duplicate of sig-cmu-velocity-fade — same study, same vendor, second speaker; merge option in Review note 2
data.name: Cmu ai productivity spike reverts

data.brief: Carnegie Mellon study: AI coding agents give a 3–5× initial velocity boost that dissipates back to baseline within ~3 months, driven by rising security, maintainability, reliability, and complexity issues — technical debt generated as fast as the code
data.name: CMU: AI coding velocity boost fades to baseline within ~3 months

data.brief: What cheap code does to the function: FDEs used to translate customer signal back into the product (stability, data integration); now they can build end-to-end solutions with coding agents themselves, and simultaneously — observed at Sierra — product engineering is becoming client-facing. The role is not narrowing but converging and stacking: product, infra and agent engineers are absorbing DevOps and deployment concerns while FDEs absorb product development.
data.name: Cheap code makes FDE and product engineering converge and stack rather than narrow

data.brief: The entire software culture, infrastructure, and company landscape was built on the assumption that writing code is the expensive part; writing code is now ~free, so produced code volume will explode and the discipline reorganizes around design adequacy, verification, and architecture — "superhuman syntax generation" is settled ("when Gemini writes a function, I can't do better — it's over")
data.name: Writing code is now ~free; the discipline reorganizes around design and verification

data.brief: Code mode is spreading as an agent interface (shipped in the Anthropic API, talked up by Cloudflare); Witan extended it to a REPL with persistent state and saw sequential-tool timeouts (5-minute budget, previously common on 10–15-call explorations) drop to zero
data.name: Code mode spreads; persistent REPL dropped sequential-tool timeouts to zero

data.brief: A code-review vendor CEO, fresh from a leading lab: code-review benchmarks "did not change a lot" across the latest models; the gap is context. Given the codebase's standards, architecture and history, current models surface the right issues; without them they emit generic advice. The scattered state of that context (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/skills with inconsistent standards, invisible MCP/RAG inputs, factory-generated code) is the actual blocker to trusted review
data.name: Code review benchmarks flat context is the lever

data.brief: Prediction from a DeepMind research VP: within a year, model-generated code will ship with nobody reading it — the compiler-assembly analogy (nobody checks compiler output anymore); replacement process is "active guardrails," and vulnerability discovery becomes a never-ending deepening cycle: models find a layer of bugs, get smarter, find subtler ones
data.name: DeepMind VP: within a year model code ships with nobody reading it

data.brief: What actually happens when teams adopt the model: "people start to plan and then not implement their plan — and this is a really good sign," because exploration and triage replace reflexive building; velocity shifts "from code velocity to idea velocity." And the review economics invert: aligning on key decisions up front moves the review point earlier — "the hardest part of any code review is *what actually matters here*; if you move that earlier, the code review becomes much simpler" — which is his answer to the unmergeable-PR flood. Closing claim: "the future of engineering is multiplayer… multiplayer by default sooner than we think"
data.name: Code velocity to idea velocity

data.brief: OpenAI open-sourced the entire Codex stack around the model — harness, app server (the same path its own apps use), plugins, AGENTS.md — and states "we're not building one system for OpenAI and a second simplified one for developers"; the harness is fed into model post-training; ecosystem proof: opencode inspected the reference implementation, an outside dev built Codex Monitor on the app server before the Codex app launched and was then hired to build Codex for iOS; Codex subscriptions now work in opencode, Pi, Droids, OpenClaw, Xcode, JetBrains
data.name: OpenAI open-sourced the entire Codex stack around the model

data.brief: Practitioner observation: out-of-the-box coding agents converge on two interaction patterns — one giant end-to-end diff, or approve-pings on every file change — and both reduce the developer to a rubber stamp, logging accept-skewed binary labels on code blocks instead of rich structured decisions (bad assumptions, trade-offs, stylistic preferences) that could actually improve the system
data.name: Coding-agent UIs converge on patterns that reduce developers to rubber stamps

data.brief: Contrarian claim aimed at this audience: "it is not the Claude Code era." Coding agents are part of the same era as ChatGPT because they are still RLHF — "it would look very, very different if it was purely RLVR" — and the familiar failure mode where a model "gets really good at agentic stuff but stops following what you actually want" is the visible trade-off between the two objectives dancing in optimization space. Neither position on that trade-off adds up to automation, so the next era is not a better agent but real automation.
data.name: It is not the Claude Code era: coding agents are still RLHF-era assistance

data.brief: What changed between 2024 and 2025 was coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) becoming the default way to build applications — and their default output is TypeScript; a self-reinforcing flywheel: more TS apps → more TS training data + deeper native integrations → better agent output in TS
data.name: Coding agents became the default way to build apps; their default output is TypeScript

data.brief: "The uncomfortable truth" for any package surface: coding agents never visit the library's website — they read the repo and node_modules with stale training data. Bundling the markdown docs into the package with an agents.md pointer cut tokens almost 50% across models versus web search and works with no skill installed; the docs must live where the agent already is
data.name: Coding agents read node modules not your website

data.brief: The bet against the corpus's own recent thread: "coding abilities are not sufficient to do well on computer use." Coding agents *look* deployable on computer tasks because those tasks are representable as code (MCP, API, Playwright), but the model must actually see the screen like a human — grounding on dense layouts, change detection across accumulating screenshots, multi-source observation over incomplete channels. Perception, not code generation, is the missing capability. A direct counter to the "computer use is just coding with a browser tool" position
data.name: Coding skill insufficient for cua

data.brief: Cognition's problem framing: coding itself is "a mostly solved problem" — models are good enough that with enough context engineering you get the code blocks you care about — and writing code faster is only ~20% of the problem. The remaining 80% is testing, reviewing, deploying and maintaining code across the enterprise, on real legacy rather than zero-to-one prompting, in languages nobody learns anymore (COBOL, JCL).
data.name: Coding is mostly solved; testing, review, deploy and maintenance are the remaining 80%

data.brief: Every AI coding tool re-learns the same codebase from scratch and shares nothing across tools or sessions (Claude Code for hard problems, Cursor for quick edits, Copilot for completions — "you explain the same codebase to three different tools", paraphrase). One shared local index + persistent memory fixed it: explain once, every tool remembers. Measured on a real project: 247 queries, 12.4M tokens saved (~$186), 84% of savings from the search layer vs compression — tracked per query as would-have-sent vs sent
data.name: Every AI coding tool re-learns the codebase; one shared local index fixed it

data.brief: An explanation, from an academic-turned-operator, for why agent success is so unevenly distributed: code is "already a language-native world" — symbolic representation, structured records, tests and rewards already in place — so it was the one domain where language agents could be dropped in whole. Evidence offered is Anthropic's revenue curve (≈400× in under two years, largely coding-driven). Outside that privileged world, deployment goes badly enough that Andrew Ng's "decade of agents, not year of agents" is quoted as still standing. The corollary is uncomfortable for generalist-agent roadmaps: the first market was not a beachhead but an outlier
data.name: Coding was the privileged market

data.brief: Composio's CTO: software engineering became fully autonomous in three years not on models and harnesses alone but because code came with the support agents need — repo, history, tests, CI/CD, review, linters, revert — and the same models pointed at support, finance and sales work blind. "For two years the model was the bottleneck; now everything else is" — infrastructure nobody has built yet
data.name: Coding went autonomous because its infrastructure was built for agents

data.brief: Deployment proof points offered on stage (anonymized case studies plus public ones): a 3-month embed delivering the equivalent of "+150% headcount"; ~82% reduction in delivery timelines measured on the customer's own pre/post agile metrics; roughly double the PR throughput versus single-point tools before an agent harness.
data.description: Also cited: Nubank's ETL migration, staffed with 50 engineers, delivered in about a third of the timeline autonomously; a large Latin American bank's tax-identification-system migration at half the required effort; and a public customer reporting ~10x weekly engineering output ("10x per week worth of engineering talent").
data.name: Cognition reports +150% headcount equivalent and ~82% delivery-timeline reduction

data.brief: Cognition dogfooding number: over the last six months, "for better or worse we might have been behind on hiring", the org shipped almost an order of magnitude more good-quality robust PRs by deploying its own agent — described as a step-function increase in engineering leverage rather than an incremental one. Enterprise-side consumption of the agent described as parabolic growth in adoption and use cases.
data.name: Cognition shipped nearly an order of magnitude more PRs in six months using its own agent

data.brief: Routing's endgame per the panel is not harness logic but trained behavior: Cognition RLs its models in both orchestration roles (model-as-orchestrator deciding delegation; model-as-executor following another model's instructions) and expects co-designing models with the orchestration system to be "a big lift in the next step"; new frontier models (Fable family, GPT-5.5/5.6) are "themselves naturally collaborative and better at delegation" — "smarter models get better and better at delegating"; NVIDIA post-trains Nemotron for harnesses including routing, and Flex Run moves the routing switch *inside* the model artifact (per-task footprint activation). Closing consensus: "models are going to get good at routing to other models"
data.name: Collaboration moves into the weights

data.brief: Practitioner claim: context compaction now works well enough that the old advice ("start a new thread after ~20 messages, one conversation per feature") is obsolete — Liu runs pinned threads 5 weeks old with ~400 sub-agents that still know their job; the pattern is pin + rename + delegate + write-to-memory + wake-on-automation
data.name: Context compaction obsoletes the start-a-new-thread rule

data.brief: The boundary condition that keeps the result honest: keep-everything stops winning when caching is unavailable or context exceeds the window — local models (a 32k MacBook window can't hold individually-large lessons; bigger model size doesn't enlarge the window) and very long contexts. There, retrieval wins (100% accuracy on pasted documents locally; stuffing the window took ~340s to emit a single token). The compaction-vs-keep-everything choice is entirely determined by whether the cache applies
data.name: Compaction wins only when uncached

data.brief: What they have built: software-engineering companies put into containerized environments. The agent must incorporate organizational context — projects, incidents, tickets, postmortems, customer conversations, explicitly including documentation that is not up to date — while dealing with failures that only appear at scale (network failures between distributed nodes, data corruption, clock skew) and reasoning about operational blast radius while serving live traffic.
data.description: Demonstrated on an ETCD consensus cluster where a conventional environment would touch only the source-code box and the capability gap lives in everything surrounding it: tickets and postmortems ("what are the train wrecks, why did they happen, how did customers feel about them"), rolling deployments that conflict or fail, hardware migration with failing and stale-deprecated nodes, and monitoring a service that cannot go down. Result claimed: "environments far more complex and long horizon than a simple code diff" — extended further just by running multiple deployments instead of one.
data.name: Whole software companies containerized as the next unit of training data

data.brief: Framework evaluation over ~3M financial records, 5 years, 4 regulatory jurisdictions: graph entity correlation + probabilistic risk scoring + jurisdictional normalization reached ~91% precision / ~87% recall (F1 0.89), a 76% reduction in false positives, and ~40% less manual audit effort vs rule-based baselines (self-reported research results)
data.name: Graph correlation over ~3M records hit 91% precision, 87% recall, 76% fewer false alarms

data.brief: x402 rails work; what blocks enterprise adoption is that a chief legal or policy officer must be "100% confident" agents will not overspend, go off-policy or pay a sanctioned counterparty. Sanctions and identity screening of bare wallet addresses (TRM) on both buyer and seller sides is the layer being built; the good-claw/bad-claw demo shows the sanctioned wallet's 0.1-cent payments rejected once screening is on
data.name: Compliance not rails gates enterprise agent payments

data.brief: Because the risk model learns from every completed audit (confirmed fraud strengthens detection patterns; false positives refine scoring), compliance shifts from reactive post-audit review to predictive governance — from "what went wrong" to "what is likely to go wrong next"; compliance becomes a continuous intelligence function rather than a periodic review process
data.name: Audit-outcome learning shifts compliance from reactive review to predictive governance

data.brief: The Miranda mechanism observed in the wild: culturally dominant representations overwrite documentary figures — reproducible today on any frontier model (a bare-model 1847 Lincoln reasons with "inherent executive authority," a 20th-century construction, in Spielberg's war-president register, while the actual 1848 Lincoln–Herndon letter argues the opposite); offline analog at the Schuyler Mansion, where post-musical visitors nearly tripled and arrived pre-loaded with wrong "facts" the staff must unteach
data.name: Cultural composites overwrite the documentary figure on any frontier model

data.brief: A personal plugin shipped while building Cora — ideate, brainstorm, overnight loop with before/after video, polish, compound — is now used by hundreds of thousands of people daily across a dozen harnesses and has spread to PMs, designers and knowledge workers. A practitioner's loop became a de facto harness standard without a launch
data.name: Compound plugin used by hundreds of thousands daily

data.brief: With code unread by design, comprehension is relocated to two surfaces. Visualization: a zoomable map of a program where clicking navigates to the exact lines, so a reader opts into which parts to understand and explicitly declares the rest "too much slop — let that be slop". Execution traces: per-file tracing at (claimed) zero performance cost, showing exactly how much time was spent in which part of the program, and navigable by Claude as well as by humans so the agent can locate bugs, errors and inefficiencies and optimize without being told. The generalization offered: the goal was never reading all the code, it was understanding the system, and tools can deliver that directly.
data.name: With code unread by design, comprehension relocates to visualization and traces

data.brief: The representation numbers: full DOM ≈ 20k tokens; a screenshot ≈ 1.1k tokens but shows only one snippet; ARK's markdown ≈ 1.8k tokens and covers the entire page — with it a much cheaper model completed tasks (downloading an Aadhaar ID document, booking a Canadian trekking date) fast, where Claude driving screenshots stalled or failed on the same sites
data.name: Full-page markdown at ~1.8k tokens lets cheap models beat frontier screenshot loops

data.brief: Dated market claim opening the talk: compute availability has become extremely scarce over the last six months and is getting worse. H100 prices reversed a multi-year decline and are ~40% above their end-of-2025 lows — abnormal for hardware. Demand side: reasoning models consume ~8x the tokens of non-reasoning models, projected to 5x again within about a year. Two consequences already visible: Google capped Meta's Gemini usage because of inference constraints, and OpenAI has effectively started selling token futures (guaranteed capacity some period forward).
data.description: Morcos's read is that forward-selling is only necessary because the labs genuinely think access to frontier API tokens may be limited — not as a business decision but because there is not enough inference and first-party products will be prioritized.
data.name: Compute scarcity has labs capping and forward-selling frontier token access

data.brief: The structural consequence: pre-training compute must be co-located and over-provisioned, while inference, post-training and agentic compute distribute well and return more per FLOP — so returns moving off the pre-training axis means they move onto compute that "does not require the same hoarding of GPUs… it's very different compute purchasing dynamics, and the person with the best idea has a higher chance of winning." A frontier-lab insider arguing the capital barrier to frontier participation is falling for structural rather than charitable reasons
data.name: Compute shape shifts who competes

data.brief: Computer use is moving from 1.0 (screenshot → reason/plan → click/type/scroll, agent takes over the human's screen) to 2.0: background, windowed, OS-integrated drivers where agents run "multi-cursor" on the user's own laptop without seizing control — Cua shipped this open source within a weekend of Codex releasing its computer-use model (~2 months before the talk)
data.name: Computer use moves from screen takeover to background multi-cursor OS drivers

data.brief: A DevRel practitioner built every ancillary asset of his 2026 conference talk — including a full Conductor product tour recreated as a Remotion/React scene — in TypeScript, calling it "the most insane statement" versus 2–3 years ago when only professional engineers wrote code for content; he's a Python-background data engineer learning React because it's now the fastest path to high-fidelity assets
data.name: A DevRel practitioner built every ancillary conference asset in TypeScript

data.brief: The safety claim is architectural, not procedural: nobody reviews the AI's code — instead, client and server are both sandboxed (null-origin iframe + CSP; dynamic-worker Durable Object), can talk only to each other over one Cap'n Web/postMessage channel, and sharing/ACL are implemented by the platform so the app "can't possibly get that wrong." Consequence, stated flatly: "there is basically no security bug you can have in this code that matters" — an agent-added paste-arbitrary-SVG feature (a textbook XSS surface) is shrugged off live because leaked script has no origin, no cookies and no egress. This is the strongest corpus statement yet of securing generation by making verification unnecessary
data.name: Confinement neutralizes vibe code bugs

data.brief: The industry is at the point of handing the general public's computers, finances, and personal lives to AI agents with no protection layer in place — Meijer ("very sad and very scary") notes even conference practitioners routinely run agents with permissions bypassed ("yes, yes, yes"), and recounts Claude Code deleting one of his files mid-talk-prep the moment his attention waned
data.name: Public computers and finances are being handed to agents with no protection layer

data.brief: Speaker's consumer app (reverse-Suno: given a song, recover the prompt) reached hundreds of thousands of users and cost hundreds of thousands of dollars in inference — far beyond anticipation; agent loops + uncompressed context on an endpoint blind to workload shape
data.name: Consumer app's inference cost blew out to hundreds of thousands of dollars

data.brief: The chat view of a coding agent is a lie about what the model saw (compaction, quirks, undisclosed thinking). Hashing every prompt part turns a prompt into a list of hashes, giving exact context provenance, diffs between runs, exact replay against another model, easier compaction and cache management — "the main advantage at scale is auditability." Verification of an agent's behavior becomes a build-system property
data.name: Content addressed prompts make agents auditable

data.brief: Role forecast from inside DevRel: 2026 was "the year of the creative technologist" (the term that got thrown around), 2027 will be "the year of the content engineer" — teams building declarative, robust content pipelines (walkthroughs, docs, screenshots, product updates) generated from code
data.name: Role forecast: 2027 will be the year of the content engineer

data.brief: The rant, and the most product-relevant finding: perfect architecture and infinite compute would still leave memory capped by what the system can observe. Demonstrated by a profile that records two mutually exclusive trips because it read a *decision-making* conversation and never saw the decision, which happened in person and left traces in connected email the assistant does not reason over. The indictment is the absence of curiosity — the system does not notice the contradiction or try to resolve it — and the diagnosis is explicit: "it's not a technology problem, it's a product problem." Compounded by fragmentation: every product builds a private memory, none shared, each rebuilt from scratch, all updated by hand when life changes
data.name: Context acquisition is the real cap

data.brief: Early results from the unified system: enterprise reps' qualified opportunities rose over 13 weeks, and users receiving context-aware feature recommendations were 63% more likely to take the next step; reps start the day with a prioritized task inbox and pre-researched drafts, and new reps learn the signals and playbooks from the best reps' encoded patterns — "shadow your best human; the chaos of tabs was the spec"
data.name: Context aware recommendations lift next step 63 percent

data.brief: Context construction is presented as the harness's first and "arguably one of the most important" jobs, with the unpredictable parts — installed MCPs inflating the tool registry, an unbounded skills list — handled by explicit mechanism rather than prompt discipline: deferred tools kept out of the window and reached via tool search, and a hard 2% cap on the skills list that degrades descriptions as it fills. The stated motivation includes a quality argument, not just a cost one: "the more context you have, the higher it is that you have contradicting information and it causes confusion for the model"
data.name: Context budget becomes explicit mechanism

data.brief: Live: Claude Code producing an optimization plan without the engine took ~2 minutes and cost more; with it, ~1 minute and sub-dollar — and it "nailed the nuances" because it found the PRs, Slack threads and docs where improvements had been discussed, with sources Claude could jump to. The value is not the upfront saving but the compounding: without the right context the agent operates on the wrong plan and loops. A customer: 50% fewer tokens, faster triage, better answers
data.name: Context engine halves cost and compounds

data.brief: Skills/MCP stacking is inheritance — inflating one general agent's context layer; the speaker cites research that installing very many skills makes an agent substantially worse, and argues 100–1,000 skills obviously hit diminishing returns
data.name: Stacking many skills inflates context and makes agents substantially worse

data.brief: The scoped counter-claim, stated pre-emptively against the room: "some of you are thinking it's just a matter of context — just give it more context." His answer: even the complete financial record of a company (general ledger, P&L, cash flows, invoices) handed to a frontier model is still just one group of data points on one company — it contains no information about what comparable businesses did and how it turned out. Worked case: an apparel company where 80% of cost came from one vendor who was also enabling 97% of revenue — the textbook "cut your biggest cost" answer yields "great margins on zero dollars". Analogy offered: given a very smart, freshly-read adviser and an experienced one, everyone picks experience.
data.name: Context is not experience: one company's full record is still one observation

data.brief: Independent practitioner corroboration of context rot: "if you fill the context window too much, the quality of the answer gets degraded too" — stated as the structural reason a single big-window CAG can't just swallow the collection and buckets must be sharded; KV-cache cost is acknowledged as real ("can be pretty expensive") and managed via per-cache lifetime
data.name: Overfilling the context window degrades answer quality

data.brief: "Context Rot" paper: performance starts degrading after ~25% of the context window is used; practitioner heuristic puts the "dumb zone" past ~40% — an agent loaded with instructions + many MCPs can start its first user turn already dumb
data.name: Context rot: performance degrades after ~25% of the window is used

data.brief: "When context can influence an action, it's state" — it goes stale, conflicts with authoritative data and corrupts later actions. Short-term (thread) and long-term (files, prompts, databases, cache) memories need an explicit source-of-truth decision on conflict, and memory should be a provenance-carrying cache invalidated when the source of truth changes. Memory management framed as cache-coherence, from the systems side
data.name: Context that drives action is state

data.brief: The claim that reframes the whole track: "continual learning is already here." A running profile *is* a learning loop — profile conditions the conversation, conversation produces new information, background synthesis folds it back into the profile, repeat — running today at consumer scale. The qualifier is where it happens: outside the weights. The open question is posed as economic rather than technical: weight updates amortize across employees and customers at enterprise scale but not for an individual, so "will each of us get our own self-learning model, what data kicks the process off, and who pays for it?"
data.name: Continual learning already shipping

data.brief: Direct positional claim: for models to catch their own mistakes and not repeat them, "in some cases people want to try to do this at the harness layer or the prompt layer. But ultimately you want a system that can evolve autonomously" — with humans in the loop at the right level of abstraction. The obstacle is named as abstraction level, not capability: environment and reward design sit "far too low for it to be practical for most people". RL is also called out as poor at absorbing dense new knowledge, which is why environment-supervised world modeling is blended in alongside it.
data.name: Continual learning belongs in the weights, not at the harness or prompt layer

data.brief: Feizi (RELAI/UMD): agent continual learning ≠ model fine-tuning — the cheapest, fastest durable fixes usually land in the harness (prompts, skills, tools, code, workflow) and memory (facts, distilled skills) layers, with weight updates the expensive last resort; a good learning engine "asks for the smallest durable change at the right layer" (paraphrase)
data.name: Agent continual learning isn't fine-tuning; cheapest fixes land in harness/memory

data.brief: Prompts were the differentiator, then models — both "rapidly commoditizing" (paraphrase); the next frontier is reliability infrastructure. An agentic control plane (scheduling, memory coordination, policy enforcement, evaluation, workload routing) is emerging the way Kubernetes followed containers, and organizations that build this layer gain significant competitive advantage: "the future of AI won't be won by better prompts, it will be won by better systems" (paraphrase)
data.name: The agentic control plane is the next frontier after prompts and models

data.brief: The counter-program: model the loop on control theory — set point, sensor, measured error, controller, actuator, disturbances — because control loops change a system incrementally instead of jumping to the end state and blowing it up, which avoids over-steering and minimises risk.
data.description: Loops are appropriate exactly when you have a system you want to change, a property you can measure, and a way to get feedback on the change (what good software engineers have always been taught to do). Stated scope beyond code cleanup: conforming an API to someone else's OpenAPI spec, tracking the MCP specification version, mirroring a project from Python to TypeScript, maintaining a fork against upstream.
data.name: Agent loops should be built to the control-theory template

data.brief: A merchant agent leaks discount codes, reveals other shoppers, or becomes a free coding assistant (Chipotle's, reportedly) unless behavior evals, protocol-compliance evals, latency benchmarks and an LLM judge run before shipping; Best Buy ships the templates. Also open per the retailer: ACP↔UCP convergence, identity standards, multi-agent checkout delegation
data.name: Conversational commerce without evals is whack a mole

data.brief: "Your competitor can build your feature this afternoon too — so the cost of the average just went to zero, and so did its value." A year ago the superpower was being good at using AI; now models are so good and everyone is skilled that everyone points AI at the same goals and gets the same answer. Expo-hall products "all sound the same." Producing averageness is not free: you pay in tokens, infra and salaried hours to make yourself harder to choose
data.name: Cost of the average went to zero

data.brief: Expensive physical GTM signals are back for devtools: Typesense (bootstrapped, no funding milestones to announce) ran hundreds of SF billboards explicitly as a credibility proxy ("I didn't realize you were this big"); SF banner culture (Muni buses, buildings, highways) plus a rising norm of early-stage startups hosting their own user conferences (Supabase's, year two, cited as the model)
data.name: Expensive physical GTM signals return: billboards and user conferences

data.brief: Live A/B on identical source markdown: vector store vs Cognee/Neo4j graph store as a digital twin of his home lab, agent VLAN-segmented off the real network so it answers from memory alone.
data.description: Graph memory precisely identified WAN-exposed end-of-life software (a Minecraft server on Debian Jessie) and 0.0.0.0-exposed management ports (HAProxy, OpenVPN), following the router node to everything related; vector memory deflected ("couldn't find specifics, check your pfSense rules yourself"). Speaker patched the real holes it found afterwards.
data.name: Live A/B: graph memory finds real security holes where vector memory deflects

data.brief: Measurement critique: the existing cyber-benchmark family (CyberGym, AIxCC, BountyBench, CyBench) checks only whether the AI could crash the program. "Crashing a program is different than hacking it — you can't go steal someone's IP by simply crashing a program." Because of that definition, a headline like "Kimi succeeds at hacking 50% of the time" is an artifact of a broken metric, and the question of whether models could exploit high-value targets was still open until this work.
data.name: Cyber benchmarks grade crashes, not hacks, so their headline success rates are artifacts

data.brief: The credential-handling pattern (echoing Agent Vault as prior art but extended): the proxy holds all production credentials and injects them at egress, so "the agent doesn't ever actually see secret values" — supporting bearer headers, cookies, Postgres, ClickHouse, OAuth, and AWS SigV4. Runs off the public internet inside Tailscale/WireGuard, with Claw Patrol as the exit node and Tailscale identity gating the dashboard. Convergent with OpenAI's b18 vaults and Anthropic's b19 credential-away-from-model — a third independent lab-adjacent arrival at "the model never sees secrets"
data.name: Credentials injected agent never sees

data.brief: The first field lesson, answering a question customers ask repeatedly — how to stop the agent reading the environment file with the security tokens. Two mechanisms: the brain/hands split already separates the loop from where tools execute, and vaults store credentials so they are "decrypted only when needed at tool execution runtime," so "the model never sees your security tokens." Extended by two enterprise features: self-hosted sandboxes, letting customers run the hands inside their own VPC under their own policies, and MCP tunnels, so MCP servers stay on a private network making only outbound calls to the Claude agent loop
data.name: Credentials kept from the model

data.brief: Rare named enterprise post-training success (the speaker's own framing: "we haven't seen a lot of successes"). Intuit's Credit Karma explains why a card was recommended; prompting works but is not reliably compliant, and the long rule list required to make it compliant "blows up the latency". Fix: curate from the product's own data, tag the form-bearing spans so the fine-tuned model stops hallucinating the over-represented 0%-APR numbers, and post-train. Result: compliance, latency and throughput all improved, and the enterprise owns the model — insulation as frontier models get "more and more expensive".
data.name: Credit Karma post-trained a model to fix compliance without blowing up latency

data.brief: Mechanism behind divergent benchmark results, attributed to Anthropic's published write-ups and other researchers: cross-harness and cross-infrastructure differencing is the primary cause of benchmark performance divergence.
data.description: Named benchmarks — Frontier Code and DeepSWE — are said to carry high false-positive and false-negative rates that are not visible in the headline stats. Structural tell for contrived benchmarks: they test a single isolated in-distribution question and therefore cannot test whether a model sustains correct reasoning across a long dependent episode.
data.name: Cross-harness differencing is the primary cause of benchmark divergence

data.brief: Multilingual result plus a scientific finding. Result: on multilingual MMLU the curated models beat a Pareto frontier of Qwen and Liquid models and Cohere's best multilingual model, coming in slightly better than Qwen 3 at roughly 8x less compute budget — while only 8% of the training data was multilingual, with at most ~6B tokens in any non-English language. Finding: curating the English data alone improves non-English performance, and the size of that transfer is strongly correlated with the language's similarity to English; the reverse also holds (curating non-English helps English) but weaker.
data.description: Framed as an access argument — "I don't want to live in a future where only developed countries can access this very effectively" — because the internet is "an extremely biased view of the world that does not represent the world uniformly at all".
data.name: Curating English data alone improves non-English performance

data.brief: Educator's ground truth on the talent pipeline: a CS degree "used to be the only game in town — a guaranteed job; now, thanks to AI, it's not", and students are being redirected toward agents/AI as the growth path (soft workforce data point).
data.name: A CS degree is no longer a guaranteed job, thanks to AI

data.brief: Against "CUA agents are slow and expensive": a small-footprint CUA model matches Opus 4.7/GPT-5.5 accuracy on browser-use benchmarks (differences "within statistical noise" — the speaker declines to claim the accuracy win) while charging ~$0.80 per task versus ~$2.30 on 20–30-step tasks, with much lower per-step latency. Cost and latency, not capability, presented as the axis where CUA is being won
data.name: Cua cost collapse

data.brief: An infrastructure vendor's diagnosis of why browser agents stalled while coding agents soared: not models — "anything I believed 6 months ago I have to revisit every week" — but missing harness and tools. RL-environment investment shifted from coding to computer use in the last six months and capability followed; the gap between coding and CUA task completion is engineering debt, not model limitation. "Solving overhang is an engineering problem… the wrong answer is to sit around and wait for the models"
data.name: Cua overhang is engineering debt

data.brief: Full-stack product clones have been missing from every long-horizon SWE benchmark because unit tests can pass while the product is unusable and the frontend is broken; SWE-Marathon is (per the talk) the first benchmark to verify these with a computer-use agent driving the submitted app through its UI against a rubric
data.name: First benchmark verifying full-stack clones with a computer-use agent

data.brief: Quantified curation-only result on vision-language models, with everything but the data held constant. Curating Mammoth (~25B tokens, the set used to train the fusion adapter between the text and vision towers) produced a +14 absolute percentage-point improvement over the same pipeline on the uncurated input. Against a Pareto frontier defined by the best public VLMs (Qwen 3 series, Qwen 3.5, InternVL), the curated models sit well beyond it — with no post-training at all — and roughly match Qwen 3.5 4B within about a percentage point while using 145x less training compute.
data.description: Second-order result: curation also produced more concise answers (the three curated models are the shortest-response models in the comparison set), so on a flops-per-response axis they beat the frontier again at ~35x fewer flops per correct answer.
data.name: Curation alone pushes VLMs past the public Pareto frontier at 145x less compute

data.brief: Cursor FDEs are deploying long-running cloud agents and Cursor-SDK applications beyond the software development lifecycle — HR, finance, supply chain, e-commerce, call-center ticketing, asset management at retailers and banks — as the "tip of the spear" testing edge use cases before productization
data.name: Cursor FDEs deploy long-running agents beyond the software development lifecycle

data.brief: Cursor, an application-layer company, has scaled to frontier-scale model training in ~12 months: Composer 2.5 (May 2026) is now the most popular model in Cursor, and the next version is a full from-scratch pre-train replacing the Kimi open-source base — an app company betting its product on owning every layer of training
data.name: Cursor, an app-layer company, scaled to frontier-scale model training in ~12 months

data.brief: Cursor announced (March 2026) a partnership with SpaceXAI for training compute — full-stack from product down to Colossus datacenters (100k GPUs stood up in 122 days, +100k in 92) and Terafab in-house chips — to run multiple large training runs simultaneously
data.name: Cursor partners with SpaceXAI for training compute: Colossus datacenters and Terafab chips

data.brief: The economics of cyber are shifting dramatically: frontier models find primitives and zero-day exploits at scale, so a skilled attacker can now choose many targets at once; defensive systems must operate at scale with very limited human intervention, so defenders are bound by out-of-the-box model capability — the 20-year cyber stack was built on the opposite assumption (attackers must pick targets, defenders react)
data.name: Cyber economics shift: AI finds zero-days at scale; defense must run at model speed

data.brief: Commercial supply of RL environments as a business: benchmarks are used to locate where frontier models stop, then environments are built to push them past it — "up to 10,000 reinforcement learning environments per month" delivered to model companies, sourced from a decade-old DARPA-derived vulnerability-mining pipeline that produces genuine zero-days precisely so the models cannot be memorizing. Held deliberately pattern-less.
data.name: Up to 10,000 zero-day RL environments a month sold to model companies

data.brief: UK AI Security Institute's cyber version of the METR time-horizon benchmark (reverse engineering, web exploitation tasks) shows the newest frontier models as a step jump above the prior regression line — a discontinuous capability improvement, not trend-following
data.name: UK AISI cyber time-horizon benchmark shows frontier models as a step jump

data.brief: The structural claim: just as code provided a verifiable substrate for complex software tasks that are not inherently verifiable, data analysis may do the same for biology — an executable scaffold that makes scientific capability benchmarkable and trainable. Also the read on why agents work here at all: coding models with (to the speaker's knowledge) no biology post-training already showed early signs of doing real spatial analyses, while frontier models still "cannot be trusted to do real work" because the missing capability sits between knowing biology and writing code — extracting scientific insight from real measurement data.
data.name: Data analysis may be for biology what code was for software: a verifiable substrate

data.brief: Market-direction claim delivered as insider information: successful data companies are all pivoting to enterprise, and an incredibly large amount of their revenues are enterprise now, in ways you wouldn't expect a data business to do — because durable value accrues to the services and app layer of actual work, so data businesses do not stay data businesses, they have to be neo labs.
data.description: Once enterprises stop renting intelligence from labs and start owning it, an abstraction layer that does not yet exist is required, of which he names three pieces: (1) serve and route small models against cost, latency and performance profiles; (2) manage RL datasets across base-model migration, so swapping to a new open-source base re-runs post-training automatically instead of starting over; (3) Antikythera mechanisms translating business context into evals. He closes by announcing his own company doing (1)-(3) plus RL-as-a-service for enterprises.
data.name: Successful data companies are pivoting to enterprise and becoming neo labs

data.brief: A from-scratch image-model team's core claim: architecture is commodity, data curation determines quality — "data is everything," and for Krea the goal was preserving stylistic diversity rather than optimizing standard aesthetic scores that mode-collapse. Frontier consistency comes from mode collapse (the boring average, center-framed); Krea traded that for faster, knob-driven exploration. The b15 data-quality-as-compute-multiplier thesis, independently restated in generative media
data.name: Data curation determines image quality

data.brief: Vendor's market read, stated as a layered diagram: compute is "kind of well defined", good open base models exist, and post-training infrastructure is well served (Fireworks, Tinker, slime are named). The one under-supplied input is high-quality data and RL environments — and the claim is that this binds for frontier labs as much as for enterprises: "this also applies to frontier labs where they have all this infra setup and they are needing good quality RL environments". Environments are explicitly classed as data: "RL environments are also something I'm calling data, it's just the data is now in a very different shape".
data.name: Compute, base models and training infra are solved; data and environments are not

data.brief: Market-structure claim with sizing: the annotation layer everyone pictures (rooms of annotators labeling images, Scale circa 2019) is worth roughly $10-15B/year per lab and is the least interesting part; the scarce, badly priced supply is the data that takes a model from generalist competence to real expertise.
data.description: Two years ago vertically integrated giants — Mercor, Surge, Scale AI — had to do every step because that was the only way the unit economics worked in an immature market; today specialists outcompete them at each step (sourcing people, building environments, designing rewards, running evals) and the fragmentation is pretty permanent, not transitional. Because quality does not scale linearly with quantity, labs now mandate vendor diversification across 20-30 vendors — an explicit institutional admission that no single supplier's quality survives scaling.
data.name: The expert-data market is permanently unbundling into four specialist steps

data.brief: Datadog acquired Lin's AI SOC auto-triage startup in early 2026 (startup name garbled in captions); she now leads "self-evolving agent" development at Datadog — consolidation of agent-triage/verification tooling into observability platforms
data.name: Datadog acquired Lin's AI SOC auto-triage startup in early 2026

data.brief: Datadog experiment: 93 real security alerts run 3× through an LLM triage agent — ~25% flip-flopped their malicious/benign verdict across runs; adding episodic memory locked down ~15 points of that, leaving ~10% for human review plus semantic-knowledge disambiguation
data.name: Datadog: ~25% of LLM triage verdicts flip-flopped across repeated runs

data.brief: December 2025 named as the moment AI engineering "broke its own trendline": METR data shows models for the first time completing tasks that take engineers 16+ hours, and the curve has kept climbing since; swyx is collecting the evidence for that single moment at wtfhappened2025.com
data.name: December 2025 named the moment AI engineering broke its own trendline

data.brief: Stated as the talk's most important point ("so important I wish I had a slide for it"): at Decagon forward deployed engineering is identical to product engineering — same hiring bar, same reporting structure, often the same team, reflected in the org chart. Rationale: when a Fortune 20 customer expresses a pain point in a call, that is a product feature that has to be built and prioritized, so the delineation between "forward deployed person" and "person who works on the product" is "gone". Independent corroboration of the Sierra observation that the lines are blurring, from a vendor that has already restructured around it.
data.name: At Decagon, forward deployed engineering is identical to product engineering

data.brief: Org-scaling data point with dates: 50 to 500 people in a year (and not slowing) forced the generalist agent-software-engineer role to split into two specialized lanes — agent builder (configures the agent brain in the UI: tonality, literal voice, user intents to hand off to a human, back-end actions like password resets) and agent software engineer (upstreams customer asks into the platform) — plus vertical expert staffing so knowledge compounds across logos in a vertical and every deployment is faster than the last.
data.name: 50 to 500 people in a year split the generalist FDE role into two specialized lanes

data.brief: Guardrails and the gateway itself are dependencies that fail: choose fail-open vs fail-closed per guardrail by the worst case you can live with, budget guardrail time so the LLM is the rate-determining step, segregate keys per route, shed load under retry storms — and reconsider the company-wide central gateway: what teams want is centralized governance (cost tracking, rate limits) over decentralized traffic, one team but not one deployment
data.name: Decentralize the gateway centralize governance

data.brief: Governance for organizations that may have millions of agent members: any member proposes a policy, members trade pass/fail tokens, and reward-seeking LLM agents converge on better decisions than persuasion produces. A market mechanism, not a vote, as the org's judgement layer
data.name: Decision markets govern agent organizations

data.brief: With code taking one to two months instead of 9–12, the two months to decide to build a product and the two months of launch reviews and approvals are now the long pole; frontier engineering teams inside Amazon "spend more time making decisions than writing code." The prescription is fast, reversible decisions — judgement and governance processes, not generation, set the pace
data.name: Decision speed is the new bottleneck

data.brief: Three ways to render generated UI, ordered by control: controlled (agent picks a finished component — ChatGPT's restaurant card), declarative (A2UI, JSON Render, OpenUI — a catalog-validated UI spec rendered natively, design-system compliant, copy under control), open-ended (LLM-written HTML in a sandboxed iframe — "good luck"). commercetools chose declarative; the catalog became the contract between agent and UI
data.name: Declarative ui protocols are the middle path

data.brief: System progression V1→V2: the deep research loop was retargeted from the public web (which required manually handpicked "golden links" and produced generic results) to the second brain, which supplies golden links organically because its contents are already filtered by the owner; V1 (web-only) still generated 35 course lessons "really quick", but the inward-aimed version anchors research in personal notes, values, and prior work
data.name: Deep research retargeted from the public web to the second brain

data.brief: Third failure account, on the Laguna S run: adding FP8 training on DeepSeek's open-source DeepGEMM FP8 kernels introduced a race condition, visible as illegal memory accesses and NaNs in the gradients, and — the unobservable part — roughly 0.5% of gradient values silently replaced with random values.
data.description: poolside traced it back to the kernels and has a fix in a public PR that is not yet merged upstream. The finding doubles as the limit case for their own defence: replica hashing cannot catch it, because real runs carry no two replicas holding the same weights and the same data, so forward/backward equivalence is never checkable; a dry-run hash checker is in progress.
data.name: A DeepGEMM FP8 race condition silently randomized ~0.5% of gradients

data.brief: Schillings' team is actively working on the "grail": instead of detect-then-patch, teach models to write correct/secure code from the start (very hard, deeply context-dependent) — plus teaching models correct planning/problem decomposition ("inductive architecture") for 35-million-line-codebase-scale engineering, where the frontier still moves
data.name: DeepMind targets correct-by-construction code over detect-then-patch

data.brief: Google DeepMind now keeps evals alongside every internal skill and gates changes on them: any diff to a skill file triggers the eval run, and the change does not merge unless it improves (or extends) the test cases — skills regression-tested exactly like code
data.name: DeepMind gates every internal skill change on its eval run

data.brief: Construction numbers for a contamination-resistant benchmark: 113 original software-engineering tasks across 91 repositories (median 1 task per repository, vs SWE-bench Pro's thousands of tasks drawn from only ~40 repos); languages TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go with more planned; repository criteria >500 GitHub stars, actively contributed, and SME-validated as real-world representative.
data.description: Prompts are deliberately half the length of SWE-bench Pro's (>4,500 characters average) and stated at objective level rather than as a to-do list — yet the tasks stay long-horizon: average solution is 5x the lines of code, touches ~7 files, and emits 2x the output tokens per rollout.
data.name: DeepSWE: 113 authored tasks across 91 repos with half-length prompts

data.brief: DeepSWE leaderboard as of 2026-07-01: unlike SWE-bench Pro — where top models cluster with overlapping confidence intervals and can't be told apart — DeepSWE shows a clear gap between the leaders and 10th place (Gemini 3.1 Pro), and separates models within the Claude and GPT families. Fable 5 holds the top spot.
data.description: The public leaderboard also reports token efficiency, cost, token usage, context window and peak context alongside score. Adoption evidence: DeepSWE replaced SWE-bench Pro in the Artificial Analysis coding-agent index, and multiple frontier labs cite it and work with Datacurve to track their models on it.
data.name: DeepSWE separates frontier models where SWE-bench Pro clusters them

data.brief: DeepSWE v1.1 shipped explicitly as anti-reward-hacking maintenance: the verifier runtime is now fully separated from the agent runtime, test reports are emitted in a standardized format, and all git refs and commits except the agent's base commit are trimmed — closing the git-history channel measured in sig-git-log-golden-patch-rates.
data.description: Stated open work: harness-comparison benchmarks, task-mix gaps (long-horizon focus under-represents bug localization and refactoring), a wider repository pool, and hybrid verification (LLM-as-judge alongside deterministic verifiers) so prompts can drop the residual methodology hints that currently steer agents.
data.name: DeepSWE v1.1 separates verifier runtime and trims git refs as anti-cheat hardening

data.brief: AWS developer-advocate field observation: default agent-loop behavior silently multiplies token spend — the full conversation history is resent on every turn ("hundreds if not thousands of tokens"), large tool results are re-injected into context on every loop iteration, and uncapped tool loops run 10–20 times or go infinite; none of it is visible without pre-deploy observability of per-tool call counts and durations
data.name: Default agent-loop behavior silently multiplies token spend

data.brief: GitHub ships delegation as product: /delegate from Copilot CLI hands the session to GitHub (job + draft PR from sandboxed agents), and the GitHub UI assigns issues to the agent — "delegate, delegate, delegate, and go have a coffee"; whole product backlogs fanned out with draft PRs as the human review/merge gate
data.name: GitHub ships delegation as product with draft PRs as the review gate

data.brief: Organization distortion as an AI-native failure mode: as signal travels through layers of management, legal and sales it gets rewound toward the average at every handoff — the founder sweats the un-averageable details because the outcome is theirs, others "ship it to spec, close Jira tickets." A long delegation chain plus a convergence machine is a factory for automating the signal out of the company. The wrong fix is more process; the right fix is a thin signal layer that validates and carries the original intent across handoffs intact
data.name: Delegation chain automates the signal out

data.brief: Demand-side evidence predates AI by decades: enterprise professional services / forward-deployed engineers as an entire industry line item, engineers hand-rebuilding dotfiles on every machine, Excel as millions of people's personal programs, algorithmic feeds beating one-size-fits-all content on every metric — plus feature flags, segmentation, and A/B testing as pre-agent attempts at divergence, forced into pre-declared buckets. Demand was never the constraint; production cost was
data.name: Demand for personal software predates AI by decades; cost was the constraint

data.brief: Businesses report engineers no longer bring PowerPoints — they bring working demos; the MVP has become cheaper to produce than the slide deck about it
data.name: Engineers bring working demos instead of PowerPoints

data.brief: Capability density is compounding on a ~3.5-month doubling cadence ("densing law", Nature Machine Intelligence): Qwen 3.6 27B dense now beats Llama 3 405B (summer 2024 → March 2026, ~21 months) and even Qwen 3.5's ~397B MoE at ~15× its size with only ~40% more activated parameters — driven by research and compounding architecture gains, not chance
data.name: LLM capability density is doubling on a ~3.5-month cadence

data.brief: A routine dependency-bump PR from the agent changed ~70,000 lines — an attack/review surface far beyond human verification, produced by "just bumping a couple of dependencies"
data.name: A routine agent dependency-bump PR changed ~70,000 lines, beyond human verification

data.brief: Factory's positional claim: it explicitly refuses professional-services work — asked to run a codebase modernization the customer has already price-quoted from consulting firms, the answer is no, even when the work would use Factory's own product, because it does not make the product better and "is not the way you scale a business out enormously".
data.description: Deployed engineers are instead "the tip of the spear of the product": the information stream from the largest, most critical customers' engineering leadership and on-the-ground engineers, flowing back to rapidly adjust the product to fit the customer's environment. The product must then self-assemble — at 45,000 people, hundreds of thousands of engineers and tens of thousands of codebases, manual installation is not available.
data.name: Factory refuses professional services: deployed engineers are the tip of the product spear

data.brief: The market read behind the research: models have breadth no human can match and none of the depth a specialist accumulates, and the three visible symptoms are the training cutoff, thin long-tail skills like AMD kernel authoring, and the total absence of personal or company knowledge. The Terence Tao exhibit sharpens it — the world's most famous mathematician values AI for cross-literature connections while noting it lacks a graduate student's five-year intuition. Depth, not breadth, is framed as the unclaimed axis
data.name: Depth is the unclaimed capability

data.brief: FDE defined as the early-startup design partnership ("give me your context, I'll build you a really good solution" — how most B2B startups find PMF) scaled up into the enterprise, with one non-negotiable condition: if each FDE builds from scratch you do not have an FDE function, you have a dev shop. The differentiator is building on top of a platform of shared primitives.
data.name: FDE is design partnership at enterprise scale, built on shared platform primitives

data.brief: A product designer who had never shipped work code built a design-system status tracker solo as a full proof of concept in ~2.5 weeks — live component previews, ingesting GitHub/Storybook/Figma links, sorted/tagged/searchable — after an engineer questioned whether it was even buildable; then deployed it as an internal tool plus a curated public-facing site. "I moved from a designer to a design engineer" — pushing code to production in a large established system
data.name: A product designer shipped a production internal tool solo in ~2.5 weeks

data.brief: Two designers went zero-to-working iOS chat proof of concept for WooCommerce merchants in 6 days — wordpress.com auth, Jetpack connection, a widget inheriting site theming, and a site-scanning AI answer agent that discerns when it can't answer — using a shared Claude Code project folder (all chats/ideas recorded to the file system) as the collaboration substrate; alignment was easy because both think user-first
data.name: Two designers built a working iOS chat proof of concept in 6 days

data.brief: Deterministic, idempotent document-structure graphs (containment tree + next-section + named links, hierarchical URIs) as the lightweight on-ramp vs LLM entity-extraction GraphRAG: no LLM at ingest, faster, stable across reruns, whole-graph rebuild safe; LLM extraction reserved for messy or domain-ontology-heavy corpora (e.g. life sciences).
data.name: Deterministic document-structure graphs as the lightweight GraphRAG on-ramp

data.brief: Pinterest trialed LangGraph's deterministic workflow mode to make Medic more predictable and found it brittle compared to the reasoning-and-acting agent paradigm — a practitioner datapoint against hard-coding agent control flow for diagnostic work
data.name: Pinterest found LangGraph's deterministic workflow mode brittle vs ReAct agents

data.brief: Vendor-side diagnosis of the demo-to-production gap: demos are trivial to ship ("writing code is very easy"), but once promoted to pilots with new customers the agent meets data it has never seen and production bugs arrive by the hour. The four candidate culprits are dismissed in turn as swappable on a schedule — a new model roughly every 3.5 months, new chips roughly yearly, a new framework any day, and the agent loop itself — leaving dev-loop velocity as the thing a team actually controls. Model capability rises exponentially; the developer's daily job is automating their own loop to keep up.
data.name: Dev-loop velocity, not the model, chips or framework, is the binding constraint

data.brief: Show of hands in a capacity AIE room (mid-2026): almost nobody still "codes like they used to" — the audience has shifted to a systems approach; Noring: "you are stuck with an AI tool — there's no longer an option not to use one"; devs still write code but are "very precious" about what they write by hand
data.name: Almost nobody in a capacity AIE room still codes like they used to

data.brief: Peer-reviewed (IJCNN, open-source) result: an SAE trained on activation *differences* isolates the backdoor as one feature at 0.4 backdoor-isolation score vs ~0.01 for crosscoders/joint features (≈40×, confidence intervals not touching), with precision 1.0 and zero false positives (recall ~25% per feature — ensemble for coverage); layer-independent across four middle layers, holds under both LoRA and full-rank, and a 4× SAE matches a 32× one — cheap enough to run on every build (demonstrated on SmolLM2-360M)
data.name: Diff-SAE isolates backdoors ~40x better than crosscoders with zero false positives

data.brief: Sky Valley/Differ's product bet: instead of one codebase gated by flags and shipped to everyone, one canonical stem with every user running her own live-adapted divergence — "from the least-worst version for everyone to the best version for anyone." Example: a CRM that observes an investor's usage (intro paths, skipped fields, deal-checking habits) and reshapes itself, or implements user-requested changes within developer-set boundaries without going back to the developer — letting horizontal SaaS address far more personas without increasing R&D spend
data.name: Sky Valley's bet: one stem, every user runs a live-adapted divergence

data.brief: The convergence signal: diffusion training now mirrors the LLM recipe — pre/mid-training, SFT, preference optimization, GRPO with reward servers, a prompt-expander LLM, and multi-expert on-policy distillation — deliberately "stealing from LLM research to reuse kernels and literature." The post-training methods coined for language (b5/b19 OPSD) crossing into image generation, with image generation framed as a proxy for VLM progress
data.name: Diffusion adopts llm post training

data.brief: The scalable-curation method: use a large VLM to make a filtering judgement, then distill it into a SigLip-sized classifier cheap enough to run over a billion+ images (paralleling the essential-web-data text approach), plus SAE-based unsupervised tagging — ~30–40 in-house classifiers total. Data infrastructure, not model architecture, as where the differentiated work lives
data.name: Distill big vlm to cheap filter

data.brief: The methodological stance, offered as a standing frustration with the field: "a lot of distillation work is done assuming you have some kind of golden answer that you can distil into the model, and this is often not the case." Applied Compute's whole taxonomy is built to work without a golden rubric per task — behavioural priors and rollout-derived hints substitute for ground truth. Paired with the infrastructure prediction that closes the loop: "as the infra collapses between serving and training, we're automatically going to raise the ceiling continuously via online distillation"
data.name: Distillation without golden answers

data.brief: Character.AI distilled its committee of experts into a small VLM that scores a 15-second video in ~3 seconds and returns the reason for the score rather than the score alone. A larger model produced better results and was rejected because the added value did not justify the slowness; the team frames the whole build/serve decision as unit economics — the committee of experts would have worked, at one-or-two-video scale, but not at tens of thousands per day.
data.name: Character.AI distills its judge committee into a VLM scoring 15s video in ~3s

data.brief: Evil Martians' PMF-compass data (37 successful devtools analyzed; early-stage client base): 9 of 10 early-stage devtools show product signal stronger than revenue — distribution, not product, is the binding constraint in 2026; "building software has never been easier, which means the bottleneck has moved" (and technical founders hate marketing)
data.name: 9 of 10 early-stage devtools show product signal stronger than revenue

data.brief: The company that solved laptop-to-cloud portability builds a new microVM runtime (spx) for agent safety: credentials injected as stubs the agent can't read, network policy and MCP control, per-task scoped sandboxes (GitHub-only for review, Notion-only for write-up), the same sandbox and policies portable to the cloud, parallel fan-out and scheduled orchestration. A runtime vendor productizing the "model never sees secrets" boundary
data.name: Docker pivots portability to agent safety

data.brief: Form3 ran an agent with host Docker-socket access in production and backed off: privileged-container escape makes it "game over" (env vars, process memory, SSH keys); the built-in sandboxes of Codex/Claude-class agents can't contain a Docker socket, and Linux sandbox primitives don't compose with containers
data.name: Form3 backed off host Docker-socket agent access: container escape is game over

data.brief: The mechanism: make the doc, not the chat, the atom of work. Chats are isolated, ephemeral and "brain off" (the agent proposes, you hit the recommended option without thinking); decisions made there vanish into code. Docs bring key decisions forward for the team, and the deeper flip is architectural — pull the state out of the session: doc as state, agent as stateless action, parallel agents spawned from one shared context, agent bankruptcy dissolved ("the result of their work is in the doc — to rebuild your human context, you just read the doc"), and a durable decision log with no LLM-summarization lottery. HELD PATTERN-LESS — bears on the uncoined pat-agent-memory-layer and pat-durable-execution candidates, on the *convention* side: the state layer here is a shared document, not a memory product (see review note 4)
data.name: Docs replace chats as work atom

data.brief: Traffic to documentation websites coming from coding agents jumped from ~10% to ~50% in one year — docs' primary reader is becoming the agent, but docs are still written for humans (intuition, follow-ups, "just Google it")
data.name: Coding-agent share of docs traffic jumped ~10% to ~50% in a year

data.brief: The harness-engineering case restated for browsing, with the coding evidence: Factory outperforming Claude Code *on the same model* with a domain-optimized harness; "Cursor actually started this." The claim is scoped carefully — "it's not clear yet if custom harnesses will beat out durably RL'd models, but we're not debating that today; adding a harness on a model improves results" — and democratized: "you don't have to be a lab to build a good harness"
data.name: Domain harness beats raw model

data.brief: Current agent systems flatten operationally distinct claims — done-to-merge vs done-to-deploy vs done-to-announce — into a single green checkmark; an agent passing tests, updating docs, and commenting "looks done to me" is a producer *claim*, not verification
data.name: Agent systems flatten distinct done-claims into one green checkmark
