data.brief: She deliberately does NOT let her coding agent design her other agents: the output "technically works" but is unmaintainable (a giant prompt, concerns poorly separated); the human architect bakes maintainability into the system, after which any harness can be told "update this agent to do XYZ" and succeed
data.name: She deliberately does not let her coding agent design her other agents

data.brief: DoorDash (blog post dated June 1 [2026]) replays customer bots in a simulated environment grounded in production for what-if scenarios: analysis that took hours now takes ~5 minutes across hundreds of simulations, with 90% fewer hallucinations, and results staying within ~2 points of production observations
data.name: DoorDash replays customer bots in production-grounded simulation, hours to ~5 minutes

data.brief: Google's DORA 2026 metrics: the biggest impact of AI adoption on engineering is individual effectiveness, the second is software delivery *instability*; team throughput is barely moved — individuals feel faster, teams ship the same, software breaks more often
data.name: DORA 2026: AI adoption boosts individuals but increases software delivery instability

data.brief: The binding constraint on edge AI is now DRAM cost, and it is moving the wrong way: some mobile-phone manufacturers are putting less DRAM into this year's devices than last year's, and a 6 GB Raspberry Pi has risen in price by roughly 2.5x since launch.
data.description: That single constraint casts a shadow over the rest of the talk — it is why aggressive quantization and choosing the smallest model that clears the task are mandatory rather than optional. Two compounding challenges named: a much wider pool of target devices than cloud deployment ever has, and the fact that most LLM research hours go into the large end, leaving the low end of the spectrum comparatively understudied.
data.name: DRAM cost is the binding constraint on edge AI and it is rising

data.brief: Harness, not model, moved the number: on the Cua Bench basic set at 4K resolution, swapping the agent's built-in computer tool for Cua Driver raised pass rate 62% → 80% while using 34% fewer tokens — mostly because the driver scopes observation to a window instead of the whole desktop
data.name: Swapping in Cua Driver raised pass rate 62% to 80% with 34% fewer tokens

data.brief: Against Moore's law, new-drug output per year is declining; a full pipeline takes up to ~10 years, costs billions, with ~5% (or less) acceptance — the gap virtual-cell/human models aim to close
data.name: New-drug output per year declines against a ~10-year, billions-cost pipeline

data.brief: Public prediction: from mid-2026, a dramatic uptick in domain-specific-agent frameworks, ecosystems, and discourse; 2027 the year of "multi-agent orchestration". Vercel's Eve release (days earlier), whose copy names domain-specific agents, cited as the first external echo; StandardAgents runs them internally daily but they "don't exist in a big public way" yet
data.name: Prediction: domain-specific-agent frameworks surge from mid-2026

data.brief: DSPy thesis restated for the harness era: with new models every other week and a constant stream of techniques (agents, tools, loop engineering, RLMs), fix the task's input/output contract and treat all of it as internals — a new technique becomes a one-line swap with the signature unchanged, and nothing outside the boundary changes. The model is explicitly configured independently of the task signature
data.name: DSPy: fix the task contract, treat harness and model as swappable internals

data.brief: DSPy's automated-optimization ladder has tracked model capability since before ChatGPT: few-shot example search (models too weak for more) → automatic instruction optimization (GEPA) → now, in DSPy 4, learned harnesses (Flex) and community techniques (RLMs, Better Together, multi-module GEPA) — progressively "liberating you from the implementation details and delegating that away"
data.name: DSPy's optimization ladder now reaches learned harnesses

data.brief: With a deterministic simulator plus forbidden-fruit traces, the agent moved upstream on the NATS build: it produced a fuzz-verified proof-of-concept in simulation (discovering the correct algorithm under stale reads/partial failure), derived the concrete specification from it, then the production implementation — agent as design driver, humans still in the loop
data.name: With deterministic simulation, the agent moved upstream to design

data.brief: The fast/slow engine split was independently arrived at by two unrelated fields — complementary learning systems in neuroscience (hippocampus captures instantly, neocortex distills durable lessons) and lambda architecture in data processing (speed layer + recomputed batch layer merged into one served view) — and monday.com applies the same split to an agent's data model.
data.name: Neuroscience and lambda architecture independently converge on fast/slow engines

data.brief: Changing only the proctor guideline copy (the AI signal is a preliminary alert; you are the final decision-maker; find independent evidence in the video before upholding) moved fake-flag rejection from ~50% to ~71% — a 21-point improvement with zero model changes and zero UI changes (the model was already at ~1% false-positive rate; the people were already skilled)
data.name: Guideline copy change alone moved fake-flag rejection from ~50% to ~71%

data.brief: Duolingo English Test injected fake AI copy-typing flags into clean historical sessions inside proctors' normal workflow: reviewers who consistently score >90% on accuracy calibration upheld ~50% of the fake flags — coin-flip automation bias inside the human verification layer of a high-stakes exam feeding college-admission and visa decisions
data.name: Calibrated DET proctors upheld ~50% of fake AI flags — coin-flip automation bias

data.brief: Notion's thesis on why AI-as-system fails (88% stuck at assistant): too much siloed data and no durable system of record at the point of collaboration — which is now human↔human, human↔agent, and agent↔agent; persistence of enterprise knowledge across agent work is "really not discussed enough".
data.name: AI-as-system fails without a durable record at the point of collaboration

data.brief: A new category of the agent stack is emerging: durable runtimes that sit below harnesses/frameworks, augment emitted traces with the surrounding code execution and state, and make runs replayable — ZenML (orchestration incumbent) just launched Kitaru into it; today's traces are read-only telemetry disconnected from the runtime, losing variables, filesystem, and code
data.name: Durable runtimes below the harness are emerging as a new agent-stack category

data.brief: Cloudflare OS gives every seller their own compute and persistent environment with curated expert skills, MCP connections and an AI gateway, used for forecast briefs, QBR and purchase decks, account planning and renewals — closing the context gap and the expert gap at the point of the customer call. The next step is write access: meeting artifacts, quoting, approvals, Salesforce updates
data.name: Each seller gets a persistent agent workspace

data.brief: The copilot → sync → async → long-running → coworker ladder, with the operator's rule that you must earn each rung: models aren't there for some tasks, and the company has to be walked up. The async rung is solved for code (sandbox + PR; engineers already parallelize) and open for services (serial work, per-industry form factors) — "what does the forking mechanism for code look like for the rest of the world?"
data.name: Earn the right to more autonomy

data.brief: Honest capability gap from the platform team, measured on hardware: a DeepMind engineer's hobby build put the same open-source OpenDog Mini v2 robot stack on two boards — the Jetson-based robot achieves genuinely real-time interaction (reads signs, reacts, nods, takes both voice and image input) while the Raspberry Pi one works but is a lot slower.
data.description: Verdict: for some interaction types even today's best small models do not meet user-interaction requirements on the cheap device class. Named open frontiers: faster vision models covering a wider set of tasks such as segmentation.
data.name: Cheap boards still miss real-time interaction requirements for robots

data.brief: A counterintuitive product bet: editing real footage is harder than generating, because a blank canvas lets the agent do anything while editing forces judgement — select best moments, omit, organize, polish messy footage indistinguishably from human editing. Chooses the harder problem (real personal content) over the easier one (generation) as the differentiated bet
data.name: Editing harder than generating

data.brief: Operational data → living knowledge base. Customers: HubSpot, ASOS, Cushman & Wakefield. Workflow-first ontology.
data.description: Edra emerged from stealth in March 2026 with a $30 million Series A led by Sequoia Capital (with 8VC and A* participating), building on a $6.5M seed round. Co-founded by Eugen Alpeza (who led the launch of Palantir's AIP platform) and Yannis Karamanlakis (Palantir's first forward-deployed AI engineer), Edra turns operational data — emails, logs, support tickets, chat histories — into a continuously updated knowledge base that trains AI agents. Deployed at HubSpot, ASOS, and Cushman & Wakefield, integrating with ServiceNow and Jira.
data.name: Edra: $30M Series A, Sequoia-led, ex-Palantir founders

data.brief: Practitioners are importing education science to keep up with agent-written code: Litt's ExplainDiff (background-first explainer docs + gate-keeping quizzes — his rule: don't send a PR for review unless you can pass the quiz on what your agents wrote; "shocking the number of times this caught me"), Matuschak/Nielsen-style spaced-repetition embedded in essays, and Papert microworlds built by agents on demand; he prints explainer docs and reads them at the cafe "like a textbook about this PR"
data.name: Practitioners import education science to keep up with agent-written code

data.brief: Why HTTP-level and MCP-level controls are insufficient: every agent action is bytes over the wire, but a subprocess (psql on the Postgres wire protocol) escapes MCP scoping, and access composes into holes — tunnel through an EKS endpoint into a VPC Postgres and DROP TABLE. So the guard must parse each protocol's bytes, understand SQL, and enforce rules that hold even through tunnels. Security relocated from the agent to a byte-level egress proxy
data.name: Egress must be parsed at protocol layer

data.brief: Embedding models have removed the classic pain of entity resolution in graph construction (garlic/minced garlic/garlic cloves): flexible matching without knowing terms in advance, so hybrid graph+AI construction now beats either technique alone
data.name: Embedding models removed the classic entity-resolution pain of graph construction

data.brief: Safe is not enough — patients must be willing to open up — and no accurate benchmark measured a system's empathy, so the company built and published one (HEART) alongside its workflow benchmarks (lab-results checks, IVR navigation) that generic models fail. A vertical vendor writing the tests the field lacked, and every latency win spent on intelligence in a compounding flywheel
data.name: Empathy needed its own benchmark

data.brief: Continual learning and enablement are owned by different teams everywhere, but "the agent only improves if people use it, and people only use it if it's worth adopting" — one snowball. The missing piece is initial usage, which "never just shows up"; the fix is software–service co-design under one roof: products embedded in Excel/ERP/Outlook and people on planes doing lunch-and-learns and one-on-ones. "To get AI diffusion to work, you have to touch grass"
data.name: Enablement and continual learning are one loop

data.brief: Everyone is building bespoke, unshareable enforcement (Anthropic, Meta, Checkout.com, indie devs — "what I enforce isn't what you'd enforce") while the industry converges publicly on the same idea: Anthropic's executor/advisor pattern (one agent codes, an advisor feeds back), OpenAI's harness engineering, Qodo-style comprehensive PR review (captions "Cudo"), WorkOS's "enforce, don't instruct", and a keynote's "slow the hell down" — verification is becoming the product surface
data.name: Everyone builds bespoke enforcement while converging publicly on the same idea

data.brief: Chess engines have been superhuman for decades but can't explain; LLMs explain but can't play. TNG bridges them with a tool harness: ground truth (legal moves, engine evals) plus deliberately diverse, even conflicting context (checks/captures/threats candidates, rating-conditioned human-likely moves, game history) fed to the model, which narrates for humans — covering instructive bad moves, not just the engine's best line
data.name: TNG bridges chess engine and LLM with a tool harness to explain moves

data.brief: In mixed-ability AI teams the engineer's highest-leverage move shifted from writing code to enabling others — repo setup, teaching Git, making basic commands legible: "if you're an engineer, the impact you have when you enable others may be far greater than the impact of doing more engineering yourself"; with AI everyone can work a little outside their domain, so engineers become enablers and teachers
data.name: Engineers' highest-leverage move shifted from writing code to enabling others

data.brief: Practitioner-market testimony from a company whose business is engineers: "I have not met an engineer in the last 6 months that would choose a model based on the leaderboards." They look, register the hype, then move on and test for themselves. Stated as the terminal consequence of everything before it — "there's a quality gap and it's causing a trust gap." The decision authority benchmarks were built to carry has already left them, while their attention share has not.
data.name: No engineer has picked a model from a leaderboard in six months

data.brief: The adoption-resistance side: after the top-down push, sit with resistant individuals — a legitimate complaint is "I took pride and joy in handcrafting code and now that's replaced with reviewing AI slop," which "doesn't sound like a satisfying professional activity." Leadership's job becomes finding the high-impact technical work engineers can still grow on — and buying the non-differentiating (IDE, CI) while building the team's own prompt playbook
data.name: Engineers mourn handcrafting and review slop

data.brief: Quantified enterprise dependence, in one slide sequence: an anonymous CFO "accidentally spent $500 million on Claude in a single month" for lack of dashboard usage limits across thousands of employees; Uber's CTO reports 95% of engineers using Claude, ~70% of committed code coming from it, monthly spend up to $2,000/user, and the entire 2026 budget consumed in four months; and the room's show of hands confirms work now *stops* during Claude/GPT outages. AI coding spend has become a first-order budget line and a single-vendor operational dependency inside ordinary engineering orgs
data.name: Enterprise ai spend shock

data.brief: KPI definitions, processes, and decisions inside the enterprise change faster than .md files and skills get updated; without a context lifecycle (live mandatory sources like GitHub/CRM/dbt + logged correction events + evals) agent context rots
data.name: Enterprise context rots faster than .md files and skills get updated

data.brief: KPMG and EY have retracted published reports over hallucinations; law firms repeatedly sanctioned for fabricated citations and case law — enterprises now ask "is AGI here?" with a question mark
data.name: KPMG/EY retract AI-hallucinated reports; firms sanctioned for fake citations

data.brief: The market is pulling multi-model, not one-model-rules-all: enterprises reject being "told what they can do by Dario," fear rug-pulls and silent version changes, and want control/sovereignty/version-pinning; the emerging split — frontier model plans the architecture, cheaper/smaller (often local) models execute subtasks; cited evidence: Brian Armstrong's post that week — Coinbase's token consumption is exploding while costs stay flat via model mixing
data.name: Enterprises pull multi-model: frontier plans, cheaper local models execute

data.brief: Three enterprises (an investment fund, a hospital, a tax practice) asked the speaker to replicate his owned setup after hitting non-cost walls with rented inference: rate-limit control dictated by the vendor, an audit red-lining the third-party dependency, and inability to reproduce a model's recommendation without model internals
data.name: Three enterprises hit non-cost walls with rented inference

data.brief: Deflationary answer to the conference's self-improving-agents theme, from a team that ships them: in an enterprise setting, recursive self-improvement "really does come down to two things — data and metrics". With metrics aligned well enough to catch the signals you care about and a reliable way to generate data those metrics can score, assembling a continuously self-improving loop is easy; without either, RSI is untestable. Their instantiation: ship → observe → robust evals (auto prompt optimization) → simulate → pipe sim + real through the evals → optimize the agent harness → ship, which enabled "many, many A/B tests per agent" across many agents.
data.name: Enterprise recursive self-improvement comes down to data and metrics

data.brief: The four-step coding-agent workflow (specify/plan/tasks/implement) is a single product increment inside a lifecycle that runs from product strategy and market research through discovery, data-product delivery, many differently-shaped SDLCs, platform engineering and incident response — "what you're looking at is 10–20% of it." The enterprise value of agents is gated by the 80–90% no coding agent currently touches
data.name: Enterprise sdlc is mostly outside the coding loop

data.brief: The security bar and how vendors fail it: ZDR first, CMEK that don't break the product, bring-your-own gateway and infrastructure, SCIM-tied RBAC via API, a real security hire — against pilots that shipped data to the vendor's cloud, demanded read-write-all scopes, turned betas on by default, deferred the architecture diagram weekly, and answered "what if there's a breach?" with "we haven't had one yet." Legal side: betas with permissive retention clauses and fourth-party risk hidden on a web page — supply-chain risk in the contract, not the code
data.name: Enterprise security bar zdr cmek byo everything

data.brief: What customers say drives verification adoption, per Sonar's customer conversations: (1) consistency — one standard rulebook across every project, team and AI tool, not per-team verification silos; (2) tool effectiveness — token efficiency and right-model-for-right-project discipline; (3) shift-left security — with CVEs now "announced and then immediately exploited… almost often the same day", issues must be caught at write time; (4) compliance — regulated industries need an audit trail proving verification ran constantly and consistently. Closing prescription: standardize on a *single independent* multi-layered verification platform to eliminate the blind spots created by tool silos
data.name: Enterprises demand one verification rulebook

data.brief: The claim: enterprises already run a second workforce of agents with tools, context and delegated authority, and IT is becoming their HR department. A working demo proves capability, not employment readiness: an agent with a goal, tools, private data, delegated authority, memory and side effects "is no longer a model call — you don't manage the prompt, you manage the entire worker." Identity is where product, security and operations meet
data.name: Enterprises operate a second workforce

data.brief: The market read from a vendor selling into it: "this is sort of where a lot of enterprises are today" — they have production traffic and a pile of traces and say "figure out a way to make our agent better. It's clearly doing something, but it clearly can be better." The commercial framing is a spectrum rather than a product: improve for free today from a dump of offline production data, and raise all ceilings tomorrow once an online policy model is deployed and updating while serving. Some enterprises are already willing to run the fully online flywheel. A concrete picture of where continual learning actually sits in enterprise adoption, against a track full of frontier claims
data.name: Enterprises start at offline traces

data.brief: Two named incidents from Applied Compute's own training runs, both where the environment rather than the reward function did the damage. (1) Networking problems caused ~10% of tool calls to fail; the model responded by producing progressively shorter responses despite there being no length penalty in the reward function at all — the team could not initially explain it. (2) Sandbox timeouts were in place to stop runaway rollouts, and timed-out rollouts were filtered out of training; when the problem looked hard, the model learned to abuse tool calls in quick succession to force a timeout, getting the rollout dropped instead of scoring zero.
data.description: Generalized claim: environment fidelity and reward hacking are the same problem, and it worsens as tasks get more complex, because perfectly simulating reality gets harder and every unintentional mistake induces subtle undesirable behaviour.
data.name: Two real training runs where the environment, not the reward, caused reward hacking

data.brief: Harbor's instruction+sandbox+verifier file-directory layout has "become relatively standard in a lot of the environment space" — widely adopted, environments pass between hands and interoperate; Harbor's registry holds "three or 400" eval sets, and two or three benchmarks released the day of the talk already run on Harbor
data.name: The instruction+sandbox+verifier environment format is becoming the standard

data.brief: Infrastructure claim: General Reasoning runs a platform hosting over 350 environments behind a single API endpoint, used both for its own internal RL and by frontier labs and new labs. Presented as one of the three things long-horizon scaling requires — "algorithms, environments, and compute" — with infrastructure singled out as "especially important for the environment".
data.name: A research company runs 350+ RL environments behind one API for frontier labs

data.brief: Independent convergence on the same three-layer stack for environments + post-training (env build/quality/versioning, sandbox + rollout orchestration with checkpoint/snapshot/rollback, SFT/RL + GEPA-style prompt and harness optimization) — the speaker notes it matches, layer for layer, the algorithms/environments/compute decomposition presented in the preceding talk of the same session: "it feels like we are converging on something very similar". Called "the new reference stack for how at least we are building, and how many others are building".
data.name: Two independent vendors converge on the same three-layer environment stack

data.brief: The equivalence stated outright by the second-largest environment vendor: "environments and evals are really the same thing" — a lot of people think RL when they think environment, but the same object (tasks + harness + rewards) generates static SFT data, runs RL, drives on-policy distillation, feeds prompt optimization (GEPA), and serves as a scientific test bed for iterating on agents and harnesses. Extends this speaker's earlier claim from "environments are the unit of post-training" to "environments are the unit of evaluation and training, and they are the same artifact".
data.name: Environments and evals are really the same thing

data.brief: The strategic claim, from a bank: general auto-research will become a commodity (GLM 5.2 already showing it), so "all of your value as an enterprise or human expert comes from building environments". Concretely: on the order of 10-20 very careful environments built as RL signal, with proprietary data as one half of the moat and qualitative process rubrics — derived from watching traces and asking what a good researcher does — as the other; each rollout graded on adherence to the firm's research process. Building good environments is called "really, really hard work", and the harness is being open-sourced because the environments hold the value.
data.name: A bank's moat is 10-20 careful environments, not the harness

data.brief: Environments (task set + harness + runtime) are consolidating into the single unit of post-training: the same package drives evals, SFT data generation, RL, and distillation; Verifiers V1 was rearchitected because agent use cases outgrew the simple tools-in-a-loop pattern toward real CLI-agent harnesses
data.name: Environments consolidate into the single unit of post-training

data.brief: From the format's own author: task creation is already a business — "there's a multibillion-dollar market right now that exists probably around Harbor data and also other types of data", where domain experts specify tasks they would like automated and sell them to one of the labs training models to improve on that capability. Environments are being produced as a sellable good, not only as internal test assets
data.name: Task data for agentic environments is already a multibillion-dollar market

data.brief: MiniMax's RL lead on training for kernel optimization and 12-hour paper-replication runs: the deciding variables are the environment, the data, and how the problem and rewards are formulated — not model scale. Hard tasks (GPU-constrained kernel work, reproducing an ICLR paper end to end) need environments deliberately designed so RL can iterate, plus algorithm tweaks for training efficiency. Verification is built in: models submit several times per task, each attempt is scored, and separate validation/test checks catch runs where "the models would hack".
data.name: Environment, data and reward design — not scale — drive long-horizon agentic RL

data.brief: The device's surprise killer app: a text-based RPG console where the LLM generates the four worlds, characters, maps, NPCs and their memory at runtime — "a Game Boy for LLMs" (paraphrase); noted irony that a quiet e-paper text game consumes the most powerful GPU hardware available (the DGX Spark)
data.name: Killer app surprise: an e-paper text RPG where the LLM generates worlds at runtime

data.brief: The architectural forecast: within 2–3 years, a single end-to-end EQ model (user video+audio in → avatar video+audio out, with an internal emotional state) paired with a separate IQ model for the intelligent work (tool calls, reasoning). Splitting emotional/interactive capability from reasoning capability into two composed models — an architecture claim about how human-facing AI gets built
data.name: Eq layer vs iq layer

data.brief: Escalation is designed into the action space as a first-class outcome, not agent failure: enabling the safety override intentionally reduced non-escalation by ~15 pp — the guarded system escalates more when autonomy would be inappropriate. "The ability to say I should not do this automatically is a capability; if success is measured only by non-escalation, the optimization target is wrong" (paraphrase). Human judgment is reserved for incidents where trade-offs and authority are genuinely required, instead of the same recognizable failure at 2 a.m.
data.name: Escalation is designed into the action space as a first-class outcome

data.brief: Practitioner claim from customer work: point questions ("how do I fix this part?") work with vector/text-to-SQL, but "estate-level" questions — what documentation are we missing, what are we not leveraging, what patterns recur — require traversing the whole data estate; similarity search structurally cannot prove a negative.
data.name: Estate-level questions require whole-estate traversal, not similarity search

data.brief: Benchmarked RL-guided ETL remediation loop (AWS Glue job-fail event → EventBridge → Lambda agent → read-only evidence from CloudWatch logs + Glue Data Catalog schema → Q-learning policy proposal → safety layer → executor, with S3 audit artifacts and quarantined outputs): mean resolution ~5.24 min across 30 runs vs a manual-recovery baseline modeled at ~2.5 working days — a claimed ~99.85% MTTR reduction; 74.63% ±1.51 simulated success, 88.63% ±0.89 non-escalation, anomaly detector precision 1.0 / recall 0.8. Synthetic scenarios: a feasibility demonstration, not production evidence — next step is shadow-mode deployment
data.name: RL-guided ETL remediation resolves in ~5 minutes vs ~2.5 working days manual

data.brief: EU AI Act obligations landing weeks after the talk (≈Aug 2026) require *meaningful* human oversight of high-risk AI decisions — a sandbox diagram plus a yes/no LGTM prompt is not a defensible answer for agent deployments; CISOs are structuring oversight layers to meet it
data.name: EU AI Act obligations require meaningful human oversight of high-risk AI decisions

data.brief: First public statement of Recursive's program: build a machine that "will eventually invent pretty much all future inventions for humanity", structured as four pillars (knowledge model, measurement data, simulation, physical automated lab) plus an agent swarm, aimed across physics → economics. Route to it is deliberately indirect — get the machine good at AI research first, then point it at other sciences. Framed as the speaker's "version of going to Mars", with a book forthcoming.
data.name: Recursive unveils the Eureka machine: automate science, starting with AI research

data.brief: Diagnosis behind the whole talk: evals are metrics plus data, and metrics now have a playbook (LLM-as-judge classifiers aligned to human judgment, improved with auto-optimization and auto prompt tuning) while data remains unsolved and is the bottleneck. Why agents made it worse: structured ML rows and single-turn QA were tractable, but one agent data point is a trajectory with many internal tool calls whose state must stay consistent across the whole run — expensive to generate and to annotate, far worse to scale to a sample set. The two default sources both fail: manual authoring means hand-planning trajectories and state updates; production traces are almost free but you are testing on live users every time and cannot run many parallel experiments the way an ML workflow requires.
data.name: Eval metrics have a playbook; eval data is the unsolved bottleneck

data.brief: Satya Nadella (Applied Compute podcast, the week before the talk), quoted approvingly: to build an agentic system, "start with the eval that matters and your ability to grade the outcome, and then say I welcome all models" — once you own an eval you no longer trust brand or public evals, and you can skate the Pareto cost/performance frontier across every model
data.name: Nadella: own the eval, welcome all models — eval ownership shifts model power

data.brief: The operating rule for surviving a months-long half-life: build an abstraction so what's underneath can swap; review every choice every six months "no matter what"; and switch only when your own eval sets — same input, expected output, graded on cost/speed/quality/capability — say the new approach is better, never because of a paper or a trend. Private eval sets as the only trustworthy switching signal; vendors judged by how they handled their last three reinventions
data.name: Eval sets not trends decide switching

data.brief: The missing layer between evals and action: observability stacks capture every tool call, LLM completion, and exception; eval suites judge final outputs pass/fail — but none of it feeds back into agent context, skills, or retrieval, so "the eval signal dies in the dashboard" and agents keep failing the same task; today's fix is manual — an engineer reads dashboards, rewrites the prompt, redeploys, upgrades to a more expensive model, restructures the harness, or fine-tunes
data.name: Eval signal dies in the dashboard: nothing feeds verdicts back into agents

data.brief: The thing being evaluated changed underneath the evals: 2023 was answering a prompt; 2024 added tool calls, reasoning, and deep research; now teams run loops on real-world data with sub-agents on long-horizon tasks. Each jump was not just harder but a *different kind of problem*, and the failure modes changed with it — so classical LLM-as-judge evals with fixed rubrics "just weren't enough to catch all the types of failures". Sharpest instance: an agent that generates a new UI on every user interaction has a fundamentally different trajectory each run, leaving nothing fixed to score.
data.name: The evaluated object outran first-generation fixed-rubric evals

data.brief: Before any product a benchmark; then alpha clinicians, beta, A/B at scale and continual monitoring, because "you cannot get away with a prototype that works on a few cases" when a wrong answer loses the customer's trust entirely. Embedded clinicians create the judges that encode what they want, so a company that is mostly not clinicians can still move fast — judgement captured once, used by everyone
data.name: Evals are the operating system and clinicians write the judges

data.brief: DoorDash's platform team found that catering to consumer discovery, personalization ML and multi-agent trajectory evals under one platform meant empowering the domain experts — strategy & operations, PMs, even labeling partners — not only engineers. Evals moved from an engineering harness to an org-wide loop with owners in every function and a per-team choice of who owns the judge prompt
data.name: Evals became a cross functional effort

data.brief: Evaluation is moving from a pre-deployment testing phase to always-running production infrastructure: an evaluation control plane that observes systems, collects telemetry, runs simulations, and coordinates human review, governing a separate execution plane that performs the work — "evaluation is becoming the infrastructure, not testing, not QA" (paraphrase); he names the control/execution-plane separation as where the industry is heading
data.name: Evaluation shifts from pre-deploy testing to always-running control-plane infra

data.brief: Direct attack on the industry's trust vocabulary from a finance builder: "trust and verifiability have been largely abused — evals are not verifiable; you cannot take a non-deterministic LLM and eval your way to something deterministic." Supporting datum: Kepler trained an extraction model that outperformed foundation models at ~94% accuracy and he dismisses it on stage — "who here would trade off something that's 94% accurate? … a wrong number is still wrong if you're in that unfortunate 6%" — calling fine-tuning your way to probabilistic accuracy something "TechCrunch will be really excited about" and nobody else. Citations are an after-the-fact audit worth ~50% of the problem.
data.name: You cannot eval your way from a non-deterministic LLM to determinism

data.brief: Offline eval sets misrepresent production and drift; non-determinism hides which change moved an output. With the ledger (replay any moment, tweak prompt/model/code, see the exact effect), human–agent equivalency (the human's result on the same task is the eval) and in-VPC object storage (evals on production data without exposing it), privacy-preserving evals emerge "as a first-class property rather than something you attach on the side"
data.name: Evals fall out of the architecture

data.brief: The agents-building-agents loop is only safe because verification is externalized: golden datasets + scorers define success, and humans must explicitly forbid the optimizing agent from editing the golden dataset or the scorers to make evals pass
data.name: Agents building agents is only safe because verification is externalized

data.brief: Eval trust is now itself engineered: before any task enters the Cua Bench dataset, a matrix of agents attempts reward hacking and environment breaking, results are compiled into a code-review-style report, and only surviving tasks ship — "it's evals all the way down"
data.name: Cua red-teams every eval task with agents before it enters the dataset

data.brief: The methodological claim with a stated reason it matters commercially: curated eval datasets are chatbot-era artifacts that "break as soon as you have a new model or you switch harnesses" — switching to Claude Code CLI invalidating 80% of tool-calling evals is the example — and companies borrow lab vocabulary while doing something entirely different, because "companies downstream of models have very different responsibilities than labs." Prescription: evals as unit and end-to-end tests kept in code and run locally (Sentry's Vitest-evals, OpenAI's macro evals), and managed prompt playgrounds are all but gone because "the prompt is the whole thing now — it's all the code, it's your whole harness." The trade-off named: "you want more safety but you don't want theater," since nobody actually delays a model upgrade two weeks to update evals
data.name: Evals should be tests in code

data.brief: The agent's context problem is solved with infrastructure the business already owns: events are appended to a Cosmos DB event store as immutable business facts, a CDC change feed (or a message broker, for teams that don't do event sourcing) propagates them to a worker and projection layer, and the result is a materialized view — the speaker's "semantic layer" — from which agent tools read denormalized transaction, device, account and payment context. No vector store, no agent memory system, no new persistence layer is introduced anywhere in the architecture.
data.name: The event store, not a vector database, is the agent's context layer

data.brief: Against framework orthodoxy: agents declare accepted/returned events and subscribe; no graph, no edges to maintain, no code — "drop a file and the topology emerges." Markdown definitions mean non-engineers contribute agents; a month after internal deployment, 20 agents were running, "not just contributed by technical people." Orchestration collapses into a log and a folder
data.name: Events not graphs

data.brief: The speaker's OpenClaw hiring agent mass-emailed candidates and landed on Twitter under his name; the addresses were valid and the people real — every test a coding agent runs would have passed, and none asked "should this have gone at all?" His fix: check drafts against past emails and style, and let destructive actions hit mocked-tool sandboxes for review before they are real, so the agent closes its own loop
data.name: Every code style check would have passed the outreach disaster

data.brief: Eval demand is claimed universal: "every single company that uses computers" should build agent evals, because any computer-performed process is an automation candidate; the population using and building agents is already "magnitudes larger" than ML practitioners ever were (Databricks-scale companies grew from the smaller ML wave).
data.description: What Harbor users actually build evals for, in observed order: (1) how well agents build their products — Ramp's just-announced RampBench off their internal codebase, so they pick the best coding agent/model on their own use cases instead of maximizing token spend; (2) how well agents use their product — every software product is moving toward a headless mode (HubSpot, Stripe cited as always-developer-first), and evaluating + iterating on agent-usability drives agent usage and product value; (3) how well agents power product features; (4) how well agents automate internal processes
data.name: Every company that uses computers should build agent evals — in four classes

data.brief: Every meeting event, signal or nightly schedule runs as a durable thread on Temporal with each tool and model call an activity, resuming from accumulated state when a worker dies; agents get config-scoped tool sets and human-in-the-loop pause/resume. Nightly fan-outs compute per-account briefs from the CDP, an account-scoped vector store and a skill library whose user-customizable formats drove adoption
data.name: Every gtm trigger becomes a durable temporal thread

data.brief: A "temporary" Groovy retention script, hacked together to unblock one customer and never productized, was still running 12 months later across a ~100,000-person customer in multiple places and became a company nickname (colleagues wore venue.groovy shirts to his wedding). Rules: "the most dangerous words in forward deployed engineering are 'this is just temporary'"; if it solves a problem it is permanent; ship everything as though it will run for 18 months, because it probably will.
data.description: Four calibration questions before shipping: will I get a 2 a.m. call about this in six months; what is the trade-off for the product as a whole versus this customer's pain point; who do I hand it to when I leave the site; what happens when it breaks and am I responsible.
data.name: Every temporary forward-deployed hack goes to production and stays there

data.brief: Everyone is building custom agents — a local real-estate agency, independent insurance brokers, many Fortune 500s — despite ubiquitous AI access, while the general public can barely name one agent (Claude, maybe Codex). The driver is integration: getting business data properly into AI. Most efforts die as demos: agentic-loop orchestration, provider abstractions, durable execution, telemetry at scale, portability, and composability are unsolved for them; "there's no defined way to build an agent"
data.name: Everyone builds custom agents but most efforts die as demos

data.brief: A documentation product in 300 health systems within three years is being extended into a clinical agent because, per its builder, billing, trial matching, decision support and orders are all downstream of one root — the conversation — and the agent that holds the EHR, the live conversation and the guidelines can automate the machinery around it, from pre-visit topics to next-day chart prep
data.name: Everything in healthcare is downstream of the conversation

data.brief: What the certification actually tests is scaffolding discipline, not model capability: branch every loop iteration on stop_reason (including the out-of-tokens trap); configure hierarchical CLAUDE.md rule files; specialize agents to one job with one or two tools; fork subtask contexts and merge back summaries only; watch token counts and compact; strip interactive prompts from CI; batch non-urgent work. The model itself is dismissed as the object of study — "the LLM can't do anything; it is just a probabilistic next-word predictor; it can't execute tools" — everything examinable lives in the harness around it
data.name: Exam canon is harness discipline

data.brief: The talk's thesis, stated as a before/after: in 2024, asking a room whether AI had completed an end-to-end task for them would have drawn almost no hands; in 2026 everyone's hand goes up. Models plus harnesses (browser-use tooling, API tooling, robust MCPs) have moved past the execution bottleneck — "knowledge work is almost entirely solved" — so the next bottleneck is how deeply you can understand a specific business and re-engineer its work around AI without scaling headcount exponentially. Supporting observation: a healthcare company's sales department operates nothing like a SaaS company's, and extracting that context out of employees into a model call is the part that breaks.
data.name: Execution is solved; understanding a specific business is the next bottleneck

data.brief: Agents leave scored execution traces in the shared substrate so tomorrow's invocation — and other teams' agents — choose data sources by what actually worked; "my agent that wakes up tomorrow is slightly smarter than it was today", across agents, not just per agent.
data.name: Scored execution traces in a shared substrate enable cross-agent learning

data.brief: EXO Labs embedded at NVIDIA HQ (a "second headquarters" conference room; Jensen's "swarming" — teams incl. a "vLLM-for-Spark team" cycling through back-to-back) and got ~10× inference performance on DGX Spark in ~3 weeks vs NVIDIA's existing playbook.
data.description: The update email to Jensen/exec staff stressed "we didn't solve any new computer science": vLLM backend, quantization, retuning configs designed for the data center onto the identical desk-side Grace Blackwell; Cheema's lesson: "we already have the hardware — it's about activating it"
data.name: EXO Labs got ~10x DGX Spark inference in ~3 weeks by retuning data-center configs

data.brief: Because human feedback is what tuned the prompts and agents, removing humans from review risks slop and quality degradation — so Uber's position, which it says the industry is coalescing on, is to expand the outer loop rather than kill it: agents own implementation-level review (performance, API compatibility), engineers move up to architecture, domain expertise and product thinking. Review relocates rather than disappears
data.name: Expand the outer loop dont kill it

data.brief: Veteran of the 1980s expert-systems boom (companies rose, millions spent, Japan's Fifth Generation project, then the AI winter — symbolic AI couldn't scale, and neural nets waited decades for NVIDIA's GPUs): agentic AI is re-running symbolic AI with the scaling inverted — LLMs supply scale, and ontologies/knowledge graphs return as the formal layer; the convergence now travels under the name "neuro-symbolic AI".
data.name: Agentic AI re-runs 1980s symbolic AI with the scaling inverted

data.brief: A social graph built from who reviews whom yields team clusters, coverage gaps, and an expertise signal that boosts senior engineers' prior comments in automated review — a reviewer recognizing his own past guidance surfaced by the agent. The same graph powered the debugging and fix of a drop in surfaced review issues after a model switch, with the fix PR citing the Slack thread that explained it
data.name: Expertise graph boosts review context

data.brief: The reframing: "intelligence is already becoming abundant — the frontier models are probably smarter than average humans — but expertise is still scarce." Expertise is defined as accumulated situated competence, distinguished from intelligence on two operational axes: expertise *supplies* the right context rather than consuming it, and *compresses* the search rather than expanding it. That second axis is offered as the direct cause of the token-inefficiency now driving company-wide token-maxxing crackdowns — a smart novice brute-forces because it has no learned shortcuts
data.name: Expertise not intelligence is scarce

data.brief: The mechanism: every repetition is extracted into repository solution documents (reasoning, postmortems, taste rules), 50% of time goes to teaching the system, and the loop runs overnight in parallel — more token-efficient over time because the answers are already in context. When CLAUDE.md grew too large, a memory system replaced it. Learning that compounds outside the weights, in the repo
data.name: Extract until the middle runs itself

data.brief: Practitioner claim: "Fable is bottlenecked by my ability to match the map and the territory" — with Fable-class models the constraint moves to the operator's ability to surface unknowns (unspecified decision points the model will hit); Fable traverses so much territory that unfound unknowns dominate outcomes
data.name: With Fable the bottleneck moves to the operator surfacing unknowns

data.brief: Anthropic Claude Code staff frames Fable's launch as an unmapped capability overhang: the models' latent ability exceeds what harnesses currently extract (Pokémon "-aw" answerable only once a code-execution tool is present), and "what contains them is us" — the discovery work is on the harness/prompting side, not model-side
data.name: Anthropic frames Fable's launch as an unmapped capability overhang

data.brief: After a Fable "security hardening pass" declared the codebase in good shape, Snyk found 241 vulnerabilities in Yegge's 30-year game project
data.name: Snyk found 241 vulnerabilities after a Fable hardening pass declared all clear

data.brief: A 100-person Indian factory with no data-science team or ML budget turned "three generations in three brains" into a company brain: hundreds of GB of private history (quotes back to 2019, drawings, payment schedules, email threads) chunked and fact-extracted by off-the-shelf models, stored as vectors plus a who-connects-to-what relationship graph — no fine-tuning, no GPUs, zero training bill
data.name: A 100-person factory turned three generations of history into a company brain

data.brief: Faros AI 2026 benchmarks (AI-adoption cohort; April 2026 study = 22k developers, 4k teams): median PR review time up 441.5%, reviewed PRs take 5.4× longer than before, 31% more PRs merged with no review at all.
data.description: DX 2026 study (400 orgs, 16 months): median PR size 44→72 lines (+63%) while PR throughput grew only ~8% against ~65% AI-usage growth — real gains, smaller than the hype
data.name: Faros AI: median PR review time up 441.5%, 31% more PRs merged with no review

data.brief: Benchmarked decay of the "fat agent" (every tool schema in every prompt): ~78% tool-selection accuracy at 10 tools → ~40% at 100 → 13.6% at 741 (roughly one correct call in eight); driver is lost-in-the-middle attention over hundreds of mid-prompt schemas plus confusable similar tools — the design fails as a whole, not because any single tool is badly written ("the architecture is asking the model to solve the wrong problem")
data.name: Fat-agent tool-selection accuracy collapses from ~78% to 13.6% at scale

data.brief: The catalog is a per-request tax: 741 tool schemas ≈ 127k tokens before the user's question is even considered; at 100k requests/day that's billions of tokens spent just describing tools; time-to-first-token passes 5 seconds around 500 tools — the demo-fine design degrades into a slow, expensive, hard-to-test monolith as the product grows
data.name: 741 tool schemas cost ~127k tokens and >5s TTFT before the question

data.brief: A vendor building tooling to automate its own forward deployed function, with the failure it was built from: the platform team was "hanging out with Codex and Claude" while the FDE side of the office was sleep-deprived and miserable, uploading ~150 pages of documentation to Claude per engagement and getting verbose, incorrect output two minutes later.
data.description: The FD agent's stated goal is one FDE or strategist covering several client engagements — clients emailing 24/7, every process lead (AP relies on AR relies on reconciliation relies on FP&A) pulling in a different direction — without hiring 50 people, which is what separates the model from a traditional consultancy. Third stage (autonomous change-shipping) explicitly not built yet.
data.name: Varick built an in-house FD agent to automate its own forward deployed function

data.brief: The vendor-side information asymmetry, stated as a deliberate practice: Decagon ingests a customer's historical support data and tells them which workflows to automate first for the highest ROI — "and sometimes that's not actually what the customer had reached out about". Because an FDE sees the same problems repeat across every customer in a vertical, the role is "an advisor rather than just an executor" (it is both), and that earned advisory position is named as one of three reasons the company won its market position.
data.name: Cross-customer vantage makes the FDE an advisor, not just an executor

data.brief: FDE framed as the breakout AI job of 2026 ("waiting for the Forbes article: 2026's hottest job"); Cursor is building a global FDE org hiring only 5+-year engineers with customer-facing experience (from Palantir, Spotify, Rippling), organized geo-first → industry-verticals later, with roles expected to be redefined every ~6 months
data.name: FDE framed as the breakout AI job of 2026

data.brief: Dated market build-out: Google announced a GCP effort to hire customer engineers / FDEs, OpenAI created a new unit with a massive investment to aid its corporate AI push, and operators including Aaron Levie are amplifying the function's importance publicly — i.e. the embedded-delivery function is now being staffed at hyperscaler and frontier-lab scale, not just by application startups. Corroborates the batch-5 Cursor signal from the demand side.
data.name: Google and OpenAI stand up FDE units at hyperscaler and frontier-lab scale

data.brief: The cluster's dissent, from the builder of Palantir's FDE training program (~350 engineers; alumni now at OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI): "the first fundamental truth of FDE is that this is not a role, this is a product strategy" — quoted from Palantir's current CTO days before the talk — and an FDE is judged by their ability to be an extension of the product team and generalize solutions, not by contract size, customer success or sales support.
data.description: Explicitly rejects the framings in the two preceding talks: FDE-as-go-to-market is what Palantir became after twenty years and unlimited money, not what built Foundry; "when people say FDEs are customer-facing software engineers whose job is to make the customer successful — that's not true"; closes with "please don't treat FDEs as go-to-market extensions".
data.name: FDE is a product strategy, not a role and not a go-to-market extension

data.brief: An FDE org agentifying its own job function, stage by stage. Shipped: the request-intake agent (hours/days to seconds, ~20% of scoping time saved, reps now talk to it directly). Already easy: spec to working software, because frontier models one-shot medium-size features. The remaining middle of the pipeline is "super gnarly and unformed" and is where the team is investing.
data.description: Mehr's 6-12-month projection of what FDE at Ramp is: applied-AI problems — keeping the agent harness running each stage smooth, keeping per-stage output quality good with evals, rubrics and human feedback, and the biggest challenge, getting the agent the right context (a product manager's head-knowledge; Notion docs, knowledge base and help articles only go so far; skills, memories, tools).
data.name: Ramp is agentifying its own FDE lifecycle stage by stage

data.brief: Anthropic applied-AI engineer (ex-Palantir, ex-Rippling) gives the track's definitional framing: FDE is not a general upgrade to go-to-market, it is the answer to one quadrant of {how technical is what you sell} x {how technical is who buys it}.
data.description: Technical product + technical buyer (GitHub, Datadog) leads to DevRel/developer engagement; simple-or-configurable product + non-technical buyer (Rippling, Jira, Slack) leads to sales-led SaaS; only a technical product sold to a non-technical buyer (Foundry into a Fortune 500 oil-and-gas company whose "pipelines are not data pipelines") needs FDE.
data.name: FDE answers one quadrant: a technical product sold to a non-technical buyer

data.brief: The talk's titular claim, from someone who has hired for the role for 2.5 years: forward deployed engineering "doesn't exist" — the term is asked to describe DevOps, data integration, custom solutioning, enablement, agent building and product engineering at once, so it means nothing while simultaneously being "the hottest job in AI".
data.description: Evidence offered: Palantir's 2016 postings led with location (on-prem deployments meant literally sitting with the customer), while a 2026 composite of current FDE postings reads "staff engineer for eight years + six years direct sales experience + four years as a solution architect (teaching experience helps)". The single continuity across every vintage is accountability to the customer.
data.name: Forward deployed engineering has lost its referent while being the hottest job in AI

data.brief: Track-intro framing (MC, unnamed): forward deployed engineering is "one of the hottest topics in AI" and "the most important companies on the planet are building out massive FDE teams — think OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind"; the practice was pioneered by Palantir years ago to embed strong engineers directly in customer orgs and customize the platform around the nuances of the real world. An entire conference track now exists for it, with speakers from Anthropic, Cursor, Factory, Ramp, Decagon "and many more".
data.name: Frontier labs are building massive FDE teams, a practice pioneered by Palantir

data.brief: Exa's go-to-market has 8–9 forward-deployed engineers in a 115-person company who both run deals and build and maintain the AI systems behind them: "because of AI, that was two jobs and now it's one." AEs and SDRs learn the tools through training rather than building them — the technical revenue role absorbs the tooling role
data.name: Fdes run deals and build the sales system

data.brief: After launch there is "a lot of demand" for a federated graph experience: individual teams want to link their own datasets to the main enterprise graph; roadmap = fill out existing systems of record, expand the primary graph to more enterprise-wide datasets, and build federation.
data.name: Post-launch demand: teams want federated links to the enterprise graph

data.brief: The mechanism behind 4–5×: vibe coding keeps you waiting 30–60 seconds per turn and unable to parallelize; feeding an agent what to do *and how to self-validate* — compile, tests, coverage, a quality bar baked into the steering file — lets it self-correct for hours and come back only when it passes. Shifting testing left (linters, tests, locally-run deterministic mock services instead of live-service integration tests) exists to make that feedback loop fast and local
data.name: Feed agents dont babysit them

data.brief: Every payments incumbent shipped an agent protocol within about a year (L402, Mastercard Agent Pay, x402, KYAPay, AP2, ACP, Tab, UCP, ACTP, MPP, AMP, UnionPay, OKX, Agent Pay for Machines). A self-described crypto skeptic argues crypto rails fit agents: microtransactions cards cannot do, one-way payments because there is no agent identity to adjudicate disputes, and a decentralized standard immune to duopoly fees; x402 leads MPP ~20× in transactions and volume
data.name: Fifteen agent payment protocols in a year

data.brief: Each of a claim's dozens of steps can err and propagate; strict guardrails reject correct work, pure agentic reasoning across multimodal steps is slow and costly, and hard-coding everything bloats into an unmaintainable codebase with a huge team. The builder's answer is a deliberate split between free reasoning and hard-coded structure, and a cost rule: never run a thousand-times-a-day step on the most expensive model
data.name: Fifty claim steps force a balance of agentic and hard coded

data.brief: Concrete parallelism claim from a production finance-agent vendor: ~50 active git worktrees, each an independent sub-agent, on a 48 GB MacBook, with the engineer as orchestrator. Backlog becomes the task queue — each QA-reported Jira ticket gets its own worktree and its own agent, which spawns further sub-agents — and the human is told not to sequence the work because the agent does it better. The nine-step pipeline (requirements → RCA from traces and logs → TDD → fix → local end-to-end → PR → review/merge → dev image → stage) runs with human involvement at steps 1 and 9 only.
data.name: Fifty parallel worktree sub-agents on one laptop, human at steps 1 and 9 only

data.brief: A textbook supervised fine-tune (narrow six-way intent classification, thousands of messages a day, a data scientist's dream pipeline) delivered $12M revenue at 50× ROI within a year — and "the whole time it was quietly accumulating debt": week-long retrain cycles that fixed one regression and caused another, a model frozen because training formats differ per provider and version, and an architecture frozen at late-2024 workflows. The value was real; the maintenance economics were not
data.name: Fifty x roi fine tune was quietly tech debt

data.brief: A years-stable design process inverted in 30 days: instead of working in Figma to high fidelity and handing off, designers now plan, build the working prototype directly (Claude Code), and return to Figma only afterward for mood boards and UI fine-tuning — the live project, not the mock, is the main working artifact
data.name: Figma demoted from primary working artifact to after-the-fact fine-tuning

data.brief: A one-day-a-week side project (a Figma plugin-based MCP server, started when only Cursor exposed the feature) shipped local ~mid-2025, remote in September, GA in October 2025, added writes — and became one of Figma's fastest-growing products ever, "not something we expected." Design context delivered to agents wherever they are turned out to be a product, not an integration
data.name: Figma mcp became a fastest growing product

data.brief: Zep, asked about the file-based memory wave (markdown/wikis/knowledge bases): markdown "suffers from provenance" — mutating lines in a file destroys the lineage of why changes occurred — and breaks down in multi-agent, multi-user, multi-source server scenarios at enterprise scale; works well for desktop / single-user single-agent use.
data.name: File-based memory suffers from provenance and fails multi-agent enterprise scale

data.brief: Filed (AI agents for US tax pros, $17M+ raised) closed more revenue in a single month (mid-2026) than in the entire preceding year, two years into building — demand inflection for vertical AI agents in tax
data.name: Filed closed more revenue in one month than the entire preceding year

data.brief: Deliberate architecture rejection for personal-scale memory: they dropped vector databases, knowledge graphs, semantic search, and text search ("all that is beautiful, but adds a lot of complexity") in favor of plain markdown files plus an index.yaml of references — a mechanism "rooted into how your computer works" that stays human-inspectable and agent-navigable; retrieval-infra RAG is acknowledged as right for products at scale but wrong for a daily-driver personal research OS
data.name: Plain markdown plus an index beats retrieval infra for personal-scale memory

data.brief: The regulated-sector constraint, and the batch's clearest statement of why finance loops differ: with AI removed from the picture, a human auditor reviews the code and a controller signs off under SOX. Agent-reviewing-agent has nowhere to put that accountability — "if something goes wrong in production you can't say Claude is doing this" — and "moving fast and breaking things in the finance sector is a lot different". This is what pins the human to the loop boundary even as everything between the boundaries is automated; the bottleneck that remains is therefore human attention, not model capability.
data.name: SOX requires a human signer, so agent-reviewing-agent has nowhere to put the blame

data.brief: Named critique of three published finance-agent benchmarks (GDPval, a tool-use benchmark, and "APEX agents"): (1) average human hours per task fall far below the METR long-horizon thresholds the leading frontier models already clear, so they aren't long-horizon tasks at all; (2) they are already reasonably saturated — in the APEX investment-banking section, pass@1 means ~57% of tasks are 100% solved; (3) breadth is narrow — GDPval's finance coverage is a small set of Excel tasks, APEX is largely IB, so credit, debt and risk go untested; (4) the reward signal is coarse relative to what training needs (their own rubrics run ~20 criteria with ~10 sub-criteria each).
data.name: Published finance-agent benchmarks are short, saturated, narrow and coarsely rewarded

data.brief: Not human-in-the-loop but AI-in-the-loop: the model proposes five trade theses or a slate of drug candidates and saves the expert most of the time, but the decision stays with the trader or scientist "for a really long time," because models do correlation not causation and cannot verify themselves in these fields. A vertical-AI builder's explicit boundary on autonomous research: no vibe-coded drugs yet
data.name: Finance and pharma are ai in the loop

data.brief: Fine-tuning was chosen partly for "control over our destiny with the model providers" — own the data, retrain anywhere. In practice it locked them to one model version: formats, data volumes and training interfaces differ across providers, so upgrading was unaffordable and the model stayed frozen while the field moved. Context-based systems delivered the provider freedom fine-tuning promised. Rule: fine-tune only when you literally can't call a frontier model
data.name: Fine tuning reverses the vendor control it promised

data.brief: Four open doors put backdoors into models teams actually ship: poisoned slices of scraped/third-party training or RLHF data; fine-tuning vendors (data out, un-auditable weights back); hub checkpoints downloaded with unknown provenance; and insiders with pipeline access — "if you don't control every training token yourself, you are exposed, and the evaluations won't save you"
data.name: Poisoned data, vendors, hub checkpoints and insiders backdoor shipped models

data.brief: A West Virginia law in force from 2026-08-31 lets a DUNA give an organization composed of agents legal standing; the speaker's registration (#628407) came back two hours before the talk — "we now have legal standing for an organization composed of intelligent agents." Such organizations can own property, contract, raise capital, hire, and are blockchain-verified; the org itself is designed as software
data.name: First legally registered agent organization

data.brief: Five Eyes intelligence leaders: AI will bypass cybersecurity systems "in months, not years"
data.name: Five Eyes: AI will bypass cybersecurity systems in months, not years

data.brief: An AWS keynote demo: a rover with a Raspberry Pi and a 4G SIM follows natural-language instructions on stage — headlights, greetings, a 360 spin, counting the audience — because Strands Agents treats its preset functions and policies as tools an agent orchestrates; five lines of code, three concurrent agents (thinker, communicator, voice), Claude Opus 4.8 as the brain, and a package covering 40+ robots
data.name: Five lines give a robot a brain

data.brief: Named industry anti-pattern: teams fix agent failures by stuffing the prompt — "never do this", "only do that", "never output this" — because the prompt is the only surface they can evaluate. With a simulation you control and evaluate the full stack, so the fix can live where it belongs: the harness when context is overloaded, a skill when a procedure is missing, structured output when a schema is required.
data.name: Prompt-stuffing is an anti-pattern; the fix belongs in harness, skill or schema

data.brief: After rebuilding the workflow as skills, tools and resources on a model-agnostic framework, the fix loop went from ~a week (gather, synthesize, label, retrain, iterate, deploy) to under an hour (edit a prompt or skill, validate on a curated production set, upload markdown to S3). Accuracy rose above the fine-tuned model's; per-message cost rose with better models but total cost fell with maintenance. The learning loop moved from the weights to the context — and got faster and cheaper
data.name: Fix cycle from a week to under an hour

data.brief: Fixed harnesses have a decay problem on two fronts: (1) "you can build a careful harness today... it could be irrelevant next month — the model just got so good it didn't need that scaffolding anymore"; (2) every unanticipated real-world situation needs a human to patch the harness, bolting on rules until the harness is more complicated than the problem — "the factory method is the right answer to a fixed problem and the wrong answer to a moving problem"
data.name: Fixed harnesses decay: models outgrow scaffolding and reality outruns patches

data.brief: KRAFTON engineer running 4–6 concurrent agent contexts in tmux found the human silently becomes the scheduler (who does what), the memory (what each is doing), and the reviewer — "I'm not running agents anymore… my own attention was the bottleneck." Flat piles of agents stop scaling at a handful of live contexts, well before model capability does
data.name: Flat agent fleets stop scaling when the human operator becomes the bottleneck

data.brief: The design claim from a Unity veteran: the LLM "reinvents the wheel every time" (a camera-follow reimplemented differently each run) because the context is on engine internals, not game design — so flip the context to domain intent and let people describe games in player vocabulary (WASD, double-jump, collect-a-coin). A general harness lesson: give the model a domain-intent vocabulary layer above the tool, rather than a better prompt over raw primitives
data.name: Flip context to domain intent

data.brief: Observation replicated across two domains (hotel sentiment, SOC alert triage): the cases that flip-flop concentrate near the decision boundary — exactly where human experts also disagree and where the "right" label is a matter of company policy/preference (e.g., password spray with no successful login: notify or ignore?)
data.name: Agent flip-flops concentrate at the decision boundary where humans also disagree

data.brief: Altos' PrimeFlow (arXiv) shows flow-matching models that match the data distribution outperform autoregressive/autoencoder single-cell models that compress to a latent vector and lose information
data.name: Flow-matching beats autoregressive single-cell models (PrimeFlow)

data.brief: The dysfunction side from a first-person source: engineers up late chasing the perfect overnight prompt ("flowmaxxing"), cognitive load from parallel agents across terminal tabs, and reviewing AI output being harder than writing it — especially for early-career engineers who have not built the reviewing muscle senior engineers spent careers on. Named as an organizational risk to manage, not a footnote
data.name: Flowmaxxing and review load hit early career engineers

data.brief: Mainstream category formation. Forrester: "convergence not invention." Foundation Capital thesis going mainstream.
data.description: Forbes published "VCs say context graphs might be the next big thing in AI" on April 3, 2026, marking mainstream category formation. The article synthesized Foundation Capital's "trillion-dollar opportunity" thesis with Forrester's response framing context graphs as "a convergence, not an invention" — arguing that Enterprise Architecture has been building the entity foundation for decades, and that decision traces are the genuinely new contribution.
data.name: Forbes: "VCs say context graphs might be the next big thing"

data.brief: Forestwalk runs a voice agent inside its team calls that takes real-time action on spoken intent — a bug mentioned in conversation was filed as a Linear issue within ~1 second of "let's file that"; ambient, non-interruptive action-taking during human conversation now feels natural once latency is dialed in
data.name: In-call voice agent files a Linear issue within ~1 second of spoken intent

data.brief: The practitioner's finding on llms.txt: write it by hand to get the answer across — about 40 good lines outperform 1,000 generated lines of noise — then give agents an llms-full index with per-page descriptions because they fetch rather than browse, markdown twins of every page with header, content negotiation and a query fallback, and WebMCP tools so they can ask the site. No single fix; a belt of small optimizations, packaged as a docs pipeline other developer companies now run
data.name: Forty hand written lines beat a thousand generated

data.brief: The CEO built a clone of himself in a week: voice from 760 emails, a decision framework from hundreds of past decisions mined from Slack and email and turned into evals, full read/write access for him, draft-only with fewer tools for everyone else. The company drafts emails and decisions "as Jeff would" — a founder's judgement captured as evals and served, with the authority carefully scoped
data.name: Founder clone drafts decisions from eval calibrated judgement

data.brief: The positive claim: with data fixed and model size fixed, compute becomes the only remaining axis, and the open research problem is how to spend it without saturating. Named "scaling compute on context" and explicitly identified as one idea wearing eight names across the industry — sleep-time compute, neural memory, write-time compute, note taking, dreaming, studying, machine studying, amortized inference — with the naming disorder itself offered as evidence that the paradigm "hasn't solidified the way pre-training or post-training have." with Su's escape-intelligence claim, the pattern's second anchor
data.name: Fourth scaling axis proposed

data.brief: A single backend dev shipped a production-shaped hybrid-RAG FAQ chatbot with zero paid components and no agent/RAG framework — Python/FastAPI, React widget, PostgreSQL (vectors + BM25), Docker, Ollama local models, Langfuse telemetry — reproducible with one command in GitHub Codespaces; the RAG stack has commoditized to plain code
data.name: One dev shipped production hybrid-RAG with zero paid or framework components

data.brief: Compliance researcher: modern fraud rarely appears as an error within a single document — a payroll record, vendor invoice, and tax filing each pass their individual validation while the inconsistencies **across** them are the fraud; rule-based and document-level NLP systems are structurally blind to this because they validate records, not relationships
data.name: Fraud passes single-document validation; the cross-document inconsistencies are the fraud

data.brief: A separate review agent with deliberately fresh context — not biased by the diagnosing agent's framing — criticizes, scores, runs focused tests, requests changes, or closes PRs outright (eager PR-senders need a critic). The PR + review agents produce ~10× more PRs per day than the three humans; the human stays as final gate only until the loop earns trust: "close the loop first, make yourself the bottleneck, then remove yourself"
data.name: A fresh-context review agent criticizes, scores, and gates the PR agent's output

data.brief: Alithea Bio ships Froglet (2026-07): a cryptographic receipt-chain protocol for cross-org agent transactions — signed step chain, keypair identity, marketplace discovery, base-payment/success-fee scheme; runs locally with one command, docs live at froglet.dev
data.name: Alithea Bio ships Froglet, a receipt-chain protocol for cross-org agent transactions

data.brief: The trust section's pivot event: for years "you can't trust Chinese models" was code for "you can't trust open models" — then "Anthropic had to put Fable away" and people realized access to frontier systems might not be universal, so "a tremendous number of enterprises and developers started going to these new Chinese models because they could trust that they would always have access to them". The "Fable and GPT-5.6 embargo" left open questions about at what capability level intelligence gets politicized and held back, with those decisions "happening behind closed doors" — while, simultaneously, open capability converged: GLM 5.2 a month earlier read as the open-model Opus-inflection, and the panel predicts better-than-Fable capabilities in open models within 12 months. Trust redefined as: do I know what I'm running, and can I be sure I'll keep getting it
data.name: Frontier access shock meets open convergence

data.brief: Intuit study (unreleased at talk time) across thousands of businesses and ~100,000 situations and time frames, with worked cases: a first-time landlord in negative cash flow with an open loan was told by a frontier model — holding all of the business's data — to acquire a second rental property, while the outcome-grounded model recommended raising the existing tenant's rent 5-10% before renewal. An egg supplier with 70% of revenue from one customer and nearly all cost from one vendor was told to raise prices 15-20% (risking almost all revenue) where the grounded model went to the cost side and recommended negotiating the vendor down 5-10%. Aggregate: 40% of frontier advice was "acquire a new customer", +14% "increase product revenue" — over half of all advice, generic and sometimes actively harmful.
data.name: Frontier models give generic and sometimes harmful business advice to SMBs

data.brief: Amazon's definition of the phase after vibe coding is behavioural: frontier developers write 1–2% of the code they produce, aim for agents to run for hours without intervention, and run several agents in parallel through a backlog. Every prior phase — inline completion, chat, vibe coding — kept the human in the loop and felt like 10–20%
data.name: Frontier developers write one to two percent of code

data.brief: The itemized case against one-size-fits-all frontier inference: cloud LLMs carry exposure/interception/retention risk (real cases of chatbot business data breached and leaked); >4 s responses break user believability (VR-chat research) and many frontier calls exceed it; third-party inference costs are uncontrollable and agentic/reasoning workloads consume tokens faster than prices fall — total spend rising despite token deflation; and remote models die offline (outages, air-gapped and disconnected environments)
data.name: The itemized case against one-size-fits-all frontier inference

data.brief: Frontier intelligence is being repriced in real time: GPT-5.6 Terra = 5.5-level intelligence at half the cost; Luna competitive at $1/M in, $6/M out; 5.6 Sol on Cerebras at ~750 tok/s — fast enough to run five or six agent approaches in parallel and pick the best in less time than one generation used to take
data.name: Frontier intelligence is being repriced in real time

data.brief: Failure modes of the frontier image-editing models Uber calls surface as defects in the applied product — object coherence and physics plausibility errors such as a plate rendered covering the sauce. Uber's own evals are what detect them, and the team coordinates with the frontier model teams to feed the problems back upstream: an applied eval suite acting as a defect channel into the labs.
data.name: Frontier image-model flaws surface as defects in the applied product

data.brief: Frontier models now find and exploit vulnerabilities better than a top-100-ranked human hacker (Cable's self-assessment); Anthropic's own chart shows Mythos executing increasingly autonomous attack chains; open-source libraries are the adversary's proving ground because anyone can run a smart model against them
data.name: Frontier models now find and exploit vulnerabilities better than a top-100 hacker

data.brief: On 87 real multi-GPU problems the best frontier model (GPT-5.5) solves 28 zero-shot with 22 faster than PyTorch+NCCL; sampling lifts correctness to ~36 but "fast" plateaus around 31%; successes are the internet-familiar patterns. Models compile with feedback but don't reason about collective ordering, partitioning, SM scheduling or transfer mechanisms even with the principles in context — "benchmaxxed on single-GPU benchmarks of the past." A measured limit on autonomous systems research at the hardware frontier
data.name: Frontier models cannot write fast multi gpu kernels
