data.brief: A ~30-person PhD AI research group inside an investment bank built an automated quant-research harness and open-sourced all of it — full code on GitHub plus a ~40-page tech report, released ~April 2026 — on the explicit reasoning that the harness is not where the value is. Custom code rather than any off-the-shelf agent framework; provider-agnostic functional tool calling; three tools (shell, web search, Slurm job submission); three phases (research → eval building → mass experimentation) ending in trained containerized models. Motivation stated in production terms: a lot of shipped algorithms where more search cycles would find improvements, transferable models across desks (credit bonds → muni bonds), and new desks with little ML where "even a reasonably trained model" moves the needle.
data.name: Morgan Stanley open-sources AlphaLab, its multi-agent quant research harness

data.brief: The demand-side sufficiency claim, from the HF seat: "most of the jobs still do not require a Fable-level thing — we are kind of in a bubble as software developers"; businesses distill midsize models down to very small ones for tasks like reranking "that don't require LLM outputs, cutting millions of costs"; quantization buys concurrency and in-house deployment most companies don't know exist ("people aren't aware of it… it's kind of shocking to me"). Compression's business value is mostly *not* frontier chasing — it is right-sizing work that never needed the frontier
data.name: Most jobs below frontier

data.brief: Off-the-shelf ASR is benchmarked in quiet rooms; on real phone lines a Spanish "sí" becomes the letter C and Arabic drug names hit 30% word-error rate — "most of what looks like model reasoning failures end up being the model mishearing." Conditioning a decoder-only audio LLM on the conversation and the domain (medication list, task, policy), preserving prosody, biasing on synthetic patient data and re-scoring one-word answers cut medical WER by over 50% and P99 latency 3×
data.name: Most reasoning failures were mishearing

data.brief: "There is general acceptance that you need to run that flywheel; in practice a lot of teams don't" — evals are static, and even without architectural change they stop measuring what matters. Through generational shifts the stagnation compounds: known-failure harvesting continues, novel failure modes go unseen
data.name: Most teams run static evals

data.brief: Mozilla Firefox monthly security bug fixes went from a ~20/month 2025 average to ~60–70 in Feb–Mar and ~400 in April (~20x last year's average), about two-thirds attributed to Claude Mythos preview; Mozilla explicitly credits agentic harnesses for making previously false-positive-ridden LLM scanning practical
data.name: Mozilla Firefox monthly security bug fixes hit ~20x last year's average

data.brief: Reported outcome: mean time to discovery dropped sharply — detection works off a single time window instead of waiting across multiple windows, made near-real-time by an async split into a hot path (Kafka/stream processing for fast decisions/automation) and a recon path (slower, more accurate).
data.name: Detection from a single time window sharply cuts mean time to discovery

data.brief: Collapsing the agentic tier's output into a single metric or if condition regressed straight back to the rule engine's behaviour — "many false positive cases". The fix was structural: fan out to a risk analyzer and a behaviour analyzer with distinct toolsets, then add a third agent whose only job is to read both responses and decide, publishing the verdict as an event. Business rules from the old engine are being migrated into agent tools rather than deleted.
data.name: A dedicated verdict agent beats collapsing agent output into a threshold

data.brief: Scaling from one machine to three (MacBook + two always-on headless Linux boxes, one control plane) broke five ways: orchestrators doing the work themselves instead of dispatching (fixed by a CLI harness + skills making dispatch the only available path); managers spawning tmux panes until capture-pane couldn't read them; OOM with swap full under stacked Claude Code + MCP processes; git credentials colliding across workspaces (fixed with fully separated per-workspace environments); laptop sleep/power loss killing in-flight jobs.
data.description: Context moves between machines by committing files + git push, then tmux send-keys over SSH to pull; per-machine dirs for machine state, shared state changed only via pull request; per-machine review gateways collapsed into one on an always-on box ("your one point of control can't be a thing that falls asleep"); Discord bots (one per machine) became the single router, phone as fleet remote
data.name: Scaling an agent fleet from one machine to three broke five ways

data.brief: Risa beats indeterministic single-source LLM extraction by reconciling multiple evidence sources (patient notes + prior authorization letters + a payer-rule KB); only where sources concur is confidence high enough to skip human review
data.name: Multi-source evidence concurrence gates when Risa skips human review

data.brief: Sonar partner/customer telemetry: organizations using multi-layered verification report AI-derived production outages 44% less frequent than those that don't
data.name: Multi-layered verification cuts AI-derived production outages 44%

data.brief: Practitioner: uploading raw documents to cloud LLMs taxes you tokens before the first question and hides how the document was chunked (28-page handbook → meaningless chunks like "signature date" → slower answers, more hallucination); converting to markdown locally on CPU via Docling and chunking deliberately eliminates the cost and makes every answer traceable to its chunk
data.name: Raw docs tax tokens and hide chunking; convert to markdown locally first

data.brief: The market shift the first war story tracks: "AI infrastructure is becoming increasingly multimodal — no longer about text; companies now need pipelines for video, metadata, transcripts, subtitles, and structural context around the content." A 5PB/month video-data-for-training ask that grew into a full suite (downloader, transcripts, subtitles, search, channel info) is offered as evidence the demand is real and escalating — the supply-side signal for the training-data and multimodal threads
data.name: Multimodal web pipelines now required

data.brief: Applied science loops now routinely wire multiple specialist models into one agent loop: a multimodal model (Gemini) reviews registration/QC images as a skill, a large reasoning model (GPT-5.5 Pro via Oracle CLI) generates and critiques hypotheses adversarially/collaboratively each iteration
data.name: Applied science loops routinely wire multiple specialist models into one agent loop

data.brief: What replaces the solo-illuminated-by-monitor era: "planning isn't before, and review isn't after — we iterate on the direction together, AI takes a step, we iterate more." Ace's answer: sessions as branches in cloud microVMs, chat + terminal + preview in one place; the agent acts on the whole team backscroll; plans are markdown docs edited *together*, then made real — "to change something about my application, I'm going to edit a document and tell AI: make the document true." Slack is dismissed as the wrong substrate ("designed to be better than email for the average office worker — never for making software"), but chat matters as the home of facts-not-in-code. The conviction line: "I don't email Word documents around anymore; I create and collaborate in the same surface. This is coming for code, a trillion percent." HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-ai-native-org ledger (uncoined): realtime-multiplayer + ambient awareness as the team's operating surface, from the platform incumbent, same-batch-independent of Ref's decision-doc version
data.name: Multiplayer surface for realtime dev

data.brief: Shipped multi-tenant bug: silently defaulted brand-identity fields made every venue's agent email as sage@[the flagship venue's domain] — a white-label leak where venues spoke in a stranger's voice and users just felt something was off. Resulting principle: in a multi-tenant agent system identity must never have a default — a missing brand identity is a crash (fail loud), not a fallback
data.name: In a multi-tenant agent system identity must never have a default

data.brief: Mutagent ships its first two agents in research preview (evaluator + diagnostics): structured root-cause analysis over production traces with failure-mode clustering and learned, code-checkable indicators per failure mode — because LLM-reading millions of traces "costs more than the execution itself", it multi-tier-samples representative traces (or does guided search from a user-reported issue) instead; output is an HTML diagnosis artifact plus remedies as coding-agent task definitions / auto-raised GitHub PRs
data.name: Mutagent ships evaluator and diagnostics agents in research preview

data.brief: Opus 4.6 near-0%. Mythos: 181 working exploits. 4-vuln browser chain. FreeBSD RCE CVE-2026-4747. Emerged from general reasoning.
data.description: On April 7, 2026, Anthropic published a technical assessment of Claude Mythos Preview's cybersecurity capabilities. Where Opus 4.6 had a near-0% success rate at autonomous exploit development, Mythos Preview produced 181 working exploits out of several hundred attempts on Firefox 147 JavaScript engine vulnerabilities (all patched in Firefox 148). The model also autonomously discovered and exploited a 17-year-old remote code execution vulnerability in FreeBSD's NFS server (CVE-2026-4747), granting full root access to unauthenticated users. It wrote a web browser exploit chaining four vulnerabilities with a JIT heap spray escaping both renderer and OS sandboxes. These capabilities were not explicitly trained — they emerged as a downstream consequence of general improvements in code, reasoning, and autonomy.
data.name: Mythos Preview: 0% → 181 working exploits on Firefox benchmark

data.brief: 2026: export controls imposed on the Mythos and Fable frontier models; industry letter urged the White House to lift them (defender benefit outweighs risk; Anthropic added defender-skewed safeguards to Fable); distillation attacks are collapsing the closed-to-open-weight lag anyway; Cable testified to Congress days before the models shipped, recommending an American open-weight frontier ecosystem
data.name: Export controls imposed on Mythos and Fable; industry urges lifting them

data.brief: Microsoft's CEO, in a clip Kramer plays as the state of the art (No Priors / Latent Space crossover, ~2 weeks prior): "you kind of want the harness to define the models, the data and the tools, so that you have a loop across those three" — and every Microsoft product, "whether it's GitHub Copilot or the security copilot… or the discovery for science," is being built as a multi-model harness with tool access, progressive disclosure of tools for token efficiency, and rich context. Kramer's gloss: the frontier is "agents plus" — copilots embedded in every piece of software and organization-level harnesses
data.name: Nadella org level harnesses

data.brief: Braintrust study + the tau-bench self-consistency stat (60% pass rate ≈ self-consistent only a quarter of the time): naive swaps to cheaper models look faster/cheaper on paper but can destroy value delivered (unresolved support requests); one replay is an anecdote — ZenML's own cohort analysis of a "cheaper and same result" single replay returned the verdict *don't ship*
data.name: Naive cheaper-model swaps look economical but can destroy delivered value

data.brief: The Nanda index is shipped and onboarding now: identity → signed agent-facts card → message box, with adaptive resolution; onboarding tiers for enterprises (own catalog/domain), existing websites (DNS records), and individuals (hosted agent URL via host39.org)
data.name: The Nanda index is shipped and onboarding now

data.brief: Nanda Town is already running real coordination experiments — marketplace price negotiation, auctions, agent voting/ballot counting, consensus, supply chains — to find where agentic-web protocols break before they become load-bearing on the real internet
data.name: Nanda Town is already running real agent-economy coordination experiments

data.brief: Gas fees and shared block space make sub-cent on-chain settlement uneconomic and unpredictable, so Circle moved it off-chain: escrowed USDC in a smart contract, signed off-chain authorizations relayed to Circle, funds confirmed in a few hundred milliseconds, gas-free for the seller, cross-chain, down to a micro-cent. The rail is reshaped around the agent's transaction size and frequency
data.name: Nanopayments take settlement off chain to agent speed

data.brief: Nearform's production cadence: collect traces with user thumbs-up/down + comments or SME annotations (114 traces in the shown example); a skill instructs the coding agent to cluster failure modes, adversarially review them, and root-cause against the agent's actual code; SMEs triage; a coding agent then implements fixes — often an entire failure suite from one prompt when given context + regression tests — and every failure mode becomes a golden-dataset regression
data.name: Nearform clusters production failure modes and agent-implements the fixes

data.brief: Nemotron 3 Ultra (garbled "Neatron") proved NVFP4 low-precision training works — the hardware footprint for training, fine-tuning, and building small specialized models is dropping too, not just inference, making owned-hardware economics viable sooner
data.name: Nemotron 3 Ultra proved NVFP4 low-precision training works

data.brief: Neo4j ships a free hands-on workshop/course teaching graph "shapes" as agent context over lakehouses (BigQuery, extendable to Databricks/Snowflake): vector search + text-to-SQL access the data fine, but agents fail on the right slice — the fix is shaped graph views (outline, themes, connections), not more query access.
data.name: Neo4j ships free workshop teaching graph shapes as agent context over lakehouses

data.brief: The second and larger result — one finding amplified across the fleet. A Spectator metrics counter object being allocated on every iteration of a hot path was found in one service; via cross-repo code search the agent then found the same anti-pattern in 7 different services, with an estimated 0.5-4.6% of CPU cycles recoverable if fixed across all of them. The generalization is the point: a human fixes the instance, an agent fixes the class — and the finding it produced (an O(N^2) implementation) was noted as language-independent, so the catalog entry transfers across languages and frameworks.
data.name: One anti-pattern found in 7 Netflix services, with 0.5-4.6% of CPU cycles recoverable

data.brief: A large-scale platform team stating an autonomy ceiling and its reasoning. Netflix runs at level 2 — a fixed, predefined workflow (trigger profiler, download, analyze, canary, suggest fix) with tools, integrations, harnesses and hooks, on a weekly scheduled run per service so regressions are caught close to when the code was written.
data.description: The agent never pushes to production: "I'm still keeping the confidence bar to just send a code review, and that's by intent", because "you're modifying an existing code that is running just fine in production in order to optimize it, which is very risky" — without business context and test coverage you break things. Level 3 (agent plans, reasons and acts) is described as available but gated on heavy investment in evaluation and sandboxing, "because prompt injection and other security attacks a typical agent infrastructure currently cannot always solve for". Guidance: start at level 1, move to level 2, "and you get maximum benefits".
data.name: Netflix stops at level-2 autonomy: the performance agent never pushes to production

data.brief: Long-term agent memory at Netflix is markdown files in a central Git repo, explicitly chosen over "very fancy vector search or a vector database": "a stateful catalog and a stateless LLM together become a full fleet-wide memory". Entries carry symbols/query hints, the services where the pattern was confirmed, a rising confidence level, and both the anti-pattern and the good pattern.
data.description: Deliberately central rather than team- or product-specific, so a pattern discovered by one service's profiling run is available to every future agent profiling a different service "without having to redo all the exercise that the first agent did". Git-repo-by-design so humans and agents can both read and author it — including humans writing entries at framework-build time, when the context is freshest. Bootstrap sources named: Jeff Dean's C++ optimization blog post, PyTorch's torchfix repo, and internal performance playbooks.
data.name: Netflix's fleet-wide agent memory is markdown in a central Git repo, not a vector database

data.brief: Netflix's first result, on live production services: fed profiling data, a coding agent identified an immutable-map copy inside a tensor-merge call path consuming 8.8% of CPU time during the profiling window, recognized it as quadratic rather than linear from the call stack alone — not from reading the code base — then, given instructions as a skill or prompt, checked the Git repo out at the exact commit running in production, located the implementation, traced the call path and opened a code review, end to end in under 5 minutes on a very large code base.
data.description: Baseline it replaces: ~20 minutes of a human engineer's time just to identify hot paths in a flame-graph visualizer, before any fix. Real production CPU and latency savings were measured for the optimized reimplementation, with figures shown on slide only and never spoken.
data.name: A Netflix agent found and fixed an 8.8% CPU hot path end to end in under five minutes

data.brief: At ~1,000 tokens/second on Cerebras (GPT-5.3 Codex Spark), the constraint on an agent loop stopped being inference and became the network: per-tool-call HTTP/SSE overhead and the re-sending of unchanged state. The fix is transport-level — a persistent WebSocket with stateful context that returns only the changed item — and the framing generalizes past this vendor: as inference approaches free, the remaining latency in agentic systems is the plumbing around the model
data.name: Network is the new agent bottleneck

data.brief: About 90% of Anterior's datasets are now synthetic; in blind review clinicians distinguish synthetic from real records only ~60% of the time; and because data can be created from scratch quickly, eval sets are built just in time for each customer deployment — edge cases modeled and tested before go-live instead of waiting for customer data
data.name: Ninety percent synthetic and clinicians cant tell

data.brief: Gates deliberately built no chat app: the chat interface, UI, and even general agent interaction were judged non-defensible; users are already in Claude and ChatGPT, so the platform is served where they are through forked Neo4j MCP servers, with constrained workflow experiences (MCP apps as entry points, sandboxed agents) delivered through surfaces like Claude Cowork.
data.name: Gates built no chat app: agent surfaces are non-defensible, serve via MCP

data.brief: A virtual copy of the market cannot come from one source: one provider covers half the phone numbers, so enrichment cascades across many vendors, cross-checked and reconciled per entity, refreshed selectively by field volatility and cost, while accounts keep changing under your own marketing. Data engineering, not prompting, is the first job of a GTM engineer
data.name: No vendor has the full picture so enrichment is a waterfall

data.brief: With every primitive exposed via API, non-engineering teammates at Warp — developer relations, social — built their own Slack-bot agents (mention triage, sentiment, proposed replies) and research agents, without engineers. The "builder" expands to non-developers when the platform exposes primitives instead of a UI; the generalization is that domain experts, not developers, hold the most interesting intents
data.name: Non engineers ship agents on the sdk

data.brief: Inside YC's own transformation the shift crossed the technical line: media, events, and finance staff who never opened a terminal are writing skill files and cron jobs; one finance person collapsed ~100 Excel workbooks into an app she built with internal OpenClaw + the company brain — "she's not a programmer, she's a manager of agents now, and everyone at YC is"
data.name: YC media, events, and finance staff now write skill files and manage agents

data.brief: Nori runs its real artifacts as agent-written HTML in production: actual board decks, sales decks, docs, and marketing videos ("literally just divs all the way down") built end to end by coding agents from company data (call transcripts, email); claim: a 10-hour deck is really ~25 minutes of thinking once formatting/branding fiddling is removed — against a world pouring "~34,000 human years a day" into slides
data.name: Nori ships real board decks, docs and videos as agent-written HTML in production

data.brief: Dated product moves toward shared human+agent workspaces: Notion launched HTML blocks in pages the morning of the talk (agents can embed interactive simulations in docs); the week before, it launched coding agents living inside Notion (Claude and Cursor); Notion's team now builds much of its own code inside Notion for the shared-space benefits — plus multiplayer chat threads where multiple humans and multiple agents converse in one visible space ("one-on-one conversations → Slack channels") and agent-written plan docs that teammates comment on in place
data.name: Notion ships HTML blocks, in-doc coding agents, and multiplayer human+agent threads

data.brief: Notion's auto model handles ~75% of its AI traffic; the harness is built as model interoperability (multi-model, cache-kill and mid-transcript switching investment), routing by traffic pattern (Opus-class for large-scale data analysis, never for email triage — "we'd be ripping you off and ourselves"), with whole-trajectory evals (Parallel web search) driving choices.
data.name: Notion's auto model routes ~75% of AI traffic across vendors

data.brief: Notion runs its own software factory in production: agents orchestrated inside live collaborative documents (not markdown files) — Claude agent scopes a spec via the new managed-agent capability, humans and PMs get tagged in, Decagon collects customer-voice data, Claude Code opens the PR, Codex reviews it; almost all polish/large-feedback work internally is coordinated this way, with >3 minutes saved per task at customer scale.
data.name: Notion runs a production software factory orchestrated in live documents

data.brief: Enterprise-scale numbers for AI-skill risk, from a regulated bank's product-security team: over 2,000 skills scanned before marketplace distribution (stated as the baseline for the talk — "now there is much more than that"), yielding more than 1,500 identified risks (a single skill can carry several, so this is not a count of bad skills), of which roughly 1,000 were remediated immediately and a small number were blocked outright before reaching the marketplace. A historical back-scan of skills created before the gate existed surfaced further risks, which were filed into the standard vulnerability-management programme rather than handled ad hoc.
data.name: Nubank scanned 2,000+ AI skills before distribution and found 1,500+ risks

data.brief: Headline production claim with numbers attached: generating eval data in simulation instead of waiting on production data lets Nubank ship agents 20x faster — the loop drops from weeks to under a day, sometimes hours. Breakdown given: changing the agent harness (prompt, tools, anything around the LLM) still takes a few hours; running offline evals goes from days to fast because a simulated user replaces hand-curated data; and confidence that a version will do well in production goes from an A/B test that "takes forever" to a few hours. Production evidence: average TNPS across five production customer-support agents rose over a few quarters from "not so great" to approaching human quality; one agent's TNPS doubled; self-service rate improved across the board and by 4% in one case; simulation caught a regression and a self-service-rate drop before either reached production. A KDD paper on the work is to be presented in Korea in August.
data.name: Simulated eval data lets Nubank ship agents 20x faster

data.brief: Nvidia's 2025 position paper "SLMs are the future of agentic AI" cited as the production-readiness stamp: small language models are sufficiently powerful for agentic task loads at a fraction of LLM energy per task (~25%; task-specific models less still)
data.name: Nvidia position paper: SLMs are the future of agentic AI

data.brief: Nx built Polygraph: metadata analysis over thousands of repos → unified dependency graph → multi-repo sessions that read/write anywhere, with per-repo agents wired together and cross-repo CI treated as one vector (when module1's CI fails, it works out whether module1 needs a patch or the upstream UI lib is broken and everyone needs one). Savkin notes other organizations he's talked to have converged on similar solutions — "look at the problem and the solution conceptually, not the specific tool"
data.name: Nx Polygraph creates multi-repo agent sessions over a unified dependency graph

data.brief: The unit-economics story of AI retrieval infra, with numbers at both ends: in 2022–23 vectors-in-DRAM made obvious features unshippable (Readwise's working recommendation engine: $30K/month against $5K total other infra — killed; Cursor's founders: "the unit economics of all the vectors in DRAM are not working"). Moving source-of-truth to S3 with cache hierarchy repriced the category — ~$1/million vectors vs ~$100 for the cheapest prior working option — and Cursor, ~8 people, migrated everything in about two weeks for a 95% bill reduction (promised on napkin math before the software deserved it). Context that forced retrieval in the first place: 2022 context windows of 4–8KB meant "you had to reach for search very quickly." The generalization is still early: S3-for-KV-caching "barely anyone is doing… I think it will happen"
data.name: Object storage collapsed retrieval economics

data.brief: The bridging claim, stated as a hot take by a vendor sitting on both sides: "there's a very tight coupling between what observability is and what continual learning is" — agents act in environments and produce traces; learning is reading those traces and updating. The commercial corollary is blunt: "if you're a continual-learning company, you need traces, and if you have traces, you can try to do continual learning over your agents." A structural claim that the observability category and the continual-learning category are converging on the same asset
data.name: Observability and continual learning converge

data.brief: Observability's consumer is flipping from humans to agents: "observability used to be for humans — a UI you click, a graph you click"; 2.0 is coding agents plus skills for Pyroscope/Google Cloud, and telemetry is reframed as "smoke thrown off your system" that tells an agent which code path ran (without it, "there's a million paths it could have taken"). Vendor claim: observability platforms are becoming tied to the *fix*, not just the signal.
data.name: Observability's consumer flips from humans to coding agents

data.brief: Logs "change everything the moment we switch to agents" — too much thinking to consume. The replacement is hook-level interception emitting traces that carry the agent's goal, reasons, belief status and a confidence score per decision, so that an operator can see where a 20–30-step agent got stuck and whether an answer was inferred. Observability re-targeted from events to judgment
data.name: Observability must capture judgment not logs

data.brief: A data-quality engineer blocked a CSV-to-Parquet migration for about a year ("Parquet is way worse, it doesn't work"), with no articulable reason, while the daily ~1 TB CSV drop to S3 strained the pipelines. Watching her work on site revealed the cause: she downloaded CSVs to a Windows machine and double-clicked them to spot-check quality, and Parquet had no native viewer.
data.description: An overnight Parquet viewer got the migration approved in two days; pipeline execution fell from ~17 hours to ~2. Generalized tells that an FDE should watch for on site: any task done more than once, copy-paste between tools, tool or tab switching, phone-out mid-task, and visceral exasperation ("well, I have to").
data.name: A year-long Parquet migration block was unlocked by an overnight file viewer

data.brief: The Q1 measured result, and the surprising one. Goal: get a Qwen 3.5 thinking model on SWE-bench to stop taking up to 80 turns and call its submit tool before turn 40. Task-complete call rate rose from ~22% to ~60% with the test pass rate flat (in fact slightly up), so the behaviour was added without regression. The surprise is mechanical: the rollout is conditioned on a production trace that never called the tool, so "the teacher doesn't force the tool call — it just starts to force the reasoning path towards the tool call without ever actually changing the tool call." Adding one on-policy step to an otherwise offline setup raised SWE-bench pass rate further
data.name: Offline distillation shifts behaviour

data.brief: Running agents on-device is a three-way constraint problem — space (weights + compressed state history + planning artifacts + render headroom), time (plan within a 16 ms / 60 Hz frame or the game janks), energy (battery; NPUs not yet optimized for agentic loops) — solved via a constraint graph with soft-constraining tradeoffs; base model intelligence (ARC-AGI level) is not yet enough for the most complex game decisions
data.name: On-device game agents face a space/time/energy constraint budget

data.brief: NYT experimental thesis: move game-agent intelligence on-device for lower latency (no cloud round-trip), privacy (compute stays in the device's security zone), offline play, and personalization; the future of game AI need not be one giant centralized brain but billions of small local brains, each shaped by its user
data.name: NYT experiments with on-device agentic intelligence for mobile games

data.brief: On-device SLMs are shipping as platform defaults: Google's Pixel 10 Pro ships with one, and Chrome exposes built-in Gemini Nano via the Prompt API — web apps get local inference without shipping a model, and product AI can target what's already on the device
data.name: On-device SLMs are shipping as platform defaults

data.brief: A former VP of Engineering deliberately stayed solo (with design/DB support) to see how far AI goes before hiring, and rebuilt a full agent-native email client alone since January without writing code. Claim: one engineer with a compounding system beats full teams that use AI without one — the thin-team thesis stated as a lived experiment
data.name: One engineer with a compounding system beats teams

data.brief: Stripe's framing: about one in four people already use AI to research purchases, and in the past year Google, OpenAI and Stripe laid the infrastructure for agents that "decide, act and transact on your behalf," with UCP as the shared language for initiating, updating, completing and cancelling purchases across many agents and merchants. Research is done; transacting is the frontier
data.name: One in four shoppers already research with ai

data.brief: The largest real-world study of ambient-scribe notes: ~1 in 20 with a harm-capable error, ~1 in 5 with an important omission, >1 in 10 with a hallucination — in production, in about a third of US practices, with physician AI use doubling and no adverse-event reporting. A doctor's reading of last week's notes from three leading scribes: the dangerous errors read as routine, and almost all of them sit below what a strong automated check catches
data.name: One in twenty production clinical notes carries a serious error

data.brief: Clay's agent architecture for deal cycles that last weeks or months: an agent per account with persistent state, dormant until a trigger or heartbeat wakes it, loading fresh context from the data and orchestration layers, writing only to agent-owned CRM fields, waiting before re-engaging a lost deal. The learning phase — the agent updating what works per account — "is not yet fully resolved in GTM"
data.name: One persistent agent per account woken by heartbeats

data.brief: Cold email answers at 0.5–1% across ~20M messages and falls yearly, so each contact is precious and an agent that misbehaves loses revenue; the practical work is domain reputation (send as the rep or from agent-owned domains with reply routing), multi-channel coordination (stop sequences when a meeting books) and the human–agent handoff, which the speaker calls the hardest problem in GTM engineering
data.name: One reply in a hundred makes agent execution errors expensive

data.brief: The adoption mechanism that worked: rather than broad mandates, invest in one high-value skill — here "ship it," covering everything from code-complete to PR-ready including CI failure loops — and let its reliability do the persuading. That it often runs over an hour initially scared people and became the point: "once they saw the value they get invested, because it's one skill which tells them this AI thing can actually work for me, I don't need to constantly babysit it, I can trust it." Reframed explicitly as expectation-setting — "it's good if agents take too long, that means you can go off and do other things and you have confidence they're doing the right thing"
data.name: One trusted skill converts skeptics

data.brief: The Q4 measured result, on a real customer constraint: a coding agent had to emit a hyperlink format dictated by a customer's harness, a format "very very out of distribution for previously post-trained models." Adding a format reward degraded overall coding performance; SFT on correctly-formatted traces did too. Online hinting — roll out, then inject a hint referencing *that* rollout ("in your prior rollout you formatted hyperlinks like this; next time format them this way") — moved correct formatting from ~15% to ~80%, while applying the same static hint to every rollout climbed "far less." Direct A/B evidence that hint provenance, not hint content, carries the gain
data.name: Online hinting beats offline on ood

data.brief: Two weeks after GA only 20% of the go-to-market org had tried the assistant, and the owner spent 60–70% of the following months on demos, adoption dashboards, manager comparisons and executive sponsorship — "if we hadn't, we'd be at half of where we are." Internal AI initiatives fail in activation more than in technology, even after a pilot and a 10% beta with >70% weekly retention
data.name: Only a fifth tried it so activation became the job

data.brief: With agents producing hundreds and thousands of PRs a week, the three verification options fail on coverage or throughput — LLM-as-judge is probabilistic, tests check some inputs, human review can't keep up — and "none can say for all inputs the code is correct. Formal verification can." AWS's formal-verification product lead positions proofs as the verification layer that matches agent speed
data.name: Only proofs scale to agent throughput

data.brief: "Ontology" has moved from decades of academic niche to hype term — "probably thanks to Palantir" plus the rise of AI — and vendors are fighting the complexity creep: Neo4j's framing strips it to the key concepts of your organization and how they relate, expressed in human terms.
data.name: Ontology moves from academic niche to hype term; vendors fight complexity creep

data.brief: The macro argument: open weights will do to models what Open Compute did to servers — the industry standardizes on what it can build on, "even if it isn't the best thing," and the supply chain reorganizes to commoditize it. Fuel for the curve: ~$3T and 100+ GW of new datacenter capacity by 2030 (roughly doubling global capacity); inference hosts (Baseten, Fireworks) whose "whole purpose is to beat each other" with dedicated hardware, caching, batching and inference silicon; estimate that 1T-parameter inference costs ~90% less by 2030; and the 2014–15 cloud-price-war precedent, after which commoditized layers stopped being the competition and value moved up-stack. The plea: American labs should release open *weights* (not research — "that's what gives us the lead"; weights let others extract traces and train copycats "but not in a way that can leapfrog"), because if foreign models become the standard "there won't be a reason to switch back to GPT or Claude no matter what the marginal improvements are — and then we lose control over the development of this technology," including who funds safety research and whose values ship inside it
data.name: Open compute precedent for open weights

data.brief: Cost-floor claim for a frontier-competitive open model. Arcee AI's Trinity Large: 17 trillion tokens curated from public datasets only — no proprietary data, no closed-model usage ("no asking Claude to do this for you") — producing a fully open, US-made model that is competitive with the open frontier, matching GLM 5 and Kimi on many tasks and outperforming Claude on a couple. The team had not trained a model before the middle of last year.
data.description: Total cost, "across salaries, across compute, across R&D, across everything... including all the repetitions" and several other models besides this one: under $20M. Explicit rebuttal: "if I want to customize a model it's going to cost hundreds of millions of dollars — that's just not true", with high-six-figures-to-low-millions cited for a narrow-domain model and $20M framed as the upper bound because Trinity is general-purpose.
data.name: A fully open frontier-competitive model was built for under $20M total

data.brief: Together AI's kernels lead, from the serving vantage point on essentially every open model: the recurring "OpenAI and Anthropic are so far ahead" question should be "put to bed" — with M3, GLM and Kimi "the open-source frontier really can catch up, and it's not even that far behind". Song's version from the lab side: models were already accelerating their own development a year ago, that acceleration compounds, and it is how open-weight labs close the gap with frontier labs.
data.name: The open-weight frontier has caught up and is not far behind the closed labs

data.brief: A practitioner data point on open-model viability: "in the last 6 months open models have basically hit an inflection point in intelligence" such that LangChain no longer reaches for frontier models by default. The stated method is a waterline test — start with Opus or GPT-5.5 to establish the task is possible at all, then look back at those traces and ask whether an open model can match it. On the Harvey legal benchmark they matched Opus's trace-judging capability with an open model at roughly one to two orders of magnitude lower cost, closing the gap through harness engineering informed by reading Opus's traces. A second economic note: high-volume inference can shift from token costs to hardware costs — "run a cluster and I get unlimited inference, then spin it down"
data.name: Open models hit the intelligence waterline

data.brief: The agent moved from Claude to GLM 5.2 via Hugging Face inference providers (Together, Fireworks, Cerebras behind one compatible endpoint) — "beats Opus 4.8 on Cursor's bench and is cheaper… there's no reason not to use it." Open models "are getting great — GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 — we are able to replace closed models with open ones" for this class of background agent
data.name: Open models run the outreach agent

data.brief: The control argument extended from weights to outputs: closed providers monetize your usage the way cloud-era platforms monetized your data — usage data improves their models directly or as an acquisition signal — while their ToS "do a lot to try to obfuscate" that you shouldn't train on Claude/Fable/GPT-5 outputs. With open models you save every trace from your own harness, fine-tune smaller models on them, or mine them for signals to build environments — "owning your stack, owning your intelligence… it's also owning your outputs." The Open MDW license (adopted by Nemotron and Trinity) exists precisely to make output-training explicitly permitted rather than merely tolerated
data.name: Open outputs ownable data

data.brief: Cited 2026 Open Proof Corpus / "Beyond Correctness" result: a sizable gap between correct final answers and correct proofs even in fully verifiable math, with reward hacking observed up to Erdős-problem level; the authors conclude this poses significant risk for critical applications — and it is worse in domains where the final answer cannot be verified at all
data.name: Open Proof Corpus: correct answers outpace correct proofs even in verifiable math

data.brief: Proposed answer to shifting offense economics: the defense must be the models themselves — specifically an array of strong open-source models, post-trained per-environment for cyber and run fast on specialized hardware, made available to every company, rather than relying on "two companies everyone knows"; speed (attacker vs defender) is the decisive variable
data.name: Proposed cyber defense: per-environment post-trained open-source models

data.brief: Once replay existed and cost ramped, he rebuilt every request against open-source models and switched: "I don't have any third-party APIs anymore," including a local model on the laptop — "good enough for what I do; for coding, I don't know." For the background-agent class (briefs, transcription, triage) the frontier model was swappable
data.name: Open source models good enough for background agents

data.brief: "A year ago 'open superintelligence stack' felt like marketing; now it's just what it is" (paraphrase): open models are superhuman at many things, and a full open stack exists to train/deploy your own — 10,000+ GPU marketplace, Prime RL, Verifiers + Environments Hub, hosted lab; customers train models on their own production workflows
data.name: The open superintelligence stack is now real, from GPU marketplace to hosted lab

data.brief: Open-data counterweight to lab-private corpora: after DeepSeek-R1 showed what reasoning data buys, Bespoke started Bespoke Stratos and then formed the OpenThoughts consortium (Stanford, UC Berkeley, UW) to publish both the dataset and the curation recipe, with a paper whose main figure is a scaling curve for the recipe. Counterintuitive findings released with it (multiple answers per question beats more questions; stronger teacher is not a better teacher; answer filtering and synthetic rewriting underdelivering). Uptake cited on stage: Microsoft's CSO tweeting the work, John Schulman describing internal use at Thinking Machines.
data.name: An open consortium publishes a reasoning dataset and a scaling law for its recipe

data.brief: The steel-man the moderator explicitly asked to arm the audience with: trust ≠ safety (a "weaponized" conflation), and on trust the asymmetry runs *against* closed models — "you don't know what went into them; the same is true for closed models, even more so." Open models are files of matrices you can inspect, served by code you can read (Prime RL, vLLM, SGLang); it is "rather straightforward to validate what data went into a model" from the weights alone; NVIDIA additionally publishes the data-mixture spreadsheet ("a couple trillion tokens of this data set…"), the datasets, and the environments. The only way to be sure the output is what you expect is a model you run or can fully validate
data.name: Open weights are inspectable trust

data.brief: The platform's value proposition is balancing accuracy, latency and cost — for models and now for agents — and "cost is the number one concern these days," so DoorDash paired its LLM gateway with open-weights model hosting and has "seen significant impact already." A large consumer company moving inference in-house on cost grounds
data.name: Open weights hosting for cost at doordash

data.brief: Nelson's closing warning: "the importance of open models is becoming increasingly in question" — continued access to use/change/adapt weights is something the community "could feel less control over absent advocating"; a dedicated advocacy site (righttointelligence.org, per captions) launched days before the panel to organize non-technical supporters around "freedom of intelligence"; panel consensus: open source is why local AI exists at all, and it now needs active defense
data.name: Open-weights access is increasingly in question and needs active defense

data.brief: "We're at an inflection point where raw intelligence lead doesn't matter as much anymore": open-weights models (largely Chinese) are powerful enough that "you don't always need the best one," and cost now dominates. Cline's real-repo test — skeptical of benchmarks, they ran GLM vs Opus on an actual Cline bug: both fixed it; GLM used 2× the tokens at half the cost, cleaned up dead code, and verified the build compiled before finishing; Opus was faster with half the tool calls but left type errors and broke the production build ("GLM was trained to spend more tokens verifying its output — fine, the tokens are cheaper"). Adoption following: Coinbase's CEO reports defaulting to GLM and Kimi in the internal gateway, cutting AI spend nearly in half while token usage grows; more businesses expected to build internal routing for dollar-efficiency, even at the cost of the newest closed-tool features
data.name: Open weights value inflection

data.brief: OpenAI's shipping cadence collapsed from a new model every ~15 months to roughly every 6 weeks; GPT-5.6 series previewed the week before the talk; capability phases (completion → inline prediction → command-K edits → models testing their own work → long-goal autonomy) each went from mind-blowing to mundane within months
data.name: OpenAI model cadence collapsed from ~15 months to ~6 weeks

data.brief: OpenAI's data-agent blog post: six layers of context required to make a data agent work on (structured) warehouse data; key conclusion — the dataset's source code is the most important context to preserve
data.name: OpenAI: six context layers make a data agent work; source code matters most

data.brief: An OpenAI core-data/AI-infrastructure engineer states as the talk's whole program that most production agent failures are not model failures but harness failures, and formalizes it as a production contract: the model proposes, the harness commits, the receipt proves it. The model may suggest a message, a tool, an edit or a command, but "the model is not the production boundary" — the harness owns the state transition, the authority check, the ordered commit and the evidence. Car analogy for the split: the model is the engine, the harness is steering, brakes, road rules, dashboard and black box; "a powerful engine with no brakes is not autonomy, it is a liability with good acceleration".
data.name: Model proposes, harness commits, receipt proves it — agent failures are harness failures

data.brief: OpenClaw shipped a community-contributed "trusted proxy auth" mode (Taylor's Feb 2026 contribution, maintainer-specced): an identity-aware proxy now gates the gateway/control plane, replacing an auth token in the websocket query string + per-device pairing — security hardening for a self-hosted agent that is also a UX win
data.name: OpenClaw shipped trusted-proxy auth, gating its control plane with an identity proxy

data.brief: A dated adoption discontinuity: OpenRouter's auto-router ran ~2 years with "no real usage" (people wanted specific models; it was a discovery play) — then exploded around January 2026 with OpenClaw, whose ~10-minute heartbeats to your default model made Opus-as-default economically absurd. One very popular app with two completely different intelligence needs, plus open models good enough for the low tier, segmented the market overnight; "a lot more segmentation blossomed afterwards" into today's router products. The fusion rationale generalizes it: "you want to benefit from all the data being trained on across all the labs, and not just the data from one lab"
data.name: Openclaw heartbeat segmented the market

data.brief: OpenClaw's growth measured in issue numbers: Taylor's issue was #1560; two weeks later numbering was near 16,000 — contributors must rebase constantly to keep PRs mergeable; his stale PR was auto-closed during a vacation
data.name: OpenClaw issue numbers jumped ~1,560 to ~16,000 in two weeks

data.brief: Method and finding: OpenClaw's public issue tracker is used as an open case study of harness failure, yielding five reproducible shapes — state hole, overlapping writers (load-modify-save race where two locally-correct writers produce one wrong outcome), dangling tool call (tool call with no matching result; the agent "simply looks stuck"), approval drift, missing edge proof. Claim attached: these are all classic distributed-systems failures — timeouts, retries, idempotency, locks, ordering, state ownership — not novel AI failures.
data.name: OpenClaw's public issue tracker yields five reproducible harness failure shapes

data.brief: OpenClaw (85k stars in one week) gets shell access, email, files, calendar, persistent memory. Snyk demonstrated prompt injection exfiltrating API keys via spoofed email. Palo Alto: "persistent memory turns point-in-time exploits into stateful, delayed-execution attacks." China banned at state enterprises.
data.description: Cisco's security team tested a third-party OpenClaw skill and discovered it was performing data exfiltration without user awareness. Following this and broader security concerns, Chinese authorities restricted state-run enterprises and government agencies from running OpenClaw AI applications on office computers in March 2026, as reported by Bloomberg and Reuters. OpenClaw is an open-source AI agent tool for developer workflow automation that had gained rapid adoption but whose skill repository lacked rigorous vetting for malicious submissions.
data.name: Users giving unvetted AI agents shell access + all their data

data.brief: Production migration off a framework: OpenGov's agents team started on LangGraph, outgrew it as the team scaled and use cases evolved, and rebuilt a bespoke Effect-native agent loop for full control — tracing, structured concurrency, fine-grained logging, and dependency-injected model hot-swapping come from the general-purpose effect system rather than an agent framework
data.name: OpenGov outgrew LangGraph and rebuilt a bespoke Effect-native agent loop

data.brief: Open-weight models are now strong enough for moderate tasks and RL-expandable upmarket — "Kimi [K2.6] was probably the first time an open model outperformed [GPT-5.2]; GLM [5.2] is another bombshell" — functioning as the credible alternative that lowers customers' cost barrier and puts downward pricing pressure on the frontier oligopoly; the gap to frontier gets covered in ~6 months, so be prepared now.
data.name: Open-weight models are credible alternatives pressuring frontier pricing

data.brief: The moat claim, stated as an engineering necessity: models are "incredibly capable… especially over the last 6 months," but for an ops agent to succeed it "has to have an underlying learning system" that captures how *your* system operates — service interactions, hotspots, current causal chains — and keeps that understanding current as the system evolves faster and faster. Every company is unique, so the knowledge system is where Resolve says it spends its time; the same learned context is offered over MCP to augment customers' own agents. Execution loads the dashboard; the learned context says the metric smells off
data.name: Ops agent value is learned context

data.brief: "Everyone can have the same model, the same agent, the same harness" — shipping is now the easiest part (a whole product or startup in days, 100k lines of code, lots of tokens); the internal system that closes the post-launch loop — detect, diagnose, fix, feel the health — is the differentiating asset, and the tight feedback loop is "at least as important as the product itself, sometimes more"
data.name: Shipping is now the easiest part; the post-launch loop is the differentiating asset

data.brief: Reported results: on LiveCodeBench, GRPO "saturates around Sonnet-level performance and doesn't really push the frontier," while OPSD reaches new territory because it shifts distributions rather than sharpening them. A second, counter-intuitive result on cost — where RL trains models to think longer for better scores, OPSD collapses the tokens needed on hard problems, which the speaker calls the exciting part for token efficiency. Scaled at Trajectory to 120B, 500B and one-trillion-parameter models, and to a 12B model on Mercor APEX agents requiring 100+ tool calls, where it "has even surpassed RL"
data.name: Opsd beats grpo past saturation

data.brief: The algorithmic claim: by making the teacher the same model with a hint, OPSD gets an online task distribution, on-policy sampling, parallelism of one, and per-token dense reward simultaneously — where SFT, DPO/RLHF and GRPO each sacrificed at least two. The parallelism collapse is the operationally significant part: "we don't need a group of eight to roll out, just a single example," which removes the environment-replica infrastructure that makes RL expensive. Reward density is the other: matching log-probs across a ~65k vocabulary per token instead of "drinking through a straw" from one end-state scalar, likened to being graded 87/100 on an essay with no other feedback
data.name: Opsd satisfies all four criteria

data.brief: Kus names one model change as the pivot of the last year: "Opus 4.0 to Opus 4.5 — suddenly you got a model that could do instruction following at really high scale; to me the beginning of the epoch of the new agent models." A senior enterprise builder attributing the approach-ladder's latest rungs (planning agents, recursive agents) to a model capability step rather than to harness work — a measured counter to the corpus's harness-first consensus
data.name: Opus 45 began the agent model epoch

data.brief: Concrete private-eval result: three long-horizon, hard-to-verify finance tasks taken from three real-world vendors — an ARR waterfall reconciliation, an LBO valuation memo, and a long/short pair trade — run with robust deterministic verifiers paired with a correctly applied LLM judge.
data.description: Findings: Opus 4.8 scores worse than 4.7 on many of the rubrics, traced by rubric analysis to over-engineered self-reflection introduced between the versions; and GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8 land within three points on the same task while failing in exactly opposite directions — GPT nails the arithmetic and misses the methodology, Opus nails the methodology and loses the arithmetic. Claim: agnostic benchmarking of this kind lets you read off where each team's post-training went, and the results ship to labs as an RL-environment report that no leaderboard number exposes.
data.name: Opus 4.8 regresses against 4.7 on private long-horizon finance rubrics

data.brief: The subtlest finding, and the one most useful to anyone building evaluations: even the oracle condition — handed the correct memory for every loop — does not reach maximum performance, "because the Oracle provides the right memory but doesn't force the model to use it. The model can get the right memory and still retrieve the wrong information, or choose to ignore it, or be confused." Retrieval quality therefore has a hard ceiling below perfect, and a measurable share of memory-system failure is *utilization* failure rather than retrieval failure. Ablations with arbitrary, wrong-step and most-recent-step memories all confirmed the ranked policy as best
data.name: Oracle does not saturate

data.brief: Orbis's production answer: distribute the corpus across parallel KV-cache buckets with a supervisor model interrogating them; bucket assignment is deliberately order-free because domain-organized buckets fail in practice — with dense cross-document relationships, "the supervisor tends to ignore domains that at first glance seem irrelevant"; net result claimed: knowledge-building significantly faster than GraphRAG with more accurate answers than simple RAG
data.name: Orbis shards corpora into parallel KV-cache buckets under a supervisor model

data.brief: Stated rationale for the manager layer: opening Claude Code immediately burns ~25% of context on how-to-do-the-task scaffolding (CLAUDE.mds, skills, MCPs); the manager instead holds what-to-do context — spec, goals, "all the other Slacks Jeffrey sent me in the last 2 weeks" — and compiles brief messages into reasonable specs
data.name: Claude Code burns ~25% of context on scaffolding; the manager holds what-to-do context

data.brief: Because session capture crosses developer boundaries, every developer's agent taps the whole organization's session history: ask "did anyone ever add a vector index to the PR collection?" and load the relevant prior sessions; replicate the approach of an engineer you respect so cross-repo code stays consistent instead of every implementation being bespoke; a thousand engineers' sessions are accessible to each of them — "almost like the Borg… one big hive mind", giving the agent more context than any single developer holds
data.name: Every developer's agent taps the whole organization's session history

data.brief: Stated core differentiator: making individual engineers 10x faster is fine and still valuable, but the unlock is making an organization 10x faster — "including every single person that might be technical or non-technical across the company". Single-point tools that are just CLIs or just IDEs are argued to structurally fail at this, which is why the deployment is sold as a partnership rather than a seat.
data.name: The unlock is making an organization 10x faster, not individual engineers

data.brief: Repeated unprompted enterprise demand (heard "six or seven times") for a new offering: not deployment help but organizational redesign — whom to hire, what job descriptions, how to rearrange teams and processes to capture value from AI tooling; Cursor is now standing up an offering for it
data.name: Repeated enterprise demand for organizational redesign, not deployment help

data.brief: 2026: the first partial-reprogramming ("OSK", Yamanaka-factor-based) medicine is entering human testing — ~20 years after the 2006 discovery (2012 Nobel)
data.name: First partial-reprogramming (OSK) medicine enters human testing in 2026

data.brief: Osman's public prediction: GLM 5.2-class intelligence on a single RTX 5090 (32 GB VRAM) within ~18 months (late 2027), framed as conservative — and his prior track record backs it: a viral December post predicted Opus 4.5-quality (garbled "OBS 4.5") running locally on a single RTX Pro 6000, which happened by March, ahead of schedule
data.name: Osman predicts GLM 5.2-class intelligence on a single RTX 5090 within ~18 months

data.brief: A founder who owes his company to open source declares its community half dead: GitHub has become "an archive of slop PRs and issues and security reports," the old sense of community replaced by "deep skepticism and distrust of each other's responsible use of these tools." The lockdown responses are structural, not rhetorical — Zig bans AI outright because AI assistance breaks the grow-trusted-contributors loop that PR review actually exists for; curl is DDoSed by AI bug reports into considering ending decades of bug bounty; tldraw auto-closes all PRs; GitHub productized disabling third-party PRs. Root cause named: when generation is nearly free, unverified contributions are net-negative, and the community "is just not worth cultivating anymore, especially because building software is so cheap"
data.name: Oss community collapse under slop

data.brief: Yegge + audience consensus: open models ~6–7 months behind frontier ("mythos-class") capability, gap shrinking — capable attack models becoming freely available
data.name: Open models ~6–7 months behind frontier capability, gap shrinking

data.brief: The integration shape: no code changes — a boundary annotation on any method (LangChain or otherwise) floats I/O to a tenant-resident ledger and receives control-plane actions, applied by a governor limited to developer-allowed actions; preview mode lets production teams tune thresholds before enforcing. Roadmap: the ledger feeds a self-learning module that generates and refines policies for failure modes not yet caught
data.name: Out of band annotation governs any framework

data.brief: Generalization claim: "we are entering the era of outcome-driven AI" — the question stops being which model is better and becomes how to steer AI toward the outcomes a domain actually wants. The winners will be whoever holds the best systems of record, turns them into unique datasets of situations-actions-verified-outcomes, and trains models against them — anti-fraud, healthcare, logistics, developer tools alike. Verified-outcome training is called far advanced in coding and essentially unexplored in finance and most other domains. Closing instruction to the audience: go look in your own data for situations across entities where outcomes can be verified.
data.name: The era of outcome-driven AI: the best systems of record become the moat

data.brief: Reported gains from utility-score memory, no retraining: tau-bench policy-following 66%→76% without skills, 80% with matured memories baked into skills; on multi-step agentic benchmarks (Humanity's Last Exam-style): baseline 35.7 → 47.5 with RAG → 58.2 with other memory systems → 61.3% with theirs; similar trend claimed on BigCodeBench
data.name: Outcome-weighted memory lifts tau-bench policy-following 66% to 80%, no retraining

data.brief: The metrics indictment with a dollar figure: rollout-only confidence intervals give ~20% coverage while appearing tight, so a deploy decision between models A and B is made on intervals that are actually overconfident — and "with 1M tasks and a 4% real performance mismatch at ~$12 per mistake, that's hundreds of thousands of dollars a month." An honest hierarchical interval instead reports insufficient confidence, prompting more eval rather than a wrong call. "A non-rigorous benchmark is misleading — for the field, and especially for your own decisions"
data.name: Overconfident evals cost real money

data.brief: Two more overnight units: turn a day's feedback JSONs into an eval set and let a harness hill-climb an LLM feature (or the internal code reviewer) until scores rise, without overfitting when told not to; and hand the agent business context, training data and cloud keys to clean data, synthesize more with a frontier ensemble, choose a model class, train two ModernBERT PII classifiers on a provisioned GPU sandbox and report — several pushed to production. ML work done autonomously overnight by a coding agent
data.name: Overnight hill climbs and model training

data.brief: Concrete agent-error classes formal ontologies catch that are "very tricky" to catch in English/prose rules: a second refund on the same order (functional property), a payout routed to the support rep instead of the buyer (disjoint classes), invented status values like "probably shipped" (enumerated ranges: paid, shipped, refunded — nothing else).
data.name: Formal ontologies catch agent-error classes prose rules cannot

data.brief: Build vs buy per layer: rent orchestration, email, CRM and enrichment because vendors do them well, but never outsource the context layer — the edge, the esoteric data model, the thing you must be able to debug. Internal agents turned out cheaper and faster to build than assumed; Notion's context layer is Notion — markdown agents read, hierarchies they navigate, designed for humans at once
data.name: Own the context layer rent everything else

data.brief: Product thesis restated for this talk: "the goal we're really trying to enable is more people to be able to become their own research lab — take ownership over the intelligence of their own model weights, optimize for the task they care about, with themselves as the experts steering the model", built on top of "the best and biggest open models in the world" for use cases that "don't all live in the training distributions of the big models". Paired with an honest admission that it is still too hard: "we're all here learning more about how it works because it's hard".
data.name: The goal is enabling more people to become their own research lab

data.brief: The economic thesis, from a 100-company/25-field enrichment test: rented context decays and every repeated query costs the same even if nothing changed, so renting forces corner-cutting (query less often, take fewer results, skip fields), leaving value unextracted; owned context is upfront cost then near-free retrieval and compounds as the web keeps changing. A computed tipping point (~15k entities in the test, use-case-dependent) above which building your own beats renting — driven by *frequency*, "the cost killer," which "is much lower than you think." A build-vs-buy inflection for agent context infrastructure
data.name: Owned context compounds

data.brief: A new deployment model: instead of selling software, acquire the services business and deploy AI from inside — "when the AI doesn't work, it's not their problem, it's our problem." More than half the team is technology staff deploying products into the field; the largest bet is a $6.3B take-private of the world's biggest corporate-travel platform. Forward-deployed engineering taken all the way to ownership
data.name: Owner operator deploys ai into acquired businesses

data.brief: Environment feedback as the fix for long sequences: the harness tracks page state end-to-end and tells the agent what just appeared, what disappeared, that the element blocking its target is gone, and that its click didn't happen — turning "agent debugging blind against a mute page" into an environment where it can locate failures and plan a long task sequence correctly
data.name: Explicit page-state diffs let agents diagnose failures and plan long sequences

data.brief: Adobe's content-management product assembling a personalized page per query in ~1 s of LLM time (~1.6 s round trip) at 2,200–2,300 tokens/s — Gemma 4 on Cerebras — "something we only dreamed about before." Blocks, copy, products and navigation re-composed for one user's intent; the "for you" page pre-generated from accumulated browsing signals. Enterprise web personalization moving from pre-authored variants to on-demand generation
data.name: Pages assembled per user in one second

data.brief: The MCP ecosystem is free today and, per a payments-infrastructure builder, will not stay that way: agents will need a wallet and an aggregator of paid tools rather than a credit card typed into every vendor's site. Live comparison: the same prompt with and without the paid-tool skill file — exact contact details vs a guessed email format — and a logged micro-transaction that paid for the answer
data.name: Paid mcp tools need a wallet not a card form

data.brief: Numbers offered as evidence the motion works: among public SaaS companies in the Fortune 500 ranked by average contract value, Palantir is first at ~$4M ACV, ServiceNow next at ~$1.2M, Workday ~$600K, and no other public SaaS company cracks half a million — reached at only a few thousand headcount.
data.name: Palantir tops public SaaS average contract value at ~$4M, more than 3x the next vendor

data.brief: A categorical pass-rate metric could not surface a hard instruction violation: the agent had been told repeatedly and explicitly that for legal reasons disclaimers can never be removed, and in edge cases it detected the disclaimer in an ad and removed it anyway — demonstrated on a public-parks ad whose "paid by" line the agent stripped. Only the reasoning trace showed the agent finding the disclaimer and then deciding to remove it; the aggregate percentage was silent.
data.name: Categorical pass rate stayed silent on a legally-mandated disclaimer removal

data.brief: The formal result: pass@k on a deterministic environment is proved equal to the replay agent's success rate — "a metrification of that exploit." A metric in wide use for computer-use evaluation shown to reward the exact memorization the replay agent exploits, so a rising pass@k does not distinguish capability from a compiled tape of prior successes. Construction-methodology evidence of benchmark unreliability, with a proof rather than an anecdote
data.name: Passk is a gameable metric

data.brief: Form3 (regulated payments) runs an agentic CVE-remediation system in production across thousands of repos; Infosec's framing — "is this automation or a supply-chain incident waiting to happen?" — reshaped the architecture (credentials pulled out of the agent)
data.name: Form3 runs an agentic CVE-remediation system in production across thousands of repos

data.brief: Phone, portal, X12 and FHIR answers come from different teams or vendors and can all agree on wrong information — a patient confirmed insured on every channel whose claim is then denied — so the system holds payer facts as provisional, expects updates, and learns each payer's reliability. Ground truth in claims work is earned, not received
data.name: Payer channels falsely confirm each other

data.brief: The design rationale AWS states outright: skills and inputs can be poisoned, so the payment path is decoupled from the agent's loop — deterministic, key-less for the agent, policy-controlled outside the payment stack, no agent-code change. The lethal-trifecta lesson applied to money: the reasoning that can be hijacked never touches the wallet
data.name: Payments run on a deterministic path outside the agent

data.brief: PayPal orders were synchronous; the approval token lets an agent start an order, the human confirm the instructions on PayPal, and PayPal hand back an opaque, expiring, merchant-bound approval the agent carries to checkout. Shipping to production for agent clients that offer PayPal — a large processor productizing human-in-the-loop agent purchases
data.name: Paypal approval token makes agent checkout asynchronous

data.brief: For autonomous payments among unvetted parties PayPal says the industry should converge on FIDO verifiable intents and AP2 mandates: a three-layer JWT (credential provider, user-signed instructions, agent signature) that lets each party verify its own slice without relationships. The highest-stakes row of the matrix "we haven't actually seen in production yet"
data.name: Paypal backs verifiable intents and ap2 for open payments

data.brief: Same model, same pelican, different medium: frontier models fail Willison's SVG pelican test (a wall of numbers no human could handwrite either), but asked for the same bird in HTML they succeed — structure the model can reason about, every line readable/theme-able/editable; presented as evidence against the "agents fundamentally can't reason about space" claim baked into benchmarks like ARC-AGI
data.name: Same model fails the pelican test in SVG but succeeds in HTML — the medium fails

data.brief: Amazon's answer — perception agents that read the rendered screen to complete the computer-use loop (act → confirm it worked, instead of fire-and-forget), need no API/backend (works on the majority of software that exposes none), and take point-and-annotate input as a precise low-loss instruction
data.name: Perception agents read the rendered screen to close the computer-use loop

data.brief: Amazon launched the first two pieces of its perception-agent harness open source: an annotation Chrome extension (mark screen elements → structured summary for the agent) and a design.md-driven verification tool (visual on-brand check + automated user-flow walkthrough → pass/fail report); building the rest in the open so "these patterns get better as more people use and break them"
data.name: Amazon open-sources the first two pieces of its perception-agent harness

data.brief: Enterprise agents keep memory in a logically separated database at partner, organization and user level rather than on a desktop, and it pays for repetitive multidisciplinary work — but memory across days steers users toward repeating yesterday's task, so the design must let anyone override it. A memory-layer deployment with its failure mode named
data.name: Persistent memory introduces bias in enterprise healthcare

data.brief: Persona-eval researcher/practitioner: the RPLA field's measurement apparatus — including the gold-standard InCharacter benchmark (80.7% personality fidelity) and the LLM-as-judge evaluators adopted for scale — systematically privileges fluency and personality consistency and has no mechanism to detect anachronistic compositing, the dominant failure mode; a top-scoring Hamilton "has read his own Broadway musical" (paraphrase). Full thesis: if the dominant failure is anachronistic compositing and evals measure fluency/consistency, the evals cannot detect the dominant failure
data.name: Persona evals reward fluency and can't detect anachronistic compositing

data.brief: Architectural reframe for role-playing systems: the persona lives in the configured encounter — prompt, primary-document anchors, temporal anchor, human curator — with the model as a swappable off-the-shelf component ("no more located in the weights than Hamlet is located in Laurence Olivier's body," paraphrase); context-window anchoring keeps documents intact and auditable where fine-tuning dissolves the archive into parameters, and it is a "kitchen-table capability" (free-tier model + documents + literacy) vs. fine-tuning's institutional one
data.name: The persona lives in the configured encounter, not the weights

data.brief: Three techniques converge on one finding: the persona is already inside the model and the engineering problem is elicitation and format, not knowledge. (1) Prompting works and always has — the seminal early work used a text-completion model with "I am a strong liberal... in 2016 I voted for ___" and sampled the completions. (2) Fine-tuning against known human distributions (Subpop) improved alignment on the supplied populations and nearly as much on unseen groups, which subsequent research reads as the model having a latent representation of those groups and simply lacking the survey task format — "LLMs aren't used to doing surveys".
data.description: (3) The strongest result comes from asking in the model's native format: let the persona answer in free text, then map that text to a 1-5 scale by semantic similarity to human-written anchor texts, which reconstructs not just the right value but the distribution shape that naive rating prompts flatten. Counter-finding in the same set: more persona detail is not monotonically better — one team's four increasingly elaborate persona constructions for voting patterns amplified model bias and moved results progressively further from reality.
data.name: The persona is already in the model; the problem is elicitation and format

data.brief: Two further failure modes that bound what personas can be trusted for. Prompt sensitivity: presenting the same question with the same two options in swapped order produced an order bias so strong that averaging the two runs collapsed the result to 50/50 noise — humans show a first-order bias, "but not to this extent" — so personas must be durability-tested under reorderings, rewordings and adversarial challenge. Behavior blindness: LLMs are trained on what people say, not what they do, so across a set of replicated social-science studies the model matched expert forecasters on surveys (natively text, measuring attitudes) and did measurably worse on field experiments (behaviors, which must be transcribed into text to enter the training data at all).
data.description: Working rule: triangulate toward behavior through attitudes rather than asking about behavior directly.
data.name: Option-order bias and behavior blindness bound what personas can be trusted for

data.brief: A Snap engineer's daily setup (mid-2026): a Slack-facing OpenClaw manager with task memory ("fix the skeptic agent" suffices — it remembers prior asks) drives a forked open-source agent-orchestrator that spawns git-worktree-parallelized Claude Code workers, which spawn their own sub-agents; works "maybe 70% of the time", and he judges his own managerial replies automatable — "I actually think an agent could replace me"
data.name: A Snap engineer's manager-worker agent org handles his work ~70% of the time

data.brief: The declared one-point takeaway from the creator of a major serverless platform: personal AI codegen breaks traditional cloud infrastructure. 25 years of cloud architecture "ran in the wrong direction" — one blessed version of an app on the developer's server for every user, which is convenient for developers and structurally forbids per-user customization — while mobile's alternative spent 15 years gatekept ("there's like five companies that can build mobile apps now"; easier to buy a gun than install unsigned software). His verdict on the current wave: vibe-coding platforms are targeting exactly this wrong substrate. The personal-software future needs per-user code instances — apps as numerous and disposable as documents
data.name: Personal codegen breaks cloud infra

data.brief: The practical thesis of the track's most accessible talk: the interconnected knowledge base people have wanted from personal-wiki tools for two decades is now generated rather than maintained — tags, sources, backlinks, entity indexes and browsable wikis all produced by agents over a raw markdown folder, with the human contributing only unstructured capture. "All of that is generated programmatically. I didn't write any of this, because all I have time to do is generate the raw ingredients, not connect it all together myself." Credited to a Karpathy gist and shown working over two unrelated personal corpora
data.name: Personal knowledge base as agent output

data.brief: "Age of personal software" in practice: Taylor builds his own tools (Claw Space workspace-file browser, MCP apps) by chatting with his self-hosted agent from his phone over Discord — Telegram rejected because channels aren't encrypted (his security-company CEO vetoed it)
data.name: Personal software era: building own tools by chatting with a self-hosted agent by phone

data.brief: Same-day software: the "Shape of Minds" interactive tool (commonalities across history's great minds over dimensions like thinking, obsessions, routines) was built in one morning before the talk, alongside a personal Slack-emoji search tool and on-demand learning reports — "it's all software on demand: whatever stream of consciousness you have, just ask an agent to do it for you"
data.name: Same-day personal software: whatever you think of, ask an agent to build
