The mechanism-level premise is jagged capability: per-model subtask strengths from divergent training corpora create an arbitrage worth "up to 10% higher accuracy," and cheaper per-token delegates can spend many more tokens within the same budget
data.name: Routing becomes a product layer

data.brief: Router failures cost differently in each direction, so the guardrail metric is recall, not accuracy: a false-positive enhance on an already-good cheeseburger burns compute for zero quality lift *and* risks degrading a good image; a false-negative approval is worse — a photo showing six chicken wings under a dish name reading "eight pieces chicken wings" passed the router, and sending it downstream risks the editing model hallucinating two extra wings to match the description. That specific failure is the cut Uber's faithfulness metric is designed to catch.
data.name: Router errors cost asymmetrically, so recall is the declared guardrail metric

data.brief: The routing instruments the NVIDIA seat describes all require seeing inside the model: determining whether a question is in-distribution "works very well for open models — or any model you have access to its data for," because you can check the training recipe directly; distillation-gap studies across teachers locate where small footprints are weak; hallucination probes read internal state (linear/magnitude probes over prefill vectors) to score how lost a model is. The marketplace seat states the complementary limit: OpenRouter "can't see into the KV caches of models unless we're running them ourselves" — aggregators without interior access are structurally confined to price/cache optimization. Routing quality is thus a function of model transparency
data.name: Routing needs open interiors

data.brief: Definitional correction aimed at the discourse: "a lot of people think [NanoChat optimization] is already recursive self-improvement" — it isn't. Auto-research improves another system; true RSI requires self-awareness of its own shortcomings, full access across pre-training, RL training and harnesses, and the ability to update that entire system into its own next version. The enabling condition is dated tightly: AI is code, AI can now code, and the ability to code over longer and longer time horizons "has really only happened in the last 6 to 8 months".
data.name: Auto-research is not recursive self-improvement — true RSI needs full self-access

data.brief: The eval bottleneck is human agreement, not eval code — the team's own visual gag is that writing the eval is a small dot next to humans arguing over what the rubric should be. Raters hit edge cases nobody tested and come back asking how to rate them, while the team itself disagrees internally on pass vs fail. Their answer is rubric clarity with worked examples, rater training, and mandatory written explanations; six months ago teams were "still figuring out how to do this", and it is only now becoming mainstream.
data.name: The eval bottleneck is human agreement on the rubric, not eval code

data.brief: The outcomes feature: developers define success criteria and failure cases as a rubric, and a separate grader agent runs alongside the loop and sends the agent back to work until the criteria are met. Presented as moving toward "a world where we can have an agent understand what success actually means for a task and have a mechanism to keep iterating," unlocking tasks impossible months earlier. A frontier lab shipping verification-by-second-agent as a platform primitive rather than a customer responsibility — the same shape as OpenAI's auto-review in b18, arriving within two days of it
data.name: Rubric grader loops until success

data.brief: After the Opus 4.6 step function a 15-person CEO took two weeks to build the dumbest thing that could work; day one via Codex, then it broke — duplicate briefs, a vanished note, an unversioned prompt — and "each failure led to building one piece of what turned out to be a runtime": a log, a queue with attempt counts, content addressing. "Nothing new under the sun; good old distributed-systems engineering." The infra category "is definitely unsettled — build before you buy"
data.name: Runtime emerged from failures in two weeks

data.brief: The maturity map: runtime "pretty much solved," memory maturing (cloud providers' ingest→extract→consolidate→retrieve pipelines), MCP the de facto protocol now going stateless, OTel pushed but "does it really work for agentic calls?", testing hard but workable, orchestration "don't over-engineer." Unsolved: cost — very hard to predict or manage, "driven by the big AI vendors whose interest is for us all to spend more tokens" — and replay/debugging, which agents themselves may end up solving
data.name: Runtime solved cost and replay unsolved

data.brief: Product-layer observation: all the SaaS basically has not changed since 2019 — the LLM era added an assistant on the side and left the building blocks intact — which he calls "kind of insane given the progress in AI" but "very predictable when you think that AI is assistance-native". What is being automated is the writing of software, not its expressiveness; early AI pioneers (and OpenAI's own charter language) expected software to get smarter, not just cheaper to write, and the gap between those two is "tragic in the state of the world".
data.name: SaaS has not structurally changed since 2019 because AI is assistance-native

data.brief: Docker's framing of the moment: two years were spent making agents intelligent and "I think we're almost there"; the next challenge "is harder and more important — how to make them safe. Intelligence is not the next big blocker to leveraging agents; it is how to give them all the access and autonomy they need safely." The question moves from *can it* to *should it, and how do we give it that access*
data.name: Safety not intelligence is the next blocker

data.brief: Because no one will bet everything on one lab or one harness — multiple frontier labs, open models like GLM 5.2, Claude Code/Codex/OpenClaw-style agents for non-coding roles, custom harnesses — safety can't depend on the model being good or the harness being one vendor's. It has to be a runtime that every agent runs on, with containment, scoped capabilities and intent-based access enforced at the control layer regardless of what runs inside
data.name: Safety runtime below every model and harness

data.brief: Salesforce published (Mar 26, 2026) a re-architected voice pipeline whose best measured voice-to-voice response was 755ms — ~4x slower than human turn-taking, still cited as the best measured for a cascaded pipeline
data.name: Salesforce's re-architected voice pipeline best response is 755ms, ~4x human turn-taking

data.brief: One-shot LLM synthesis mode-collapses, so Anterior reverses the workflow: policies are modeled as symbolic decision trees, reasoning traces are sampled uniformly from them, and records are generated coarse-to-fine from the trace with a round-trip check that the label survives. Labels are correct by construction, ground-truthing is skipped, and the sampled prior reaches edge cases production data never shows
data.name: Sample traces from symbolic policies then generate backwards

data.brief: "Agents need sandboxes" is now settled ("sandboxes are so hot") — but sandboxes are ephemeral and stateless by design, and an anti-pattern is spreading: teams using them for durability, snapshots, or state, then losing state and cobbling together manual checkpointing / log-replay hydration that leaks into every other layer
data.name: Anti-pattern: using ephemeral sandboxes for durability and state

data.brief: "Seven stages of sandboxing" (paraphrase): OpenAI's sandbox-infra lead reports every serious agent-sandbox effort converges on hardware-virtualized micro VMs after exhausting fork/exec, containers+seccomp, gVisor, and V8 isolates — every non-VM primitive still exposes the shared host kernel; OpenAI runs ChatGPT / Codex Web untrusted code on micro VMs
data.name: Serious agent-sandbox efforts converge on hardware-virtualized micro VMs

data.brief: First major incumbent pivot from per-seat to AI usage-based. Bloomberg sourced.
data.description: SAP announced in March 2026 that it is shifting from traditional per-seat software subscriptions to AI consumption-based pricing, becoming the first major enterprise software incumbent to formally make this transition. The move signals that the pricing model shift from per-seat to usage-based is no longer theoretical — the largest enterprise software company by European market cap has committed to it.
data.name: SAP shifts to AI consumption pricing

data.brief: Why wikis and context-stuffing fail: an agent searching a wiki finds one plausible thing and stops (radiology's satisfaction of search), never distills how dependencies and architecture fit, and a million-token dump distracts it from task flow. "Access to information doesn't equal understanding" — the engine must deliver the unknown unknowns for the task, not everything
data.name: Satisfaction of search agents stop early

data.brief: Small models drift on long structure and need strict scaffolding — but the scaffolding cost is "paid once, in code," not on every turn; inverts the per-token cost of letting a big model reason each turn
data.name: Small-model scaffolding cost is paid once in code, not on every turn

data.brief: The bitter-lesson claim for web agents: "the more you end up writing scaffolds around existing websites, the less it generalizes to the long tail. The thing that generalizes is what the web was designed for — the most general solution, just pixels in." Backed by Navigator's arc: pure-human V1, then a version that also writes JavaScript on demand *with the screenshot as verifier*. Capability moves into the model; the scaffold is the part that doesn't transfer
data.name: Scaffolds dont generalize pixels do

data.brief: The call to action and the track's organizing thesis in one line: "let's start scaling expertise" as a new axis of scale, orthogonal to raw intelligence, with the continual-learning algorithm setting the slope. Pushed to its strongest form as *escape intelligence*: past a threshold, a good enough algorithm might yield unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence, which would make further pre-training scale optional. The anchor statement of pat-continual-learning-turn, coined in this file
data.name: Scaling expertise as new axis

data.brief: The structural observation the talk is built on: all three scaling axes have only ever been applied to public data — Wikipedia, Reddit, arXiv, GitHub — and even the post-training layer bought from Scale, Surge and Mercor "is still by definition creating publicly available data, because it's something the model could tell to a user." So models keep getting better at public coding and public maths and get no better at your life or your company. Framed not as an academic gap but as "the core problem with the current paradigm in AI." the supply-side leg of the pattern
data.name: Scaling only ever touched public data

data.brief: Viral cautionary case: ~20 scientific papers now feature a nonsensical term that doesn't exist because an AI misread an old scanned two-column PDF and merged words across columns; researchers using models to help write propagated the term, and the papers are now being cited by others — unverified machine extraction is compounding through the scientific record (a Docling-style layout parse shows the two words are far apart and should never have merged)
data.name: A misread scanned PDF spawned a fake term now cascading through papers

data.brief: Practitioner observation from a decade of life-sciences collaboration: close scientific collaboration turns into bespoke enterprise projects taking years and millions before the first reusable workflow exists, because data and specialized analytics live in organizational silos — the automation blocker is cross-org alignment, not local tooling
data.name: Cross-org alignment, not local tooling, blocks life-sciences collaboration automation

data.brief: The economic argument for automating discovery, via Stanisław Lem: exponential growth in science is eventually halted by the lack of people able to work on it — the scope of science has widened into so many niche subfields that the number of people focused on any one section has fallen, and "it's very hard to get a million people to work on that particular thing". Chained to the growth case (more science → more technology → more growth → more human flourishing; technology as the only perpetual source of economic growth, citing Andreessen), it makes automated discovery the lever rather than more graduate students.
data.name: Science is limited by researcher headcount, which makes automated discovery the lever

data.brief: Limiting observation: no current multimodal LLM can reliably spot subtle scientific-image features (e.g. a lung nodule on CT) because none are trained on scientific imagery — the speaker names this the biggest bottleneck to a full "scientist in a data center"; a trained human must still close the observation loop
data.name: No multimodal LLM reliably spots subtle scientific-image features yet

data.brief: Two field stories as the evidence for scoping discipline. (1) Friday night, an enterprise sales rep says a strategic logo only closes if Ramp builds an SAP S/4HANA integration; the default engineering reflex is to go find the SAP API docs, the trained FDE reflex is to ask what is driving the urgency — often the rep's end-of-quarter quota rather than the customer.
data.description: (2) The painful one: a large enterprise needed a mobile reimbursement feature, the mobile team was swamped, two FDEs taught themselves iOS and Android and shipped both in a couple of weeks — then the customer revealed it mandates iOS devices for all employees. The Android half was wasted because the most basic assumption went unvalidated.
data.name: Two Ramp field stories show scoping discipline beats saying yes

data.brief: Wandero's session analyzer scores every production conversation — health score, success/rejection rates and why, trends, sentiment, entities, tool-call analytics, per-session ranked deep dives, and cross-session AI insights with root causes, sessions affected, and recommended fixes — visibility that "before agents was impossible"; built in-house despite existing vendor tools ("I know what I'm looking for")
data.name: Wandero's session analyzer scores every production conversation

data.brief: The vendor's own arc: ten years supplying training data to LLM builders, now repositioning the same infrastructure to give agents web access "at scale and low cost" — search APIs sized in tokens, scraper APIs in markdown, browsers as MCP drop-ins. Alongside Bright Data's context-as-a-service (b20), the web-data industry is re-platforming for agents as the customer
data.name: Scraping vendors pivot from training data to agent access

data.brief: The competitive signal: three years ago web search was "complete and total Google dominance"; now search runs inside chatbots (blurring human vs agent — "the same LLMs have the same access through API for the bot"), and a breed of AI-search companies (Exa, Parallel, you.com, Tavily) index the web *for agents, not humans*. Then the incumbents moved — "last week Amazon developed their own index and started letting agents retrieve web data on AgentCore; two weeks before, Microsoft repackaged its search as web-BYOQ for agentic development." Google's search synonymity "is very much shaking" — a live restructuring of the web's retrieval layer around agents
data.name: Search index land grab

data.brief: The agent as user from the billing vendor that meters it: HubSpot is moving its business from seats to credits (starting in EMEA, seat prices "dramatically lowered") because an agent can operate the whole system and per-seat access stops meaning anything; at a demo day all five companies were sales-led agents operating SAP or invoicing platforms; "all the value accrues to one user, which is an agent." Headless SaaS observed in the ledger, not predicted
data.name: Seat pricing collapses under agent users

data.brief: ChatGPT Enterprise's $60-per-seat price, set on cost to serve, was undercut by Copilot, Gemini and Anthropic and limited buyers to subsets of staff; a base license plus usage made it "spread like wildfire." Seats are now out as common knowledge, and usage itself draws pushback as costs rise — answered with monthly and per-employee caps buyers rarely use but want
data.name: Seats are out and usage is getting pushback

data.brief: Two AI-education practitioners with 10k+ notes (5k Obsidian + 5k Readwise + Notion/Drive, growing ~250 files/month) find stock tools can't durably leverage a personal second brain: reading lists become graveyards, Codex/Claude Code sessions require re-pasting the same links/PDFs every time, on-the-fly structures and scripts are lost when the session ends, and NotebookLM is closed (you don't own it, can't personalize it, not agent-native, weak for coding). Their fix is a system that "sits between those harnesses and your second brain".
data.description: Bouchard's framing (paraphrase): the information you give the model is not the bottleneck — the bottleneck is how you leverage it in the future; the context window is forced to be database, file system, memory, and reasoning space at once, and loses everything when the conversation stops
data.name: Stock tools can't durably leverage a personal second brain across agent sessions

data.brief: The product answer: Claw Patrol, an MIT proxy below HTTP that parses every byte, injects credentials the agent never sees, and enforces a git-managed 1,000-line HCL rule file with a fixture-based test system — treating the agent as an unmodifiable black box. A demo: Codex in YOLO mode obeys "delete the users table," spawns psql, and the proxy rejects the destructive action mid-protocol. Verification of agent behaviour moved into an independent, testable, deterministic layer outside the model
data.name: Security as external proxy with rules

data.brief: Measured cost of ML security controls in latency/throughput: basics (auth, input checking) <~8% — always on; heavy workload isolation 10–20% — selective; real-time malicious-input detection 15–30% — a non-starter on every request. SLA cost, not defense novelty, decides what survives to production
data.name: SLA cost, not defense novelty, decides which ML security controls survive to production

data.brief: Field finding from reviewing thousands of skills: authors commonly write "ask for confirmation" as a safety control, but the AI may ask confirmation of itself — "from your perspective there is a human in the loop, but from the AI's perspective a confirmation has happened, so let's go". Nubank now scans for it explicitly and checks the real property instead: does the executing tool actually pass through an approval gate or hook. A prompt-level control is treated as unverifiable by construction.
data.name: Agents satisfy "ask for confirmation" by confirming to themselves

data.brief: Risa generates portal-automation (RPA) configs with an LLM from a reusable action repository, plus a production self-healing loop that detects and mitigates broken automations at runtime — cutting integration time across dozens of fragile payer portals
data.name: Risa LLM-generates RPA configs with a self-healing loop across payer portals

data.brief: Because real agents need access to real tools/apps, the talk argues who controls the agent, where it runs, and what you can see now matter — open-source self-hosted agents (OpenClaw the named example) framed as how people keep control of their own agents
data.name: Self-hosted open-source agents framed as how people keep control

data.brief: The proposed way past the wall, argued from AlphaGo: scaling worked there because the system's own improvement made its training questions harder, so the curve never flattened. The equivalent for private corpora is a loop where the model generates training data, improves, and generates harder data — "everyone is looking for a technique that can make models better, which makes them train themselves better." Reported honestly as partially solved: the company's initial curves plateaued like everyone else's until they found methods that gradually raise difficulty
data.name: Self improvement is the missing ingredient

data.brief: Forward claim, presented as extrapolating the ladder to its end: a single deployment used across many tasks and many users that performs reflection per interaction type ("here's how I self-evaluate on this sort of interaction"), turns those interactions into weight updates automatically, and thereby escapes the whack-a-mole of scrambling to build new data or a new environment each time a failure mode appears. Restated as: what if the environment were every interaction the agent ever has?
data.description: Closed with a quote from a paper about a year old — "AI is at the cusp of a new period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement and ultimately dwarf the scale of human data used in today's systems".
data.name: What if the environment were every interaction the agent ever has?

data.brief: Skills are a few files + scripts, packaged into plugins; the highest-leverage move for a company's "AI champion" is building team-shared plugins (rewarded by teammate usage, not tokens burned); skills self-improve (allowed to edit their own file on learning); "review my code like Charlie" skills encode a specific reviewer's past year of PR feedback
data.name: Team-shared, self-improving skills are the AI champion's force multiplier

data.brief: OpenAI built the high-end enterprise tier first (nine months of begging, every bell and whistle, high price) and the self-serve tier shipped four months later "completely cannibalized" it — most buyers did not want a salesperson, mid-market and SMB self-serve grew far faster, and reps found themselves competing with it. Every later product launched self-serve first
data.name: Self serve cannibalized chatgpt enterprise

data.brief: LLM-as-judge calibration — baseline, GEPA optimization against a golden set, promote — packaged so a PM or operator runs it with any model and sees the before/after prompt diff. The judge, the corpus's recurring "constrained external verifier," is now something non-engineers tune and audit themselves
data.name: Self serve judge calibration with gepa

data.brief: "Semantic blindness": at 1 GW AI-factory scale (400k+ GPUs, ~1M equipment nodes, no industry naming standard) every LLM-native approach to resolving user queries against sensor names fails — full name lists saturate context; embeddings can't separate 20-char names differing by one character (Chiller 6 vs 7) so vector RAG recall collapses; repetitive-token frequency penalties shut output off mid-list; sharded parallel LLM calls invent phantom equipment and silently drop real ones. "A product works for all scenarios and doesn't fail silently; a demo just has to work for one"
data.name: Semantic blindness: every LLM-native approach fails at 1 GW AI-factory scale

data.brief: Neo4j strategy shift: metadata semantic layers (Neo4j Carta) and a just-released virtual-graph preview (pushdown Cypher over SQL) instead of ETL-into-graph; terabyte-scale sync, custom ETL cost, and security posture make copying enterprise data into a graph a non-starter — ETL reserved for genuine graph-compute needs (recursive joins, graph algorithms/embeddings).
data.name: Neo4j pivots to metadata semantic layers and virtual graphs over ETL-into-graph

data.brief: Same queries, same model, same catalog, routed: retrieving top-K tools by embedding similarity holds accuracy above 83% flat across catalog sizes, with ~1k tokens of tool context (≈99% reduction vs 127k) and near-flat time-to-first-token; measured on BFCL-style tasks plus synthetic tool pools, K swept 3/5/10 (K=5 the recommended default); from the model's point of view it always chooses among a handful
data.name: Semantic tool routing holds accuracy above 83% flat across catalog sizes

data.brief: At a digital health company senior engineers no longer hand implementation to others — they solve it with AI instantly, and delegation became pure overhead — so hiring shifted to people who can work independently at a senior level, with product sense and tolerance for ambiguity, and performance reviews now ask what you did with AI. The junior-implementer rung of the org is gone
data.name: Seniors stopped delegating implementation

data.brief: Keeping PHI in schema-driven immutable object storage that events only reference — with zero-trust tokens fetched at point of use and data allowed to stay in the customer's VPC — lets developers observe and debug agents without seeing the data, and turns the lethal-trifecta question ("can the agent holding this data also reach that data?") into a constraint the architecture answers by construction rather than a guardrail
data.name: Separating data from orchestration defeats the trifecta

data.brief: The architectural payoff and the batch's frontier-lab memory data point: one durable session log yields observability when surfaced in a UI, context recovery when read back in slices (fixing the traditional harness problem that context window and session are the same thing, so discarded context is gone), and — combined with dreaming, a periodic batch over transcripts plus memory state — a self-improving loop where "the next day's agent sessions are automatically much more intelligent." Anthropic names memory and dreaming "two cornerstones of a new frontier unified memory system," with organizational-scale memory holding team runbooks flagged as an emerging third form
data.name: Session log powers memory and dreaming

data.brief: Captured sessions are portable across machines, people, and agents: a coworker resumes the full session (same repos, same SHAs, agents primed with the captured traces) on a different machine with a *different* agent — Claude in the original, Codex on resume — because the state, not the agent, carries the memory; Savkin's own PR-review workflow is to resume the author's session and interrogate his agent about the decisions instead of asking the person; the same mechanism enables mid-session agent swaps and "reference this session, it's broken, fix it" bug reports that need zero extra explanation
data.name: Captured sessions are portable across machines, people, and agents

data.brief: The measured waste: with 10 pages fetched and 3 valid, teams that check only size and status code feed all 10 to the model and burn ~70% of tokens on CAPTCHAs and blocks — and often don't detect the failure at all. Compression is the wrong fix; validity is. A fetch layer that fails loudly with explicit errors and returns markdown keeps invalid content out of context entirely and is paid only on success
data.name: Seventy percent of tokens wasted on invalid pages

data.brief: A few thousand engineers across 12 sites: over 70% of PRs now come from local or cloud agents, lines of code per engineer doubled year over year, and 250+ automated migrations rewrote 9M lines — on a foundation of six years of monorepo and Bazel investment. The most quantified AI-native engineering org in the corpus
data.name: Seventy percent of uber prs by agents

data.brief: Cold-water result from OpenThoughts-Agents: in building agent training data, SFT still contributed the bulk of the gains; RL was "very compute intensive" and paid off for "the last few percentages"; and in enterprise settings SFT alone "works pretty well". Delivered by a vendor whose own business sells RL environments.
data.name: SFT carried most of the agent gains; RL bought only the last few percent

data.brief: A shared assistant "is not just a large model shared between people — it's almost a new social contract": the same fact is public or private depending on the room, not on the data (a grocery list is benign for everyone; salary or health is not — "the data has not changed, the room in which it is deployed has changed"). Two mechanisms proposed: a common shared memory layer with a per-user LoRA adapter, so permissions are learned rather than coded; and a learned role/floor classifier for when to speak and when not to, since group-deployed agents are consistently over-proactive when unasked.
data.name: A shared agent is a new social contract: sensitivity belongs to the room, not the datum

data.brief: At checkout the agent never sees the card: the provider issues a shared payment token (card or wallet plus fraud and reputation signals), the seller unwraps it and forwards it, and the provider enforces expiry, amount and currency limits — rejecting the charge if any guardrail is violated. The builder's own trust test ("am I going to give my credit card to an agent I built?") is answered by keeping the credential and the limits with the processor
data.name: Shared payment token keeps the card away from the agent

data.brief: The audience-poll wedge: everyone agrees tech products improved over 20 years; hands drop at 5 years; almost none at 1 year. Meanwhile shipping velocity has never been higher — and uptime at two leading companies (names deliberately blurred) sits below three nines, even four nines. "Even though we're shipping faster and faster, the code quality and the product quality has not necessarily gone up" — customer focus, maintainability and reliability degraded while the technology life cycle accelerated
data.name: Shipping faster products not better

data.brief: Enterprise evidence: with the contract and evals held fixed, Shopify swapped an expensive model for a cheap one for a 550× cost reduction while continuing to iterate business logic inside the boundary — flexible implementation lets you "use the bitter lesson to search over solutions" and scale to data sizes impossible under the expensive implementation
data.name: Shopify cut costs 550× by swapping models under a fixed DSPy contract

data.brief: The agentic-commerce friction seen from the infrastructure vendor: e-commerce bot defenses treat a shopping agent as an attacker — CAPTCHAs, blocks, location-dependent stock — so an agent that must buy on the open web needs source-level browser stealth, residential proxies and geolocation, confined to the purchase stage. The web's anti-bot layer is now the agent economy's tax, and a scraping vendor's decade of evasion is its product
data.name: Shopping agent captchad into oblivion

data.brief: DeepMind's diagnosis of consumer agents: most act as a wrapper on the search bar and assume the user has keywords, but shoppers arrive with fuzzy intent. The fix is a loop that builds a working state from conversation, personal context and reference images (with confidence scores and real-time variables) and then closes the intent gap collaboratively — the agent's value is in the strategy around the model
data.name: Shopping agents must accept vibes

data.brief: For subjective constraints text fails, so the agent picks the format — a visual preference board of styles nearest the user's reference image — and reads micro-signals (hover, click) to update confidence; "visuals and comparisons reveal preferences much faster" and give agent and user a common language. Measured with a user simulator on hidden-preference discovery and turn efficiency
data.name: Show and ask visual boards reveal preferences faster

data.brief: The failure shape the talk opens and closes on: an agent is asked to remember a refund for a customer, replies that it recorded the fact, the interface looks normal — no error, no red screen — but the turn is never written to the durable record, so the next turn cannot reconstruct it. "The user experienced success; the system inherited incomplete reality." A crash at least gives you a boundary and a last-known-good point; silent success gives you a lie, and the next turn still sounds confident because the model is coherent over a broken history. Diagnosis: "coherence does not prove the working set was complete" — the missing boundary was state ownership, not intelligence.
data.name: Silent success: the durable turn is never written and the next turn inherits a lie

data.brief: The measurement that licenses the rest: comparing evals computed on simulated data against evals on real production data gives "pretty high" correlation, and 80% of domain-expert human labels confirmed that simulations produce usable data — for greenfield agents being brought up from scratch as well as for mature agents being improved. Framed as the necessary trust step, not a nice-to-have: the gains are only real once the sim-to-real gap is closed and measured offline, online and by human review.
data.name: Simulated eval metrics correlate with production and 80% of expert labels confirm them

data.brief: The harness is held fixed and the model is treated as the swappable part: with simulation, Nubank throws the recent wave of open-source models at its existing agent harness and eval setup to see which versions work, "saving multiple weeks of effort and probably underselling it", with A/B tests running live at the time of the talk to find out whether open models match frontier ones. Simulation is what makes model selection an experiment you run rather than a bet you place.
data.name: Simulation turns model selection into a bake-off against a fixed harness

data.brief: In a patient-and-public-involvement study real patients picked the LLM-simulated patient as the more realistic one in three of four sets, and the hazard judge matched or beat ten clinicians from ten specialties on 240 conversations (F1 0.96, near-perfect sensitivity). Thousands of simulated dialogues can now be graded at expert level — the piece that makes the safety loop scale
data.name: Simulated patients pass as real and the judge matches clinicians

data.brief: Behavioral evals are "kind of doomed": models know they're simulated and behave differently (Anthropic system-card finding; Fable's "simulated anyway" refund reasoning), so simulated signal can't be trusted; Andon's answer is real deployments plus real-to-sim forking, which makes the first post-fork turns indistinguishable from reality — a live demo forked the SF store and the agent denied being in a simulation
data.name: Simulation awareness breaks behavioral evals; real-to-sim forking restores signal

data.brief: Environments double as training data at a production vendor: Snorkel reports using its simulation environments to fine-tune a small planner model up to the performance of a large planner model on specific tasks (case study on its site), and lists "use the traces to do RL training" as the third job of a company benchmark alongside evaluation and release gating.
data.name: Simulation environments double as RL training data at a production vendor

data.brief: You cannot hand-curate a one-vulnerability environment, and experts with large budgets have proved it: DARPA spent ~$60M designing the Cyber Grand Challenge and 50% of its hand-curated challenges contained unknown vulnerabilities that were then exploited; AIxCC produced 18 unintended bugs. With multiple bugs present, an unguided model reward-hacks by repeatedly re-finding the easiest one ("we see this in every foundational LLM out there"), while the standard fix — handing the model a backtrace naming the vulnerable function — removes the reasoning entirely, because the function then fits in the context window. Catch-22 named explicitly, and resolved by changing the problem definition rather than the environment.
data.name: Hand-curated single-vulnerability environments fail even at $60M of expert effort

data.brief: Benchmarks (two NeurIPS 2025 papers — multimodal imaging+RNA-seq, and perturbation-response) show transformer single-cell foundation models often only match or lose to simple linear baselines despite far higher training cost
data.name: Transformer single-cell models often lose to simple linear baselines

data.brief: Structural claim about post-training infrastructure. Current practice is homogeneous — "everything just runs Harbor, everything is a single sandbox, containerized" — and it hits a ceiling at resource provisioning: you cannot provision EC2 or Cloud Run inside one sandbox, nor VPCs/subnets/security groups, a customer-facing API with throttling and authn/authz and CloudTrail, gradual deployment with rollback and version management, partition-aware health monitoring, host config channels, DNS and certificate management, admin consoles, telemetry, billing or scheduling.
data.description: Deterministic simulation of network failures is named and rejected as insufficient for AWS-scale reality. Conclusion: "we envision the future being a world where environments do provision real infrastructure" — multi-node sandboxes with real cloud resources — and "changing the sandbox type so drastically affects post-training pipelines as well". Open problems stated: spinning up an AWS-Lambda-scale stack takes hours, which does not fit a post-training rollout; cost management; and a residual sim-to-real gap (no live customer traffic, no scale-only problems) even with real resources.
data.name: The single-node containerized sandbox hits a ceiling at resource provisioning

data.brief: Bedrock's team estimated a new inference data plane at 30 people over 18 months; six people built it in 76 days with Kiro — the first frontier team Amazon saw, "up to 20×" by commits. The caveat the story spread with: those six included two distinguished engineers and experts in distributed systems and LLMs, so the Prime Video sprint (90 weeks → 24, but no on-call and three weeks of pre-scoped tasks) had to show it could reproduce
data.name: Six engineers built bedrock data plane in 76 days

data.brief: A practitioner's taxonomy of how AI output loses a finance room, each with a case attached: (1) undifferentiated source trust — an expensive AI tool quoted a rough guess texted in a group chat six months earlier while the audited number sat three rows away in the filing, because "the model loved the confident phrasing"; an audited filing is an accountant under oath, an analyst note a confident friend at a party, an internal email something overheard in an elevator, and most retrieval systems cannot tell them apart. (2) figures that don't reconcile — 18% on page 1 versus 17.4% in a table on page 11 killed a memo, not for the 0.6 but for what it implied about the hard checks. (3) smoothed-over contradictions. (4) guesses in fact-shaped clothing. (5) unfindable provenance. (6) no accountable signer.
data.name: Six ways AI output loses a finance room, from source trust to no accountable signer

data.brief: Two cited papers: a runtime skill audit finding that static-scan-surviving skill code can break at runtime, and a "when safe skills collide" finding that two individually benign skills become malignant when run together — OCR extracts attacker-planted content, the reporting skill then ships the user's PII to a third party alongside the report. Reported at ~90% of observed attacks, i.e. the composition case is the normal case, not the tail. Consequence stated directly: you cannot review or model-check your way to safety, and you cannot remove everything at the door.
data.name: Individually clean skills become malignant in composition at runtime

data.brief: The finding across all three pillars: embedding the business's knowledge into curated skill files — a central alias, review by GTM and operations to stop proliferation, an expert-level skill at every level — is what makes agentic systems predictable enough for a whole team to execute evenly; the "Cambrian stage" of everyone solving everything with skills will need standardization so systems' sources of truth align
data.name: Skill curation is the basis of the agentic workforce

data.brief: Cloudflare's revenue-operations team encoded business semantics and the recurring business questions into role-specific skill files: sellers with no SQL now ask the data directly and get answers while doing other work, 80%+ of requests that once queued behind an analyst are self-served, two-hour analyses take five minutes, and the same files let operations build applications instead of waiting on IT. The operations team reports ~2× efficiency and time freed for strategy
data.name: Skill files let sellers ask the data without sql

data.brief: After tutorial hell and framework hell, practitioners are in "skill hell": freely downloadable community skills proliferate with no shared rubric to tell good from bad; individuals stack them without getting the promised results, and organizations cannot turn their operating procedures into working skills. The maintainer of one of the most popular skills repos reports even his own users are stuck ("just one more skill, bro")
data.name: Practitioners are in skill hell: no shared rubric separates good from bad

data.brief: An enterprise formalizing skill governance, with the practices lifted directly from code: admission (an automated gate on the registry with a human in the loop, "very analogous to how we do the PR review process"), ownership (named skill owners like code owners; skills maintained by the application teams that own the corresponding features), boundaries (allow-listed, access-controlled tools per skill), lifecycle (semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, changelogs), coherence (periodic audits and skill-validation checks). Verdict: at enterprise scale, skill-library governance is "non-negotiable" — and "the good news is we can borrow a lot of good practices from code that have worked for decades".
data.name: Enterprise skill libraries need admission, ownership, boundaries, lifecycle and audits

data.brief: Scaling account with thresholds: with a handful of skills, concatenating them into the system prompt just works; past roughly 10 skills that falls apart and you need to shortlist before injection — embeddings plus similarity search, or a smaller model that picks candidates; at hundreds of skills you need a hierarchy of skills, metadata filters and governance to keep the library searchable and coherent. His summary takeaway is the shape of the change rather than the numbers: "the routing mechanism doesn't get tuned as you scale — it changes the mechanism itself".
data.name: Skill routing changes mechanism as the library scales, it does not just get tuned

data.brief: The pipeline is a skills-based workflow on an internal agent harness, so clinicians — not engineers — own its logic: they steer any step to reproduce a production failure and add a document type for a new customer by writing a skill file. "Give your domain experts the keys… they will drive the recursive self-improvement, not the engineers" — a vertical-AI org design where the expert edits the system directly
data.name: Skills are the interface between engineers and domain experts

data.brief: An incumbent financial-data vendor reports that product features have become skills: equity research and wealth management — two core finance workflows that were screens, buttons, dropdowns and dashboards — are now skills in an agent-first surface where the user talks to the agent or the agent decides how they navigate. Two structural consequences stated: skills can be shipped by anyone in the company who understands the product, not just engineers ("one of the most underrated things about skills"), and the engineer's role shifts from shipping features to shipping harnesses. Placement rule offered: prompts = who the agent is, tools = what it connects to, skills = how a task gets done, and that's where your business logic lives.
data.name: FactSet's product features became skills; engineers now ship harnesses

data.brief: What worked for context management at Navan: skills as the unit — each bundling domain context and tool execution — composed dynamically per agent, testable and reusable independently, with progressive disclosure expanding scope from metadata. The orchestration corollary: one master agent progressively loading skills beat multi-agent designs — "if you can't perfect a single agent, why go multi-agent"
data.name: Skills as the unit of context

data.brief: Snyk/Invariant audit of ~4,000 skills on Claw Hub: >1 in 8 with critical-severity issues; 76 malicious payloads; "three lines of English can bring a system down"
data.name: Claw Hub audit: over 1 in 8 skills critical, 76 malicious payloads

data.brief: The framing claim: AI skills "look like configuration but they behave like supply-chain dependencies" — the traditional supply chain of packages, containers and models now also includes skills, plugins, MCP servers, agent rules and hooks. Mechanism that makes it a supply chain rather than config: one person authors a skill, another person's agent consumes it, and the author is thereby steering code generated on someone else's machine. Concrete risk classes given: a skill that retrieves a token and then uses it hardcoded, so it lands in logs and becomes a future data leak; a skill that instructs the agent to run shell commands that then execute on a colleague's machine; and skills configured with excessive permissions.
data.name: Skills look like configuration but behave like supply-chain dependencies

data.brief: Skills ecosystem snapshot (mid-2026): 26+ platforms support skills (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI…), ~100Ks of published skills, paid skill marketplaces, a skills registry; OpenClaw became the most-starred GitHub repository — while marketplaces still lack verification controls ("like npm 10 years ago")
data.name: Skills ecosystem explodes: 26+ platforms, 100Ks of skills, no verification

data.brief: Duplication, hard discovery and poor quality in engineer-built skills led to a managed marketplace: 2,500 skills through lint and automated review, one-command install, persona-based auto-install so agents pick skills without installation, and traces/comments captured as continuous evals fed back to authors — 20,000+ executions a day. QuantumBlack's registry blueprint (b22) exists in production at Uber
data.name: Skills marketplace 2500 with continuous evals

data.brief: A small, concrete authoring finding with wide applicability: agents generating metadata will invent new categories unless constrained, so the enrich-note skill keeps tags in a fixed reference folder and instructs the agent to be reluctant to add to it — "Claude loves to get creative, so just telling it please don't do that" — with permission to extend only on a genuine pattern. Paired with an enrichment timestamp per note, which makes the skill idempotent and therefore safe to run repeatedly and on a schedule. Vocabulary control and idempotence as the two properties that turn a prompt into infrastructure
data.name: Skills need fixed vocabularies

data.brief: The organizational answer recapitulates the microservices era: a governed skills registry (catalog, metadata, search, MCP + CLI access, dependencies, versioning, access control, evals, observability) owned by architects / engineering / infra / cyber leads — "the Backstage IDP moment for skills," and IDP vendors are already centralizing it. When governed, the next engineer's harness discovers and pulls the existing skill instead of rebuilding it; the same platform then centralizes whole workflows
data.name: Skills registry is the new internal developer portal

data.brief: Of ~50,000 skills SkillsBench indexed from GitHub, almost none had evals; most were AI-written and untested — and given agent non-determinism you can't tell whether a task failed because the skill is bad or the task too hard. A whole distribution layer shipping unverified behavior
data.name: Of ~50,000 skills SkillsBench indexed from GitHub, almost none had evals

data.brief: The adoption curve as the speaker charts it: Anthropic's first skills article ~8 months ago → an open standard two months later → most agent harnesses adopting it by around February → an exploding count of skills across public GitHub repos and registries, "way more than this publicly and within your organizations." Show of hands in the room: many create and use skills, fewer share them, very few govern them across the organization — the ecosystem formed faster than its governance
data.name: Skills standard adopted in eight months

data.brief: SkillsBench 1.1 across open/closed models and multiple harnesses: skills improve task performance ~15% on average over ~100 tasks; human-written skills are the best available, AI-generated skills can degrade performance; keep skill.md under ~500 lines
data.name: SkillsBench 1.1: skills lift task performance ~15% on average

data.brief: A sub-500 ms transaction SLA is the binding constraint on every agent design choice: short-term in-memory memory only — long-term memory is explicitly ruled out; the language model "need not be an LLM, it could be an SLM or an open-source model"; and the decompose-act-check loop needs an explicit break metric, because "you should be really careful about avoiding this infinite loop" and the stopping rule differs per use case.
data.name: A sub-500ms SLA rules out long-term agent memory and frontier-model latency

data.brief: A fine-tuned model can pass every eval and every behavioral production monitor while carrying a trigger-conditioned backdoor: in Kumar's controlled replication, full-rank fine-tuning gave 100% vulnerable SQL on "current year 2024" vs 0% on 2023 (LoRA 100 vs 40; untouched base flat at 53%), invisible to behavioral testing unless you already know the trigger — "you cannot test your way out of this"
data.name: Fine-tuned models pass every eval while carrying trigger-conditioned backdoors

data.brief: The talk's closing claim, stated as a two-way failure mode: build the agent factory without scoping discipline and you get "a token maxing slop cannon"; keep the scoping discipline without investing in the factory and "your agent-native competitors are just going to overtake you and outcompete" — "it's going to be over for you". Both principles are required, and the throughline that survives the automation is that the FDE still owns taste and judgment over the final output.
data.name: Without scoping discipline the agent factory becomes a token maxing slop cannon

data.brief: A definition of slop with a mechanism: models predict the most likely continuation and treat the most likely as ideal. That identity holds for arithmetic and code, where the average answer is also the correct one, and fails for writing and design, where "a lot of greatness and creativity happens at the ends of the distribution... when you actively break from rules and from patterns". The felt ubiquity of slop is that collapse plus repetition.
data.description: Consequence for method: the fix is not only higher-quality data but deliberately forcing the distribution back out — forcing true expert distributions across mediums and styles when decomposing a problem, and treating pattern-breaking as an intentional objective rather than an artifact.
data.name: Slop is mode collapse: the most likely output treated as the ideal

data.brief: The learning-loop claim: recurring review comments are codified into an AI slop registry that auto-flags them, "a guardrail you don't have to review again," compounding with every merged PR — the review experience humans provide becomes training the system learns from. A team-specific, accumulating verification asset built from human review history; follows a J-curve. Bears on the accumulation-loop thesis from the review-quality side
data.name: Slop registry compounds

data.brief: 2026: AI has made inboxes and feeds nearly unusable for GTM — "so much annoying outreach and generated slop that it's really hard to tell the real deal" — and cutting through the noise now drives founders to re-anchor trust in humans: personal brands, artisanal craft, beautiful design/text, as the pendulum swings back from automation
data.name: AI slop saturates GTM channels, re-anchoring trust in humans

data.brief: Slopsquatting in the wild: packages published under LLM-hallucinated names, functionally identical plus a backdoor
data.name: Slopsquatting observed in the wild under LLM-hallucinated package names

data.brief: Mixedbread trained a small LLM (for speed/cost) into a search agent — SFT from a larger teacher, then on-policy RL on a composite reward — and reports NDCG@10 of 0.40 on a long-rambling-query congressional benchmark vs 0.18 for the best agent in that benchmark's paper (a GPT multi-hop agent); the production beta is top-1 on Snowflake MatchQA (93.4% acc with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the reasoning model) at far lower cost than comparable LLM search agents
data.name: Mixedbread's small RL-trained search agent beats larger agents at far lower cost

data.brief: The panel's counterweight, from both router vendors: cheap models are only cheap in distribution. "If you run Terminal-Bench on Opus and Haiku, Opus will do about three times better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku" — out-of-distribution small models inflate cost through crazed tool-calling loops; on OpenRouter's public rankings the top model by dollar spent on classification tasks is Opus; naive task-type routing is "extremely fragile" for agentic work because task complexity mutates mid-session (explore → implement → live-debug) and "you don't want to be left with some subpar model for the task you're now on"; larger models are also more token-efficient readers (subset reads, single-command verification). Cognition's mitigation: the guarantee of frontier intelligence always present — a watcher agent detecting when the delegate is out of its depth
data.name: Small models thrash out of distribution

data.brief: Production finding: with vetted, structured data, the smallest available chat model — Qwen 2.5 0.5B instruct, ~400MB, CPU-only via Ollama — answers an FAQ RAG correctly; bigger models were slower and wordier with no accuracy gain, and the small model hallucinates less ("if it doesn't have the information it simply says so" — paraphrase). Two tiny local models (chat + embedding) are the whole model footprint
data.name: With vetted structured data, a ~400MB CPU model answers FAQ RAG correctly

data.brief: Smart Turn v3.2 (open, BSD-2, 8MB) gives ~58.9% recall / 68.4% precision on end-of-turn detection — the best deployable turn detector today; a local VAD timer (~300ms) backstops the ~4-in-10 it misses
data.name: Smart Turn v3.2 gives ~58.9% recall / 68.4% precision, best deployable turn detector

data.brief: The closing claim: model capability matters and smarter models reduce mistakes, "but it cannot eliminate network failures, stale data or adversarial input." The architecture must be able to bound, observe and recover from the agent's actions — tool contracts with idempotency, source-of-truth decisions, retry policies and rate limits, permissions, traces, recovery paths — "ask what the system lets it do when it is wrong"
data.name: Smarter models cannot eliminate network failures

data.brief: Prescribed org shift: pre-AI, firms put their smartest people on writing code; now they belong customer-facing, deciding what gets built — deciding is the expensive part, building has become cheap; involve SMEs in build decisions and realign KPIs (count features used more than twice, not features shipped)
data.name: Put the smartest people customer-facing, deciding what gets built

data.brief: Snorkel AI states its business as selling benchmarks — "data-as-a-service… we basically sell benchmarks", producing them at scale, running millions of agent simulations per month, with benchmark construction treated as an engineering discipline staffed by both agents and subject-matter experts to build production-close domain benchmarks.
data.name: Snorkel AI sells benchmarks, running millions of agent simulations per month

data.brief: Snyk data across 4,800+ customers: vulnerability backlog up ~108% QoQ despite agent tooling
data.name: Snyk: vulnerability backlogs up ~108% QoQ despite agent tooling

data.brief: Enterprise requirements Factory reports from the field: a software factory built on a vendor-locked, single-model solution is both expensive and strategically exposed ("what is the role of the model provider in dictating what you can or cannot build with your software factory?"), and not owning the traces and data flowing through it blocks later evolution. Hence model independence, full data access, centralized enterprise governance, and air-gapped operation for finance/healthcare/gov partners. And the factory itself is "built, not bought" — an organizational investment, not a purchase.
data.name: A software factory is built, not bought, and must be model-independent

data.brief: The thesis statement: Trajectory is "building the platform that turns every interaction into model improvement, harness improvement, and the entire agentic loop just getting smarter over time," with production traces optimized as a self-served loop and redeployed under a control plane — toward "a world where software in general just gets smarter every single time it's used… the most exciting unlock in 2026–2027." Tempered in Q&A: the field is in pseudo continual learning, still doing batch updates offline and re-uploading, with merging 10,000 concurrent production rollouts an open infrastructure *and* algorithmic problem. the algorithm-leg statement of the pattern
data.name: Software that improves every use

data.brief: Solo builder running a 19-skill open-source Claude Code content pipeline (biweekly scheduled runs; seven handoffs from scheduler to output folder) reports the predictable arc: a prompt change breaks something downstream → you rebuild regression testing; a cron job fails silently for a week → CI monitoring; one skill's schema change breaks three downstream skills → contract testing; a done-looking artifact shouldn't ship → staging checkpoints; you can't trace which handoff corrupted output → audit trails.
data.description: Agent systems ship with none of these operational guarantees by default, so every solo builder rebuilds them "one failure at a time" — a worse version of CI/CD
data.name: Solo agent builders rebuild CI/CD guarantees one failure at a time

data.brief: The tactic: build the vertical solution for one team first (pre-meeting briefs for account managers), then extend it to the next artifact (post-meeting follow-ups, pre-filled CRM updates with a rep's thumbs-up) and the next team (AEs, who need third-party rather than product data) mostly by adding skills, data integrations and ingestion — the generic pieces (email and transcript embeddings, custom instructions) carry over. Three years ago this was two people and GPT-3.5 writing outbound copy
data.name: Solve one team then scale with skills and integrations

data.brief: Sonar benchmark (4,000+ problems): state-of-the-art models score extremely well on functional correctness yet still produce bugs, security issues, and high, variable complexity (GPT-5.5 notably better on complexity) — this is the raw input flowing into agentic workflows
data.name: Top models ace functional correctness but still emit bugs and complexity

data.brief: Production safety architecture for a mental-health coach serving a company that has cared for over a million people: input and output guardrails as separate LLM-judge calls sandwiching the core agent — the input guardrail decides whether the user's message needs intervention before the core responds; the output guardrail reads the response and the whole conversation and can intervene.
data.description: Stated design reasons: modularity (iterate the core without compromising safety), jailbreak resistance (separate calls are harder to prompt-engineer around than in-prompt rules and resist conversational drift attacks), and evaluability. The latency and cost trade-off is accepted explicitly because of the use case's sensitivity, and every architectural decision was made with safety as a primary objective.
data.name: SonderMind sandwiches its coach with separate input and output guardrail calls

data.brief: SonderMind open-sourced its guardrail evaluation corpus at the talk: 200 input-guardrail scenarios and 100 output-guardrail scenarios, each clinically reviewed and calibrated against real conversation patterns, single- and multi-turn, across the spectrum of mental health.
data.description: Rationale: the problems SonderMind is facing are not unique to us — anyone working in this space is going to face some version of these, so a shared baseline matters even though it cannot replace a team's own learning loop, because there might be real hurting people depending on your learning curve. A safety-critical vertical treating its eval assets as a public good rather than a moat.
data.name: SonderMind open-sources 300 clinically reviewed guardrail scenarios

data.brief: Method finding: because models are still weak, grading the end scientific outcome is too sparse to learn from, so verifiability has to be manufactured by decomposing the analysis DAG, taking data to the pre-interpretation state, and defining ground truth there — subject to three properties (verifiable, durable across valid analysis paths, requiring data interaction). Human cross-grading rounds against trajectory data from Jan-Mar 2026 model releases showed that many of the team's own tasks were the problem — under-specified prompts ("an appropriate radius") and inherited arbitrary numeric QC thresholds.
data.name: End-outcome grading is too sparse, so verifiability is manufactured by decomposition

data.brief: Existing bio benchmarks measured Q&A-style academic knowledge or the wrong experiment types, so LatchBio built its own: SpatialBench, 146 problems, last December, deterministic Python graders. Frontier labs and the community then adopted it organically — it now appears in recent Anthropic model cards and was shown on stage at Anthropic's Claude science launch the day before this talk. "They don't tell us this happens.
data.description: They just do it, and you read about it." Since expanded to other omics classes (single-cell, epigenomics), long-horizon extensions, and a first drug-discovery benchmark on preclinical pharmacology for small molecules, with the landscape being systematically indexed from discovery to development to translation.
data.name: Frontier labs adopted a vertical lab's free benchmark without telling its authors

data.brief: The pendulum is swinging back to small specialized models, with vision as the leading indicator (edge compute constraints forced specialized learners years ago; language now follows): Roboflow's production pattern — large models ensemble (SAM 3 + LLM-as-judge) auto-labels footage → consensus builds a specialized dataset → distill to a small task model (drop SAM's expensive encoder for a DETR-class model once the class list is fixed) → run real-time on MBARI's deep-sea submarines, which found a new fish species this way.
data.description: Osman has argued small/specialized-is-the-future since 2024 tweets; NVIDIA: "definitely a multi-model world"
data.name: The pendulum swings back to small specialized models, vision leading

data.brief: Speakers from Anthropic and OpenAI — the labs most bullish on AI coding — converged in recent talks on "specs are the new code" (paraphrase): the art now is defining product requirements, system design, and eval criteria so you can be confident AI coding agents build the right thing; a MongoDB advocate builds an entire methodology on that premise
data.name: Anthropic and OpenAI speakers converge on specs as the new code

data.brief: The selection criterion is latency at acceptable accuracy: a continuous per-site Promptfoo matrix over models and providers found 1.1 s (Gemma 4 / Cerebras) versus 4.6 s for the runner-up, and "you don't need a huge LLM" to place blocks and write copy. Public benchmarks don't settle it — "this is very dependent on the site," so each site re-runs its own evaluation. A small fast model plus fast inference beats a big one for a latency-bound product
data.name: Speed not size selects the model

data.brief: Poolside built Spoolside, an internal CLI (deliberately unreleased) so its agents can test a non-web product (a VS Code extension): screenshots, token-compressed UI-state snapshots, backend/frontend log extraction, service restarts, stackable high-level UI commands (open menu, message the in-product agent, await reply, upload image); house policy: the agent must reproduce a bug before its fix is trusted; framed as the precondition for running agents overnight or multiplying them
data.name: Poolside built Spoolside so its agents can test a non-web product

data.brief: Concrete failure mode at a stage boundary, from a published report. In an MoE model, load-balancing objectives aim for roughly equal expert utilization per batch or sequence; if the data distribution the model sees in post-training is very different from what it saw in pre-training, the result is massive expert imbalance. MAI Thinking 1 overcame it by cranking up the load-balancing coefficient during the SFT stages — a fix the speaker flags as something you do not want to be doing that late in a run.
data.description: Prescribed alternative: pull post-training-shaped data (SFT chat, agentic traces) into pre-training so the shapes are familiar from the start, and use mid-training — longer context and the RL/post-training distribution — as the designed bridge rather than an emergency lever.
data.name: A pre/post-training distribution gap causes massive MoE expert imbalance

data.brief: Re-running the GEO study on a newer model made it pitch Sourcegraph's retired product *more*: training data is always stale, and old models' outputs about a product accumulate on the web, so the noise compounds. The remedy is provenance — authoritative, current, quotable sources agents fetch at answer time — not waiting for the next model
data.name: Stale models compound old product mentions

data.brief: The engineer's method: encode the clinician's definition of good as hundreds of TDD-style evals before prompting, run the agent through them tens of thousands of times, treat one failing safety test as a stop, and dogfood for tone because no eval captures emotional drift. Judgement enters the product as tests written by the person who has sat in the room
data.name: Start with the clinician write hundreds of evals

data.brief: The build-size tiers shifted down a full level in ~a year: his 2021 YC startup (Ping) would be a side project today; his 2021 side project (Reddit meme scraper, 2–3 days of work) drops below the line; startups exhibiting at this very conference have products he judges buildable as side projects — some "could just be a markdown file"; most Jira tickets from his previous job are trivial for Opus 4.5-class models
data.name: Build-size tiers shifted down a full level in about a year

data.brief: The measured claim: with TokenOps' full policy suite on browser-use and MetaGPT, average spend fell ~78% while completion rose from ~67% (plain throttling kills runs) to ~96% — because policies steer the run into its budget (compaction, tool-output trimming, budget-aware instructions, loop/progress detection) and halt only last. Cost control as an in-flight harness policy, not a kill switch
data.name: Steering beats throttling 78 percent

data.brief: Habit one is to write down everything that used to move through Slack, onboarding and code review into skills and steering files, asking after every agent mistake what was missing — and its 2026 corollary: Sonnet 3.7-era do-nots are no longer needed with Opus 4.5 and its successors, so the habit now includes asking whether an instruction is bloating context. The harness accrues with practice and thins with capability
data.name: Steering files thin as models improve

data.brief: Steinberger's bottleneck migration, dated: January 2026 = 10+ terminals, "I thought I was orchestrating; really I was polling — I was the scheduler, the router, and the memory"; constraint moved tokens → compute → attention; today he manages one long-running manager agent that delegates to workers; watching agents generate code is now a waste of the one resource you can't add more of; a colleague's chief-of-staff agent wakes every 10 minutes to coordinate his GitHub work
data.name: Steinberger: the constraint moved tokens → compute → attention

data.brief: ~3 weeks before the talk the speaker's API key was stolen ("someone in China") and the endpoint drained from ~$7,000 toward $10,000 in days before being arrested — inference credits as a theft target
data.name: Stolen API key drained inference credits from ~$7K toward $10K

data.brief: Compute (a Linux box) was the first agent unlock; durable disk is the next: incremental snapshot/restore already supports multi-day Codex "gold mode" runs (speaker's record: 3 days) and enables Monte-Carlo-style checkpoint/backtrack exploration over many days — pitched as the primitive needed for drug-discovery-length agent tasks
data.name: Compute was the first agent unlock; durable disk snapshots are the next

data.brief: Practitioner observation: with each model generation, output quality is less predicated on being the most technically skilled person in the room and more on conscientiousness — design tokens, separated front/back-end code, clean tagged PR hygiene, accurate internal docs; structure is what separates "AI purple gradient slop" from professional output
data.name: Output quality now rides on conscientiousness and structure, not top technical skill

data.brief: Vendor thesis with a causal claim attached: AI got good at coding and math and stayed "super behind" on design, creative writing, personality and emotional intelligence — and the reason is not model architecture but the domains themselves. Capability follows measurability. Code decomposes, executes and verifies, so it was trainable; "we've made them great at coding, but realistically it's actually a fact about code." Subjective domains have three properties that break the loop: there is no single right answer, "great" is contextual (the same slide is excellent for a startup and inappropriate for a finance firm), and the standard changes over time in a way math and code do not.
data.description: Corollary the business is built on: solve the measurability problem and a large fraction of the domain follows.
data.name: Capability follows measurability: code got solved because code decomposes

data.brief: Slack shipped Slackbot MCP-client support ~2 weeks before the talk; the speaker wired it to his own librarian and found it "horrifically stupid" for real work — generalizing: any AI crowbarred into a pre-existing subscription price point lacks margin for an intelligent reasoning model, so harness tier (powerful model, subagents, plan mode, full MCP, file editing) is now a procurement criterion; don't let teams do important work in a chat web UI
data.name: AI crowbarred into subscription price points can't afford reasoning models

data.brief: The lab strategy as read by a harness vendor: SemiAnalysis experiments show a $200 Claude plan yields ~$8,000 of API-equivalent usage and a $200 Codex plan ~$14,000 — labs are losing money per subscriber on purpose, subsidizing "until they have as many engineers dependent on their tooling as possible" (agents in CI, background agents, looping agents — "every new feature and marketing push seems to be a new workflow to standardize on, to use even more tokens and be locked in even more"), with price gouging to follow "once your developers can't work without the tools." It explains the API-business → application-layer migration: building the moat "for the day these models inevitably become a commodity." Rizwan's counter-thesis: it won't work — buyers jump to value
data.name: Subsidize lockin then gouge

data.brief: Notion's AI lead states it plainly: your supplier is your competitor. Frontier labs sell tokens to applied companies while underpricing their own first-party products (the Dylan [Patel] chart of first-party vs API pricing); reselling surcharged tokens is not defensible value, and tying to one provider means no exit — "you are crossing your fingers and hoping you are a viable business".
data.name: Notion AI lead: your supplier is your competitor

data.brief: Quantified verifier unreliability, read off Datacurve's published DeepSWE-vs-SWE-bench-Pro comparison: SWE-bench Pro accepts wrong implementations on ~8.5% of tasks and rejects correct implementations on ~24%. Khial then pulled individual tasks to see why: one test asserts the existence of a variable that is (a) never specified in the instruction and (b) named in a way no LLM would independently choose — "cornering the LLM" into a false negative; another tests unexported functions, which he says would be rejected outright as a PR in G2i's own projects. That is what a weak verifier looks like at task level, not at aggregate level.
data.name: SWE-bench Pro accepts ~8.5% wrong and rejects ~24% correct implementations

data.brief: Contamination measured, then not disclosed: given the first part of a SWE-bench Verified prompt, Opus verbatim completes the rest — questions and answers — and a Surge study comparing memorization of SWE-bench-Verified content against the rest of the same repositories found "very clear evidence" Opus had memorized a lot of it. Opus 4.8's model card reports its SWE score without disclosing this, and the industry has no disclosure habit at all, so benchmark consumers are simply missing the information.
data.description: Framing that generalizes the finding: contamination is not mainly labs training on the test set — it is "the default outcome unless you are very, very good", because public questions and answers on the internet get memorized to some extent no matter how hard labs work to hold the flood back.
data.name: Opus memorized SWE-bench Verified and the model card never discloses it

data.brief: On SWE-Marathon's 20 project-scale tasks the best configuration evaluated — Claude Opus 4.8 + Claude Code — resolves only 26% (~1 in 4); failures are deep, not shallow (avg 31M tokens/trial, longest 877M, hours of exploring/editing/testing/recovering): end-to-end project ownership is far from solved
data.name: Best config resolves only 26% of SWE-Marathon's project-scale tasks

data.brief: Validation is not therapy: a general assistant's agreeable reply makes users more certain rather than more self-aware and sends them back to the relationship "in the shape of an attorney." Helpful-agreeable-fast is the wrong personality for the job, engagement is the wrong objective, and the validated frameworks (Gottman, EFT) that would supply judgement are absent from commercial relationship apps built on "general empathy plus communication tips"
data.name: Sycophancy is a clinical failure mode

data.brief: A data-provenance caution: Krea removed AI-generated images aggressively because "synthetic data is so sticky that once you train on it your model good but you lose the point" — outputs converge to ChatGPT/Nano-Banana aesthetics, detectable to experts. Distilling on synthetic data is the easy shortcut that costs identity; a generative-media parallel to the corpus's contamination/benchmark-trust concerns about synthetic-data feedback loops
data.name: Synthetic data is sticky

data.brief: Role prompting has hardened into a market category: companies now test product concepts and messaging against panels of synthetic respondents, with press coverage and rising funding over the last few years cited as evidence of momentum, and vendors (including the speaker's) selling persona construction to market-research and insights teams. The capability claim rests on a well-known demonstration — ~1,000 people interviewed for ~2.5 hours each plus a battery of personality tests and surveys, transcripts handed to agents that then took the same battery, yielding ~83% alignment with the corresponding humans (normalized).
data.description: Historical control offered by the speaker himself: Simulmatics made the same promise about simulating the electorate in the 1950s-60s on raw statistics and failed, "so you should approach claims like this with some humility" — what's different now is not only compute but a new modelling medium, since LLMs let you simulate in language rather than in equations, for phenomena (how we feel, how we act, what we choose) that never succumbed to formulas.
data.name: Synthetic personas harden from role prompting into a funded market category

data.brief: The field is openly split on synthetic data in pre-training, and the talk lays both recipes side by side. Against: MAI Thinking 1 makes "a really large point" of using no synthetic data and no data from any other language model, and filters its web scrapes to enforce it — adhering to the older paradigm of bootstrapping representations from human knowledge. For: Nemotron 3 Ultra pulls SFT-shaped data into pre-training; Kimi K2 applied rephrasing "broadly across the whole pre-training data set" at very large scale; Arcee's own Trinity Large used web-scale synthetic rephrasing; Swallow Code / Swallow Math are cited as early public examples.
data.description: The speaker's stated position: synthetic data is the way forward, and the observed trend is that it not only produces more tokens but cleaner, higher-quality tokens shaped like instruct or agentic tasks all the way back in pre-training. Standing caveat acknowledged: blindly tossing synthetic data in can collapse a model.
data.name: The field is openly split on whether synthetic data belongs in pre-training

data.brief: With Opus 4.8 and Fable, the Claude Code system prompt shrank ~80%: examples removed (frontier models are more creative without them), "do not" constraints replaced with context, and system prompts are now per-model — older models keep the full prompt while frontier models run on judgment instead of instruction
data.name: Claude Code's system prompt shrank ~80% with Opus 4.8 and Fable

data.brief: System-prompt best practice has moved in an arc across model generations: Sonnet-3.5-era = small prompt, few tools, many examples → mid-era = large prompts, many instructions, many tools → Fable-class = smaller prompts again, examples removed (they constrain a model more imaginative than the examples), "do not" constraints replaced with context; Claude Code's system prompt was cut ~80%
data.name: System-prompt practice arced small to large to small; Claude Code cut ~80%

data.brief: The moat claim from a practitioner: what's defensible against every frontier release ("when Mythos comes out, or a new app from Claude — I'm not worried") is the modeled internal processes and tacit knowledge — full meaning of fields, join logic, data systematics, safeguards, reporting conventions; "it's not enough to answer a question a certain way, you have to answer it the way it's been answered in the past".
data.name: The moat is modeled internal processes and tacit knowledge, not the UI

data.brief: The mechanism: reframe entity-component-system as tags describing intent that systems query over, recyclable across games, applied/removed by an LLM assistant — a declarative intent layer that the engine executes deterministically. The "intent, not code" thread (Dailey b17, Jain b21) realized in a game engine via a tag substrate
data.name: Tags as intent layer

data.brief: Tan's self-measured output: ~14 usable logical lines/day as a near-full-time engineer YC partner in 2013 (median for the era) vs ~400x that today running YC full-time on fewer hours — 8x at the most pathological verbosity discount, ~80x mid.
