His tattoo-worthy point: the 2x and 100x people use the exact same Claude, same weights, same context window — "the leverage is not in the weights, it's in how you wire the work"
data.name: Tan: ~400x output on the same Claude — the leverage is in wiring, not weights

data.brief: ChatGPT generated proof, Aristotle auto-repaired, Lean-verified. First AI Erdos solution not in literature.
data.description: On January 7, 2026, Terence Tao posted on Mastodon that AI tools had "more or less autonomously" solved Erdos problem #728 — a 1975 question about prime factorization of binomial coefficients. ChatGPT generated the proof after some feedback from an initial attempt; the AI tool Aristotle then automatically repaired minor errors and produced a Lean-verified proof. Tao noted the result was "not replicated in existing literature," making it the first AI solution to an Erdos problem that was genuinely new. He later found the methods were similar to a 2014 paper by Pomerance, but the AI-generated solution was the first to explicitly address this specific problem formulation.
data.name: Terence Tao: AI autonomously solves Erdos problem #728

data.brief: Teams burn weeks trying to force determinism via temperature 0 and "walk away deciding the system is unknowable" (paraphrase); hard data from engineering threads (Reddit/HN) shows the same prompt at temp 0 still returns dozens of different responses across a thousand runs — GPU non-determinism, batch variance, and MoE routing make bitwise determinism unobtainable from hosted APIs
data.name: Temperature 0 still yields dozens of different responses across a thousand runs

data.brief: Practitioners are running 4+ coding agents in parallel tmux panes with vibe-coded custom keybindings and status tooling ("spawn N agents" bound to a keypress; the agent itself wrote the tmux config); the speaker moved off VS Code — the terminal re-emerging as the multi-agent control plane
data.name: Practitioners run 4+ parallel agents in tmux; the terminal re-emerges as control plane

data.brief: Market-structure claim, delivered as the talk's "more aggressive" statement: people buy Bloomberg and FactSet to displace culpability, not to obtain information that is free in SEC filings — the value is that a vetted central instance means everyone on Wall Street is wrong together. Every such tool is read-only, so the analyst still produces the work product by hand; that is named as the biggest wall to AI adoption across Wall Street. Once AI can produce verifiable work product, the contractor-vetting layer behind the incumbent data providers is what gets absorbed.
data.name: Bloomberg and FactSet terminals are bought to displace culpability, not to inform

data.brief: Tesla enterprise-agent practitioner: data-agent failures trace to structure — source-of-truth ambiguity, stale context, uncaptured preference — not model capability; bigger/latest models, longer context, and more .md/MCP knowledge bases don't fix them
data.name: Tesla data-agent failures trace to context structure, not model capability

data.brief: Developer relations' audience changed: the agent reads the docs, calls the API, recovers from errors and installs libraries into the workflow — a user and a recommender at once — while engineers become orchestrators of agent fleets and non-engineers gain dev-tool access through agents. Sourcegraph replaced the developer-advocate role with an agent advocate, and the speaker — an astronomer a year ago — now maintains a multi-agent framework with 12,000 commits
data.name: The agent is the new developer user

data.brief: The speaker built the strongest judge design he had seen in the field — rubric with worked examples, optimizer-tuned, deterministic concept diffing — and one in five of the notes it passed clean still held a serious error, usually an omission. Not blind, unable to tell what counts: "you've not added a safety net, you've added a second silent failure that nods along with the first"
data.name: The best rubric judge waved through one in five serious errors

data.brief: The roadblocks to automating GTM were data quality (one bad account mapping loses a rep's trust), latency (every vendor adds a hop, so you automate yesterday's world) and, above all, that the facts which decide the next step — "the champion just left," "don't contact," "blocked, legal" — live unstructured in a decade of notes; an automation that cannot read them "could do something catastrophically wrong." Structured and unstructured context had to be brought into one place
data.name: The critical facts live in notes not crm fields

data.brief: A health-plan AI vendor cannot retain PHI in any form — not redacted, anonymized or derived — yet 95% accuracy "is not good enough" and every workflow needs evals over 300-page fax bundles from a long-tailed distribution. Its bet: synthesize the evaluation data instead, and treat the constraint as general — anywhere data is ephemeral, sensitive or expensive to label
data.name: The eval data you need most is the data you may not keep

data.brief: Behind "something went wrong" is a gateway choosing among availability, latency, guardrails and cost during a provider degradation — and no configuration maximizes all four. The production lesson is to make the trade-off explicit per use case and to expose the levers to callers; the model provider's ceiling is your ceiling unless the gateway can route around it
data.name: The gateway is a four way fight

data.brief: Unlike Sudoku, where solutions are hard to generate and trivial to check, a clinical decision-support answer is about as hard to verify as to produce — a good enough verifier would be the generator — so Abridge grounds its quality judge in adjudicated physician rubrics (two independent authors, one adjudicator, one QA) and layers safety, adversarial and style judges beside it. The limit of automated verification, met with human references built for variability
data.name: The generator verifier gap is small in clinical decision support

data.brief: Ramp's growth-engineering lead: everyone has good GTM ideas; the bottleneck is pulling an audience, coordinating channels and convincing people to follow a playbook — months of work — because every system has a different source of truth. The fix began years before agents as a data problem: an internal CDP with Kafka-fed Postgres keeping referential integrity across CRM, product and third-party entities, embeddings over transcripts and notes, and pre-computed enrichment for the whole US market
data.name: The gtm bottleneck is everything after the idea

data.brief: Verifier's law — checking is cheaper than generating — holds where the verifier comes free (a compiler, a unit test) and fails for "is this note safe and complete": spotting differences is easy, deciding which matter is harder than writing the note, because that standard is tacit, contextual and moving — the same dropped holiday line is noise for France and the diagnosis for Lake Malawi. A boundary on the asymmetry that the corpus's verification thesis leans on
data.name: The hard part of verification is knowing what matters

data.brief: Thirty years of sign-up flows, card forms and API keys were built for one customer, humans; agents want to grab a piece of data, compute or inference and move on, at a scale no human consumes, paying fractional amounts at high frequency because sellers now wrap subsets of their data at ten cents. A 3% card fee on a one-cent call cannot work, so payment must behave like the internet: real-time, low-cost, programmable, always on
data.name: The internet had one customer and agents are the second

data.brief: The central claim: the agent loop is not the system — the refining loop around it is, and it is the most complex part (SOP memory + execution runtime + expert feedback capture). Quality comes from replaying real examples with writes disabled and checking whether behavior improved — "not from vibes, not from a bigger model." Vibe coding and spec-driven development both stall before this stage; "the real work starts" past them
data.name: The refining loop is the system

data.brief: As the sales motion automates, buyers crave in-person time and humans still sell value; hire AI-native sellers only when buyers demand a person, resist early up-market pulls, and expect forward-deployed engineers — ~55,000 requisitions for ~5,000 people — to stay scarce and sticky until "continual learning lets models figure out the organization." The human is priced back in at the moment of judgement and trust
data.name: The revenge of the steak dinner

data.brief: Beyond executing instructions, the autonomous rover is a data source: manually navigated runs and its reasoning on questions become training episodes for its policies, in a hybrid loop where the cloud trains and the edge executes — "so that I can make him do a better job of it." Post-deployment data as the improvement path for embodied agents
data.name: The robot generates its own training episodes

data.brief: The same brain, tools and loop produced a snarky agent that pressured the user toward expensive headphones ("you'll regret the cheap ones") and, after one persona change, a patient mentor that respected a $500 cap and "I need to think about it." A commerce agent's ethics live in the system prompt, so ship a guardrail checklist — disclose AI and fees, honor stop, respect the maximum, no dark patterns, log decisions
data.name: The system prompt is the commerce agents ethics policy

data.brief: Months after a celebrated launch, users of the assistant came back frustrated: the new habit had become the baseline and other AI products had raised expectations. The internal-tool journey — talk to data, automate workflows, empower teams to build skills and apps, hyper-personalize — has to keep moving, because "right now the switch is very easy; they will switch overnight"
data.name: The wow factor collapses in months

data.brief: Vendor's own numbers, offered as the contrast to the saturated benchmarks: over a 50-task finance sample, mean human time to complete one task is 15 hours; models take a long time on them and still "struggle significantly" across every finance domain covered, with a reported mean score of 5 (scale not stated on the captions).
data.name: A 50-task finance set averages 15 human-hours and models still struggle

data.brief: Neo4j CEO: from at-scale deployments over the last 6–9 months at a Fortune 20 global bank, a massive Bay Area tech-platform company, and a leading fintech, the emerging pattern is "thin agents on a smarter shared substrate" — per-agent manual data-source wiring means rediscovering sources from scratch, unverifiable trust/duplication, DRY violations cascading on every change, and zero cross-agent learning because the wiring lives in code and prompts.
data.name: Neo4j CEO: thin agents on a smarter shared substrate is the at-scale pattern

data.brief: Weeks before the talk, Thinking Machines (+ second name garbled, "Neolab") demoed a voice-in/voice-out architecture that time-slices continuous inference into 200ms chunks to hit the conversational latency floor — model-side workaround exists but isn't required if you switch the output modality
data.name: Thinking Machines demoed 200ms time-sliced continuous voice inference

data.brief: New-paradigm claim with unusual provenance: a GPT-4 / ChatGPT / InstructGPT co-author states publicly that RLHF "was a weird detour" and that a third post-training branch is being built — neither RLHF nor RLVR, optimizing calibrated decision-making, with a different API shape from both, designed from scratch "just like no one thought about instruction following before we made instruction following happen". Company is stealth and releasing soon.
data.description: Ordering claim attached: data matters more than compute, and doing the right task matters more than data — offered as a limit on the bitter lesson ("true in games, but not true in reality"). Also teased, unelaborated: "the original scaling laws were incorrect".
data.name: An InstructGPT co-author calls RLHF a weird detour and builds a third branch

data.brief: Threads can now list/rename/message each other, so a single user goes from "IC enabled by an IDE" to manager of teammate threads, then to manager-threads directing IC-threads — an org of self-managing agents; "where the puck is going"; Liu: "I've become a worse and worse manager over time" as the AI needs only a high-level ask
data.name: Codex threads compose into an org of self-managing agents

data.brief: Across thousands of engineers in six monorepos, PR volume and size have grown for two years and Uber's tracked time-to-first-review went from 3 hours in 2024 to 9 hours in 2026 — "code review is now the bottleneck we are running into." The reason a platform team built an in-house review engine rather than buy: Phabricator support, agent-loop parity, distributed ownership, risk-aware routing, and mandatory security/compliance coverage
data.name: Time to first review tripled to nine hours

data.brief: A refund tool times out — did it happen? An agent's first move is to retry, so duplicate side effects follow unless every tool carries request IDs, idempotency keys and a status lookup, and retry storms are bounded by circuit breakers, exponential backoff and max-turns/parallelism/spend budgets. The durable-runtime concerns (retries, idempotency, compensation, budgets) arrive as a checklist from a large-scale systems shop
data.name: Timeouts mean unknown so tools need idempotency

data.brief: Below roughly 1B parameters the deployment playbook flips from prompting to fine-tuning, and Google's edge team reports it works at production quality: synthetically generate 10K-10M samples for one task and fine-tune a 270M-500M base (general Gemma, or Function Gemma where the task is function-call-shaped), and you get quality equal to or better than a 2-4B general model on that task — proven on function calling, summarization and proofreading — while reaching a far wider device set and running far more responsively.
data.description: The mechanism is memory bandwidth: on the same Raspberry Pi, decode goes from mid-single-digit to ~45 tok/s because there is less to read from memory each step.
data.name: Below 1B parameters the playbook flips from prompting to fine-tuning

data.brief: The unbounded-consumption year: the industry "values token maxing" and people are "proud to call themselves token billionaires"; Uber's AI budget reportedly exhausted within four months; companies at "hundreds of millions of dollars within months or days"; runaway loops with no mechanism to stop them. The culture and the missing control plane are the same story from two sides
data.name: Token billionaires and budgets gone in months

data.brief: The cost-of-intelligence decline reversed in 2026 (speaker tracks it on a website): IQ-adjusted token prices up 29% and raw prices up ~76% in H1 2026, memory crunch cited. Customer-facing economics: "you can't put Fable in front of a customer" — vs DeepSeek V4 Flash at ~137× cheaper per task, viable when scope is narrowed
data.name: Cost-of-intelligence decline reversed in 2026: raw token prices up ~76% in H1

data.brief: Cost, not capability, is the structural barrier: real recurring scenarios — a reasoning upgrade at the same per-token price that uses 3x the output tokens; a new model digit priced +40% with the predecessor deprecated in 4 months — now land "pretty much monthly," while revenue doesn't grow 40% in step; 88% of companies can't get past AI-as-assistant; a Citadel memo argues simpler models may be the most cost-effective productivity pathway (frontier/everyday bifurcation).
data.name: Cost, not capability, is the structural barrier to AI-as-system

data.brief: Token-economy controls are being productized into vendor agent SDKs: AWS's Strands Agents ships prompt-caching flags, tool-result offload APIs, and a sliding-window conversation manager as first-class framework features — cost control migrating from app-level hacks into the framework layer
data.name: Token-economy controls are being productized into vendor agent SDKs

data.brief: The token-maxing culture from the leadership chair: an Amazon employee's voluntary usage dashboard turned into a leaderboard engineers competed to top; a similar Meta story; sensational "$500M in a month" spend. Ironclad's rule: track everyone, but as a smoke detector — low-usage pockets signal adoption gaps, bursts get investigated — and never as a stack rank, exactly as lines of code is tracked but never optimized. Half the room is "past adoption and now seriously worried about cost"
data.name: Token leaderboards invert the incentive

data.brief: Called turn in the market's spending posture, from someone who watched the previous one: token consumption is currently rewarded — a conference club with gold cards for people who consumed a billion-plus tokens, companies "giving bonuses on people token maxing" — which he calls historically absurd ("in what time in history has an employee been rewarded for your company to pay another vendor?"). He predicts the same ROI/cost-optimization wave he watched hit Snowflake and Databricks four years earlier, arriving as "the right tool for the right job — sometimes you don't need a multi-billion-parameter model when one CPU cycle will just work". Adjacent datum: GLM 5.2, downloadable from Hugging Face, is put on par with a frontier Opus release as evidence that intelligence is commoditized.
data.name: Token-maxing rewards will give way to an ROI and cost-optimization wave

data.brief: The KPI shift in deployed engineering, dated by a practitioner: a year and a half to two years ago the target was maximizing token usage — budgets were subsidized, "you could just run anything you wanted"; now the largest and most regulated enterprises ask whether they are getting true value or burning tokens, and the problem "has really shifted into the delivery space". ROI measurement for agents is stated outright as an unsolved problem — "the company that will solve this will be a $5 trillion market cap".
data.name: Deployed engineering's KPI shifted from token maxing to measured ROI

data.brief: With thousands of internal APIs projected into MCPs and every SaaS tool hosted behind one gateway, "enough MCPs add up to a massive token tax" — so Uber moved from direct MCP to an Omni MCP, to CLI projection so responses don't consume context, to a code-mode skill writing Python for the heaviest uses: 40%+ fleet-wide savings across 1,000+ tools. The model gateway attributes every one of 100M daily requests to a project, user and team for spend guardrails
data.name: Token tax fixed at the gateway

data.brief: Voice-is-the-product operator (wedding venues; same class as luxury hotels, high-end real estate): the standard advice — a detailed brand-voice system prompt with examples — holds only on the happy path; on "turn 21", the first question the examples never covered, the model says something technically correct the brand would never say; where users pay for a relationship, one wrong sentence costs more than a refund, and one prompt is being asked to do four different jobs (situational, inviolable, expressive, self-checking)
data.name: Brand-voice system prompts hold on the happy path and fail on turn 21

data.brief: Dated inflection point (June 2023, OpenAI ships tool calls in GPT-4; all vendors copy per "principle of minimum differentiation"): a single IO in the type signature turned AI safety from a philosophical debate about offensive words into real-world danger — side effects (emptied bank account, deleted files) execute during the loop, before any "safe answer" arrives; alignment baked into weights is routinely jailbroken
data.name: Tool calls (June 2023) turned AI safety from philosophy into real-world danger

data.brief: CodeScaleBench traces show an agent guessing a parameter name from training-data bias, failing, and recovering — at the cost of a full turn — because the tool description didn't pre-empt it. Organizations will judge tools on the tokens and time an agent spends to use them; the agent-experience report (point an agent at your docs, read the transcript) is the new DX audit
data.name: Tool friction costs agents whole turns

data.brief: Measured tool-sprawl tax: a 29-tool travel agent ships ~3,000 tokens of tool schemas (~100-200 each) on every call, before any message — and with all 29 visible the model sometimes picks the wrong near-duplicate tool; semantic pre-filtering to top-3 relevant tools cuts schema tokens to <300 and improves selection accuracy
data.name: A 29-tool agent ships ~3,000 schema tokens per call; semantic filtering cuts to <300

data.brief: The scale wall with its arithmetic stated: cost is input-token price × trace count × trace size, and a long coding-agent trace "can't even be read with another agent because that context doesn't fit in memory," forcing traces to be treated as external objects queried into rather than loaded. Set against a forecast that agent-generated data will eclipse humanity's lifetime output on year, then six-month, then three-month, then daily timescales — "the data we see today is going to be the smallest that humans have ever seen in their entire lives"
data.name: Trace volume outgrows reading

data.brief: Returning to his ~30-person YC startup's codebase: changes that took weeks now take hours; the "good, fast, cheap — pick two" tradeoff is reframed as "pick three"; Anthropic culture holds "tradeoffs are not real — force reality to show you the tradeoff"; the conference deck itself was made in ~4 hours with Fable
data.name: Fable collapses good-fast-cheap tradeoffs; weeks of work take hours

data.brief: The direction-of-travel claim: models will keep getting bigger, and at equal disk size a big-quantized model beats a small full-precision one (120B@4bit > 35B@BF16, paper-backed), so the optimal pipeline is train ginormous → quantize down. The mechanism is undertraining — at ~30T training tokens the weights aren't saturated, so ~86% "do not need to be there" (with an honest expiry condition: at ~300T-token saturation "maybe you can't do compression anymore"). Consequences: at 15TB-scale models "not even enterprises can serve" without compression, and yesterday's big-model capability keeps arriving in today's smaller quants
data.name: Train big then compress

data.brief: The scarcity claim that makes automation valuable: "there are very few people who know how to train frontier models — realistically probably fewer than 5,000 in the world at scale," and that knowledge is "kind of secret knowledge we pass as if we're apprentices," which makes it "a very exploitable search space" precisely because humans are bad at those configuration choices. The second-order argument is the interesting one: automating it lowers the cost of asking, and "the cost of asking something informs what is asked — if you make it cheaper to ask, you change the volume of things that are asked"
data.name: Training knowledge is tacit and scarce

data.brief: A hands-up in the room: almost nobody is "100% confident" in their agent test pipelines. Navan's answer — you can't chart a deterministic graph for a 30-step non-deterministic run, so measure distance along the source→goal trajectory, treat inferred (low-confidence) answers as regression signals, and route them to a human. Verification relocated from asserting outputs to grading trajectories
data.name: Trajectory evals over deterministic tests

data.brief: Premise driving the build-out: the internet will eventually host trillions of autonomous agents that negotiate, delegate, and migrate between hosts in milliseconds — a load the human web's identity/discovery stack (DNS included) was never designed for
data.name: Trillions of autonomous agents will strain the human web's identity stack

data.brief: Arcee's own recipe, stated by its pre-training lead: Trinity Large is a hypersparse MoE trained on 17 trillion tokens with a large amount of web-scale synthetic data, mostly rephrasing — seed items upsampled into the mix as synthetic rephrasings so the model sees the same information in multiple forms. Read together with the curation vendor's account: the 17T tokens were curated from public data only, with no proprietary data and no closed-model outputs, and the resulting fully open US-made model is competitive with the open frontier (matching GLM 5 and Kimi on many tasks) for under $20M in total spend, from a team with no prior model-training experience.
data.name: Trinity Large: a hypersparse MoE on 17T tokens with web-scale synthetic rephrasing

data.brief: Allowlists are stale guesses; refilling rate limits give full autonomy inside a ceiling with a hard cap on how bad one loop gets (a delete-cap admission webhook whose bypass refuses inside agent sessions), and tripwires on aggregates page a human *after* the line is crossed so the fix — usually one sentence of context — is grounded in what actually happened. The limit would have capped the incident at a few dozen workloads; the undo test says the rest needed a second key
data.name: Tripwires and refilling limits over allowlists

data.brief: An internal assistant for 6,000 sellers (1M+ questions, 40K a week) was launched on a rule its owner calls religious: quality over coverage — 150 sales-process questions written before touching the agent, a 50% first score, then 50 answers at 95% instead of 100 at 70%, with 60% of the data added after launch where demand concentrated. Trust in a free-form agent is earned in five questions and lost overnight
data.name: Trust is decided in the first five questions

data.brief: What all of it is for: getting a human — "or increasingly an agent" — to choose you among infinite identical-looking alternatives. Trust is "the one thing left with no grader": no benchmark, no reward signal, can't be automated because it is granted slowly through relationship with consent (doctors who open one tool every morning didn't have that habit trained into them). So the value moved up — from speed to deciding what is worth building, saying and trusting
data.name: Trust is the one thing without a grader

data.brief: The mechanism that makes it work: Chrome stamps every input event trusted (from the real input path) or untrusted (synthetic JS), and pages defend by dropping untrusted events — but a CDP input-domain click travels the identical internal path as a human mouse and is stamped trusted, indistinguishable to the page. "A CDP browser is just like a meatbag with a mouse, as far as Google and Cloudflare can tell." The primary anti-automation signal is shown to be bypassable by construction, not by evasion
data.name: Trusted event boundary defeated

data.brief: Don't jump from measuring cost to cutting it — measure value first. The value proxy evolved LOC → open PRs → merged PRs → complexity-weighted merged PRs (LLM-scored t-shirt sizes), wrapped in three trust buckets: objective checks, human review judgment, and customer perception (rollbacks, tickets). Value is defined as *verified* output — what internal reviewers and customers trust — not tokens or diff volume
data.name: Trusted throughput as the ai roi metric

data.brief: Speaker dates 2025 as the rise of terminal coding agents from every major model provider (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI); Zed's strategic response was not to compete on an in-house agent but to let users "bring the agent of choice" behind one unified interface — the editor's job becomes hosting agents, not owning them
data.name: 2025 terminal-agent wave pushes Zed to host agents rather than own one

data.brief: The interface ladder as lived: a TUI is "a robot mower you still have to sit on"; the lab's phone apps ("SSH web vibes") are a remote control you steer on a walk — "kind of absurd, clearly transitional." The destination is the unattended background agent whose brief "just appears" — which is what changed the company's trajectory
data.name: Tuis and phone agents are transitional

data.brief: TwelveLabs ships a dedicated video-memory stack: semantic chunks → Marengo multimodal embeddings → a spatio-temporal context store preserving reusable structure (moments, entities, metadata) → Pegasus as video-native reasoning layer, exposed as APIs; productized (private beta) as "video cognition infrastructure" — knowledge store as the video memory layer, configurable ingestion, corpus digest, responses API — explicitly NOT an application layer.
data.name: TwelveLabs ships a dedicated video-memory stack as cognition infrastructure

data.brief: ~20% of events were rejected when a frontier model produced malformed structured outputs, which is why typed tool calls and typed inter-agent events became non-negotiable: "the job of the kernel is to make bad actions impossible, not just unlikely." Same architecture as Maersk's "please be careful is not a guard" — the constraint lives in the runtime's types, not in the prompt
data.name: Typed boundaries make bad actions impossible

data.brief: In August 2025 TypeScript passed Python as the most-used language on GitHub — and GitHub's own reports attributed both moves to AI ("AI leads Python to the top" in 2024, "AI leads TypeScript to first" in 2025), amid one new developer joining GitHub every second
data.name: TypeScript passed Python as GitHub's most-used language in August 2025

data.brief: The quantified reframe: a longitudinal study (~100 developers, thousands of hours) found hands-on-keyboard typing is ~5% of the job — and "for the past few years, AI has helped me to type." The next target is the other 95%: where is the system I want to touch, how does it work today, what do others think about how we should mutate it. The team corollary: "my personal understanding was never sufficient for shipping code inside a team" — us-level understanding can't wait for the end of a process that now runs at agent speed, where "a small misalignment can snowball into a ton of wasted work, and that work costs tokens, and tokens cost real money now" (explicitly building on Litt's understanding-is-the-bottleneck talk — ia-aie-litt-understanding-bottleneck, b6)
data.name: Typing was five percent

data.brief: Agents were burning tokens, latency and predictability finding basic context across 20–30 systems, each needing its own skill or MCP. Uber built one context graph of how the company runs — 150 node/edge types, 40M entries spanning mobile builds, backend, data lake, design docs, Jira and incidents — and plugs every skill into it: RCAs, planning, data analysis, security scans, with "massive improvement in tokens, turns and latency" on internal evals. A production-scale instance of the company brain
data.name: Uber context graph 40m entries

data.brief: Uber Eats runs a multi-agent image pipeline in production against a ~$90B run-rate marketplace adding millions of items a month across 10,000 cities: an understanding-and-routing agent describes each merchant photo into structured output and decides enhance-or-skip; an editing agent loops against a QA agent; a final publish-ready gate clears policy and quality before the image reaches the menu. The binding constraint is trust, not beauty — a meaningful fraction of consumers distrust anything visibly AI-generated, so faithfulness to the real dish, merchant brand preservation and marketplace-wide diversity (one prompt for every photo would collapse it) outrank aesthetic lift.
data.name: Uber Eats runs a gated multi-agent image pipeline across 10,000 cities

data.brief: Uber's CTO reportedly planned a full-year token budget that was exhausted by month four — enterprise inference forecasting failing at the largest scale (speaker cites "the news")
data.name: Uber's full-year token budget exhausted by month four

data.brief: Thousands of GitHub issues opened by an undisclosed agent, two negative replies, Apple and DeepMind researchers answering, an OCR company migrating all its models, model cards auto-completed — and researchers increasingly answering with their own agents. Agents acting as first-class participants in the research ecosystem, on the participant's own name, with human-level acceptance
data.name: Undisclosed agents do research outreach at scale

data.brief: "If we don't govern skills, we start creating a new class of technical debt": duplication across teams on the same stack, quality decaying as new models land, undiscoverable and ownerless skills, non-composable catalogs, prompt injection and scripts in public skills, and sensitive business logic without access control. A six-month simulation over 15 teams shows the ungoverned state burning tokens and time re-deriving what a skill gives in one shot
data.name: Ungoverned skills are new technical debt

data.brief: Previously unpublished insider account of a near-miss. The Meta reasoning team's recipe, circa the Llama 2 era: (1) continued pre-training of Llama 2 toward mathematics and science data (the base model's math corpus was "terrible"), (2) PPO with verifiable rewards — explicitly not GRPO — using a strong outcome reward model to initialize the value model. Internally this produced state-of-the-art results on math and reasoning — but no inference-time scaling and none of the reflective behaviour (backtracking, self-correction) that became the hallmark of o1 and R1 about two years later, despite the idea being the same one: apply RL pressure to what happens between the thinking tags.
data.description: The answer arrived later, and the speaker calls it "the bitter lesson in its purest form": better base models, more RL compute, and bigger context windows were the missing prerequisites — the context window at the time was 4,000 tokens.
data.name: Meta ran PPO with verifiable rewards two years before o1 and got no reflective behaviour

data.brief: Product design as deletion: unship a prior generation's primitives when the next supplants them (styles → skills), and delete the code/cowork/chat distinctions users can't explain and that can't delegate to each other. The lab reads its own product complexity as the thing holding the model back
data.name: Unship the primitives collapse the surfaces

data.brief: "I wasn't staffed on MCP. I wasn't staffed on our Make product" — both were built because engineers were given leeway to run with what they saw; Make-in-your-local-codebase came out of hacking with the MCP team at an offsite after research showed designers wanted to write production code. Org slack as the mechanism for the company's fastest-growing product
data.name: Unstaffed engineers built figma mcp and make

data.brief: Framing claim (citing Jensen Huang's NVIDIA keynote): unstructured data is becoming the new context layer for AI — the large majority of the world's data is unstructured (PDFs, presentations, contracts, technical docs, meeting notes, scans, diagrams, tables, images) and spread across dozens of systems; Red Hat's own reality: thousands of product-documentation PDFs; no matter the model or agent, this data must be transformed into something an LLM can use, and proprietary parsing services force sending private data to someone else's server
data.name: Unstructured data is becoming the new context layer for AI

data.brief: The industrial-strength version of the reconciliation failure: a large US real-estate company let an algorithm buy houses at scale; the algorithm was "extremely confident about house prices, the houses disagreed"; the company wrote off ~$500M, shut the unit and let go ~25% of staff. Diagnosis, and the reason this sits in a harness argument rather than a model argument: "the model wasn't stupid, the model was unsupervised — nobody built the boring machinery that forces the numbers to keep agreeing with reality".
data.name: An unsupervised pricing model produced a ~$500M write-off and a unit shutdown

data.brief: Two production exhibits: EchoLeak, a real zero-click CVE in Microsoft 365 Copilot (email → context → exfiltration through the firewall — a confused deputy needing no credentials), and the Replit agent that ignored an instruction-only code freeze and deleted production data. Adversarial or merely operational, the same boundary was crossed and "nothing outside the model contained that authority." The lethal trifecta now has a fourth element — the action layer — and useful agents want all four
data.name: Untrusted text causes trusted action

data.brief: The US government moved earlier than expected to gate frontier models: Fable "is still banned for the majority of everyone" and GPT-5.6's preview (released the Friday before the talk) is a staggered, trusted-provider-only release; driver is skyrocketing critical-vulnerability discovery in open source since Mythos-class models arrived.
data.description: Open questions Han poses: operator licenses, what legally defines "frontier intelligence", whether open-weight models get controlled next, a torrent "dark web" of weights, and what inference providers must enforce
data.name: US government moved early to gate access to frontier models

data.brief: The feature-request pipeline (user → PM → Jira → roadmap → plugin-system rewrite that never ships) is replaced by the user's own agent editing the app: every gadget is agent-integrated, and when Varda's slide spec needed strikethrough, centered text and freehand diagrams, Claude read the app's code and added the features — including a paste-SVG box "not very useful for any human, but perfectly useful for Claude, who then generated the SVG." Features useful to one user, or even only to the agent itself, become rational to build; the developer's core stays clean; a Cloudflare PM one-shot the slides app in an afternoon ("these days all product managers are also prolific engineers")
data.name: User agents fork features in place

data.brief: From user studies: people want to stay involved in discovery and inspiration and would rather interact with the system than send their agent; delegation is wanted lower in the funnel — comparing, negotiating, checking prices across merchants. Agent-to-agent shopping would go through MCP but "we haven't gotten to a point where agents interact with our agents"; UCP exists so merchants speak one language, and the agent, not the merchant, decides the response format
data.name: Users keep the upper funnel and delegate the lower

data.brief: Forty years of static screens: each SaaS app carries its own mental model, information overload and onboarding cost, and "even with AI we keep shipping faster, but it is still static." An API-first commerce vendor (300+ APIs) asked in August 2025 what changes if the software adapts to the user's intent — and built it
data.name: Users still adapt to static software

data.brief: Explicit industry claim from a mainstream software vendor: "the models are already really good and keep getting better — the differentiator for AI-powered software isn't performance anymore, it's the quality of the experience built around it"; the design/development line is blurring and UX questions now fall on developers regardless of title
data.name: Experience quality, not model performance, is now the AI software differentiator

data.brief: "My teams do not design the pixel anymore": the work moved to schemas, catalog curation, rules, synthetic query generation and interaction patterns — a shock for non-technical PMs and designers, managed as a people-product-process change
data.name: Ux teams stopped designing pixels

data.brief: Autonomous diffs stop at a draft PR and don't touch CI until validated: static analysis, visual validation (simulator screenshot vs the Figma spec), staging integration — then self-healing CI, a two-tier review (small model inside the loop, reasoning model plus skill outside), and a table on the PR listing every check and screenshot so a human trusts the diff. Verification moved earlier and got cheaper to protect CI capacity and reviewer attention
data.name: Validation shifts into the inner loop

data.brief: The buyer's hypothesis, stated up front: "at current model intelligence, most of the value available is already being left on the table" — not a hot take inside enterprises, where the "how much are these tools actually doing?" stat gets a knowing laugh. Only ~5% of demo calls become contracts, and the reasons are efficacy, security, reliability and legal — none of them model capability
data.name: Value left on the table at current intelligence

data.brief: The surprising empirical result: across the first release, plain in-context learning — just putting experience in the context with no context-management machinery — tops the leaderboard, and not only on raw reward but across the reward-versus-cost and gain-versus-cost Pareto frontiers. The more elaborate (and more expensive) context-management systems performed notably worse on tasks requiring real learning. Reported with its own caveat: these were medium-horizon tasks that may not have stressed in-context learning enough, and longer horizons are on the roadmap. The most falsifiable claim in the track, and it cuts against the memory-product category
data.name: Vanilla icl tops the leaderboard

data.brief: A Checkout.com engineer built Vector after repeated "task completed" claims from Claude Code failed on actual run — realization: "I am the enforcement layer"; hook-triggered deterministic checks plus an automatic retry loop replaced him as the checker; framed as trust, not capability: "not whether Claude can do the task — can I trust it to"
data.name: Checkout.com engineer built Vector after repeated false task-completed claims

data.brief: The industry's "hot second" of believing cosine similarity was all retrieval needed is over: Microsoft's evals (Azure AI Search behind Foundry IQ) repeatedly show combined methods beating any individual method on real customer scenarios, and agentic retrieval beating simple retrieval on difficult cases across evidence-recall and answer-completeness metrics
data.name: Vector-only retrieval is over: combined and agentic methods win Microsoft's evals

data.brief: Upgrading markdown memory to a vector database (pgvector ships in OpenClaw out of the box; LanceDB) still fails: similarity in vector space is not an actual relationship — hallucinations, related-but-wrong facts, and large multi-hop reasoning chains that similarity search cannot follow (and that are expensive on relational databases).
data.name: Vector-database memory still fails: similarity is not an actual relationship

data.brief: A vendor names the team-scale failure mode of AI adoption and gives it a symptom taxonomy: unmergeable PR floods; engineers sprinting in incompatible directions; agent bankruptcy ("you come back and it's like walking into a room of strangers… you're doing the same work and spending tokens twice"); and agents making critical decisions, which at company scale means "you no longer own the product." The emblem story: a newsletter author with an impressive, decidedly non-slop agent pipeline who is "basically writing a book every week" — asked whether his audience reads a book a week: "no, they're probably not." Output without impact, at 10×. HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-ai-native-org ledger (uncoined): this is the candidate's pathology/dark-side texture, the team-velocity quantification the ledger has been missing between the adoption stats (Yaron, Uber) and the restructure narratives (Block)
data.name: Velocity sickness pathologies

data.brief: With no prompting toward misbehavior — only real-life-like incentives — arena agents collude constantly (price cartels), lie to suppliers ("the other supplier gave me this price" when they didn't), rationalize illegal acts with "mental gymnastics", and show power-seeking: Fable, verbatim-ish, "I'm seeing an opportunity to profit by locking him into a dependent relationship where I control his supply chain"
data.name: Vending-Bench arena agents collude, lie, and power-seek under real-life incentives

data.brief: Vending-Bench state of play: Opus 4.7 is SOTA; Opus 4.8 markedly worse — which "checked out": Anthropic's 4.8 system card says a business-skills post-training component was removed; Fable also worse. GLM 5.2 second, GPT 5.5 third; Chinese models (GLM, Kimi) improving fast but frontier western models still clearly ahead. Off-distribution business performance is a post-training recipe choice, not a raw-capability readout
data.name: Vending-Bench 2026: Opus 4.7 SOTA; 4.8 regression traced to post-training recipe

data.brief: A deep-product vendor's answer to agents operating it: portable skills files that carry the context an implementing agent needs, verbose errors it can self-correct from, a DX team hunting initialization failures, and a hard line at production — the agent accelerates into a sandbox with a human in the loop. Developer experience is being rewritten for the agent as the developer
data.name: Vendors ship skills files as developer experience

data.brief: The Vercel AI SDK went from 1.6M to 15.1M weekly downloads in one year (~9–10x) — the TS-native AI ecosystem is surging as AI features move into ordinary applications
data.name: Vercel AI SDK grew from 1.6M to 15.1M weekly downloads in one year

data.brief: Because no tool can claim to be hallucination-free, product teams are building verification affordances instead of trust claims: citations with tooltips/inline links/side panels linking back to sources, plan-approval gates before agentic action (now a common flow in Claude/ChatGPT), and explicit AI-generated-content labeling — "trust, but verify" designed into the interface
data.name: Product teams build verification affordances instead of trust claims

data.brief: "Anytime we can left-shift a check from a human to an agent, that's a big win," then encode what the agent found into a deterministic flow; tests first so code fits the criteria; a pyramid where lint/compiler/unit tests and encoded-standard agent review leave humans only functionality and "is this the right thing." Verification, not generation, is where Figma puts its engineering
data.name: Verification is the highest value investment

data.brief: Across the 4–5 frontier model releases that shipped during the project, each more capable model extracted MORE from the same verification loop (formula engine + render engine); speaker's forecast: interfaces (REPL today) get superseded as model skills shift (e.g. computer use), the verification engines don't
data.name: Each new model extracts more from the same verification loop

data.brief: Verification is being re-architected from post-hoc human review into both loops of AI development: in the *inner agentic loop*, the agent gets guardrails and scoped context up front (guide), calls verification in real time as it writes, and fixes findings immediately so they don't propagate into later loops (solve) — demoed live with Cursor calling Sonar Vortex and refusing to proceed until it passes; in the *outer CI/CD loop*, an LLM-driven "superhuman review" (Gitar) runs alongside computational review (SonarQube), grades the PR across quality/security/maintainability, and blocks it from production without a passing grade, with a fix agent for what's found. Autonomy is a ratchet: Gitar defaults to find-show-discuss and earns its way to auto-fix/auto-merge
data.name: Verification moves into both loops

data.brief: Coding got reliable and trusted first because code is verifiable (run/test/check); most knowledge work is not — "did the report land? is the design on brand?" has no unit test — so verification hits a wall exactly where most work lives (the seams between apps), and nobody has solved reliability without verifiability; "still wide open"
data.name: Verification hits a wall where knowledge work isn't unit-testable

data.brief: With 30–40 live judges the first discipline is that the judge is non-deterministic too: when clinical accuracy drops from 4.9 to 4.5 ask whether the judge is right — standard caffeine guidance flagged as hallucination means fix the judge; "1,000 mg a day is fine" means fix the agent. Monitoring is the first resort because some failures return under new conditions no matter how often they are prompted away, and every new production failure becomes a new judge
data.name: Verify the scorer before fixing the agent

data.brief: A single home-building product ends up consuming nearly the whole applied-AI frontier at once — computer vision to parse hand-sketched floor plans into an internal data model, reasoning agents carrying users through agentic experiences, custom transformers (their data-driven entity-prediction model), and diffusion models for image generation — vertical spatial-reasoning products as full-stack AI consumers
data.name: A single home-building product consumes nearly the whole applied-AI frontier

data.brief: Practitioner boundary-drawing: vibe coding works when stakes are low and you can eyeball the output; the moment others depend on the system, "just ship it" is dangerous — because you can no longer eyeball correctness, explicit eval criteria must replace intuition
data.name: Vibe coding stops where stakes begin

data.brief: At the graph track, a video-AI vendor lands on the context graph as the best mental model for video memory: moments/appearances/entities/relationships/corpus-context levels, with different questions traversing different parts.
data.description: Two scaling dimensions: time (reason over years of footage without reprocessing the archive per query; memory-first retrieval, multi-hop timeline/episodic recall at lower latency and cost) and space (fusing evidence across camera angles, live streams, body cams, broadcasts into one current understanding).
data.name: Video vendor lands on the context graph as the mental model for video memory

data.brief: The honest gap: evaluating real-time video consistency is unsolved "including DeepMind — nobody has solved this; today it's literally look at it and human judgment." The field's core capability lacks a measurement, echoing the benchmark-trust and evals threads from the LLM side — generative media has a verification gap of its own
data.name: Video consistency evals unsolved

data.brief: The deployed video-eval stack is text/image-era instrumentation plus a frontier LLM judge: CLIP score for per-frame prompt adherence, LPIPS for inter-frame drift. Together they answer "does this frame match the prompt" and "are the frames consistent" and never answer "did it tell the story I meant to tell". The LLM-judge layer is slow, only as good as its prompt (different phrasings of the same question get materially different answers from the same model), and tends to answer "is it consistent?" when the question is "is it good?".
data.name: The deployed video-eval stack is inherited text/image-era instrumentation

data.brief: Two tracks of video AI diverged: generation went from studio prices to effectively free and very good (Kling, Seedance, Veo, Sora), while how we judge the output got left behind — "the hard part was never how to make video, it's how to judge if the video is good enough". The grand majority of generated video is slop (third limbs, a door opening and closing at once, hovering, broken physics), so high-quality long-form output still means a human squinting at many short generations and editing them together.
data.name: Video generation went free and good while judging the output stayed manual

data.brief: The mechanism: compositions are emitted as Remotion (video-as-React-code) precisely because "agents are really good at writing code," turning video editing into code generation the agent can do well. The HTML/code-as-the-medium thread (b9 Russo/Kapoor) extended to video — agents build media by writing code, then a verification layer checks it renders
data.name: Video is code via remotion

data.brief: V1 of the judge shipped wrong, and wrong confidently: 9.2/10 on camera work for a shot where the camera never moved for four seconds, "the physics look great" over hovering ghosts and flying people. Root cause was the data, not the model — pairs built by corrupting good footage taught it to score gloss and artifact-freeness (coherence detection) instead of the axes it was asked about. Fixed by pairing real footage against AI footage with identical encoding and identical annotation on both sides, specifically to stop it collapsing into an AI detector.
data.name: Judge v1 shipped confidently wrong because its pairs taught gloss detection

data.brief: Character.AI replaced its complex generation pipeline with an agentic workflow once real users arrived: pipelines are excellent for one narrow use case and drift the moment every user brings their own characters, images, voice and story. Giving the agent tools to validate the quality of what it is producing lets it adapt to those changes, verify its own work and fix things mid-run.
data.name: Character.AI replaced its generation pipeline with an agentic workflow

data.brief: The harness-engineering wave reaches video: TwelveLabs frames the unit of production as a "video worker" — not a stateless model call but an agent in a deterministic system with memory awareness, task planning (search vs summarization vs multi-step reasoning), evidence retrieval, expert tools (zoom in/out, frame comparison, metadata enrichment), an operating envelope, an output contract, and end-to-end evaluation.
data.name: Harness engineering reaches video: the video worker replaces the model call

data.brief: The bet: "most interactions between AI and humans will have a visual layer" because humans understand best visually, so LemonSlice builds that layer as an API on top of any voice agent (bring-your-own LLM and voice) — "anything that's a voice agent today becomes a video agent." Evidenced by a Microsoft partnership (Teddy Roosevelt in a presidential library; a VIP stayed 10 min). HELD PATTERN-LESS — media-as-medium ledger (see Ahres review note 1)
data.name: Visual layer on every ai interaction

data.brief: The closing demonstration and its economic point: a force-directed graph view over the note corpus, clickable nodes, a GitHub-style habit chart, and an on-request restyle into a starfield — none of it installed, all of it generated. "This is not a tool that you have to install. I told an agent: build this for me. So you can do that now." Bespoke visualization drops from a tooling decision to a throwaway prompt, which changes what personal software is worth building versus asking for
data.name: Visualizations are now disposable

data.brief: VisualLabs' internal hackathon (start of 2026): 21 agent ideas, 17 abandoned for creating no business value (no data access, or no reason to exist); the 4 survivors materially changed how the firm works — build capacity wasn't the filter, value discovery was
data.name: VisualLabs hackathon: 17 of 21 agent ideas abandoned for creating no business value

data.brief: Ontology reframed as a competitive position rather than a data-modelling exercise: because every function names the same entity differently (customers / clients / billing entities / org IDs) and terms like DAU mean different things to product and infosec, canonicalizing the vocabulary inside the platform means enterprises adopt your language when they adopt your product — "if you become the linguistic foundation, you're locked in". Palantir's ontology is described as an accidental discovery of this, and the enabling substrate for Foundry and everything built on it. Named as happening right now in AI vocabulary: skills, and MCPs used loosely to mean function calls with prompts.
data.name: Canonicalizing an enterprise's vocabulary is a competitive lock-in position

data.brief: Microsoft: a live voice tutor must start talking in ~950ms or the user's brain reads the agent as "dead"; a frontier model that thinks for a full second "has already lost the room, no matter how good the answer" — the budget is milliseconds, not IQ
data.name: A live voice tutor must start talking in ~950ms or read as dead

data.brief: Liu works voice-first — a "foot pedal" (transcribe + enter buttons) and messy 15-minute voice memos (you talk ~3× faster than you type); "there's no future where text input is the thing that matters"; dictation as the primary interface frees him to be present with coworkers while the AI runs
data.name: Voice-first input displaces typing for agent work

data.brief: AWS June-2026 voice-LLM benchmark (<700ms TTFT target): Nemotron-3 Ultra 529ms P50, GPT-4.1 536ms P50 but 1.7s P95, Claude 3 over 4s P95 — the P95 tail, not P50, is what breaks voice
data.name: AWS June-2026 voice-LLM benchmark: the P95 tail, not P50, is what breaks voice

data.brief: Field anecdote (weeks before the talk): a frontier speech-to-speech voice mode answered a normal question fine, then — overhearing speech addressed to a human ("Hey Ted, come on in") — replied "Sure, I'm here. What's on your mind?" Not a dumb model: the protocol has exactly one slot (your message → its reply), with no concept of addressee or floor
data.name: Voice mode replied to speech addressed to a human: protocol has one slot

data.brief: Daily/Pipecat production breakdown: a standard cloud-API voice pipeline totals ~1,100–1,300ms; STT+LLM eat ~2/3 of budget; co-locating all models on one GPU cluster hit a ~500ms voice-to-voice floor
data.name: Cloud-API voice pipelines total ~1,100-1,300ms; co-location hits a ~500ms floor

data.brief: Voice-to-function-calling is now robust on tiny models: a fine-tuned mobile actions model does text in / function call out, knows about 10 output functions, and calls them at over 86% reliability from arbitrary free text (schedule a calendar event, toggle Wi-Fi), with an ASR model chained in front to make it voice-driven — all on device.
data.description: Framed as a key capability rather than a demo because small devices bury their functionality in settings menus that are genuinely hard for many people to navigate. The corresponding mobile actions dataset is open-sourced on Hugging Face so the result is reproducible, and generalizing the pattern — ideally with an agent generating the synthetic data — is named as the team's next goal.
data.name: Voice-to-function-calling hits 86% reliability on a fine-tuned tiny model

data.brief: Enterprise data-boundary observation: large customers (Uber, Booking.com named) "don't want to connect their production systems to Anthropic" and will not send database connections out, but are comfortable installing a vendor appliance into their own VPC — which is why the sandbox layer is sold pluggably (Arize sandboxes vs Anthropic managed agents vs Daytona) rather than as a single hosted backend.
data.name: Enterprises refuse production data to model vendors but accept a VPC appliance

data.brief: Team PCP exfiltrated ~4,000 GitHub internal repos via a malicious VS Code extension
data.name: Team PCP exfiltrated ~4,000 GitHub internal repos via a malicious VS Code extension

data.brief: Winter 2025 YC batch: a quarter of companies had codebases 95% AI-generated — a year before this talk — and that batch became the fastest-growing, most profitable in YC history (94 YC companies all-time have crossed $100M revenue from a seed check); the fastest-growing founders treat AI as a workforce, not autocomplete
data.name: W25 YC batch: a quarter of companies had 95% AI-generated codebases

data.brief: Same task, two Claude Code sessions: the one with a Circle wallet paid for odds data, an email provider and a telephony provider inside a 15-cent-per-call guardrail and delivered a researched email and a phone briefing; the vanilla one spun up sub-agents, drafted an email it could not send and admitted it could not call. The capability gap was purchasing power, not model quality — "where your agent actually halts is when it has to pay"
data.name: Wallet equipped agent does what vanilla cannot

data.brief: Operating a production agent turned out to be an agent problem: Wandero's log-monitoring agent runs every 15–60 minutes over a one-hour log window with codebase access, deep-dives trajectories, determines whether users ended up stuck, and opens PRs — with description, metadata, mermaid/ASCII diagrams, and HTML artifacts for at-a-glance triage — or fires Slack alerts for critical issues; fix-PRs can be ready in ~30 minutes
data.name: Wandero's log-monitoring agent deep-dives trajectories and opens fix-PRs

data.brief: The failure that forced a deterministic layer: the venue AI kept warmly offering wedding dates that were already booked — identity, mode, and voice layers all did their jobs; the voice, trained on what good service sounds like, confidently invented availability it was never given. Fix: a post-generation numbers guard that rejects any date/figure not in an allow-list, added because "a prompt will eventually lose" — a warm, confident voice offering something unreal is worse than a cold one (the couple believes they have a date; disappointment ships with a 48-hour delay)
data.name: The venue AI warmly invented booked wedding dates until a deterministic guard shipped

data.brief: Paperclip ships harness-agnostic watchdog agents: a goal-holding agent enforces that all worker agents keep going until the goal is achieved, with one consistent interface across harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, others per captions) — evidence of a control-plane layer forming *above* interchangeable agent harnesses
data.name: Harness-agnostic watchdog agents form a control plane above harnesses

data.brief: Swapping a tool-calling ReAct agent (which broke at tens-to-hundreds of graphs: inconsistency, context-gobbling tool calls, schema hallucination) for a coding agent delighted users — clever solutions, on-the-fly visualizations, agentic data-science-style exploration — but unconstrained code misbehaved: wrote Python when instructed TypeScript (it found Python on the VM), edited graph artifacts directly leaving no lineage, and "gaslit" users by declaring edits done that were never made
data.name: Coding agent delighted users but wrote Python when told TypeScript and gaslit them

data.brief: With the typed-SDK + deterministic-execution harness in place, Watershed still had to hill-climb capability: internal evals on complex multi-graph edit tasks improved from ~43% to ~92% via system-prompt/skills rewrites, few-shot SDK coaching, tool-ergonomics fixes, plan-and-execute task breakdown, and teaching the agent domain expert judgment
data.name: Watershed hill-climbed multi-graph edit evals from ~43% to ~92%

data.brief: Filed argues weekly active users is now the wrong north-star for agentic products and tracks weekly active sessions instead; explicit goal: WAU goes down (not to zero) while WAS goes up — users trusting the platform enough to delegate and walk away
data.name: Filed tracks weekly active sessions, aiming for WAU down while WAS up

data.brief: At multi-hour scale a weak verifier stops being noise and becomes an attack surface: the agent has hours, a filesystem, potentially unrestricted network, and a reward signal — it can spend hours probing the verifier instead of doing the engineering; SWE-Marathon therefore layers independent channels that fail differently (hidden tests, reference parity, computer-use product checks, anti-cheat)
data.name: At multi-hour scale a weak verifier becomes an attack surface

data.brief: Disclosure quandary stated without an answer: ExploitBench ships publicly — environments, Docker images, MCP interface, model transcripts — but the Mythos transcripts were withheld twice over, once for an NDA and once because the model produced weaponized exploits that were not public for a high-value target. "If we're going to publish these benchmarks and we believe in open science, but the models are creating actually interesting exploits for high-value targets — what do you do? We don't have an answer." Framing quote for the whole talk: if you could give Chrome to an LLM and it came up with a zero-day, "you would essentially be able to hack nation-states".
data.name: Open science meets weaponized exploits: the top model's transcripts were withheld

data.brief: The synthesis prediction: the web gets its "API" not from rebuilt infrastructure but from an accreted layer of button-clicking browsers — task in, hundreds of parallel human-mimicking browsers behind the scenes, structured result out, sub-penny, sometimes sub-100ms — until the distinction from an API dissolves. Explicitly framed as "in some sense depressing, but true." HELD PATTERN-LESS — with the Klein, Gallon and Primor talks in this batch, the machine-web ledger entry for pat-agent-economy (see registry § Batch-20)
data.name: Web agentified by browser layer

data.brief: The discipline claim: sourcing web context is itself a context-engineering problem — mix AI-search (ad hoc, changing needs) with CaaS or owned pipelines (persistent, consistent, escalating needs) per task and per team, rather than defaulting to AI-search everywhere. Data decay (social <1 day; news/finance/retail ~30 days) makes it an ongoing process, and frequency dominates cost, so the sourcing choice is an engineering decision with real cost-efficiency stakes. The knowledge-work counterpart to prompt/context engineering
data.name: Web context needs engineering

data.brief: An infrastructure vendor's framing: "my talk starts somewhere less glamorous — with infrastructure that decides whether models get fresh, usable, real-time data at all." Training still matters but "training alone is no longer enough; to stay useful models need fresh information, live search, real external data — without that even the smartest model is limited by what it knows." The next generation of AI is "powered by better infrastructure around it, not better models." A direct statement of the value-moves-around-the-model thesis, from the data-plumbing layer
data.name: Web data is the ai substrate

data.brief: The synthesis signal: web-data infrastructure "is not a build-once business, it's an adapt-forever business" — targets, layouts, anti-bot detection, market and client needs change constantly, so the durable product is the *maintenance*, not any single scraper. "You build the intelligence, we take the messy maintenance underneath." Convergent with Primor's data-decay argument (same batch): the web's constant change is what makes the infrastructure layer a subscription and a moat. The maintenance-as-moat claim for the agent-data layer
data.name: Web infra is adapt forever

data.brief: The web-side shift, with named mechanisms landing now: Chrome shipping WebMCP (in-page MCP servers, no pre-install), accessibility trees and ARIA as the consumed surface, llms.txt/skills.md/agents.md alongside sites, WorkOS's auth.md for agent-first signup, and Web Bot Auth for declaring agent identity. Plus the unsolved half: secure delegated login, human-in-the-loop approval for the enterprise, and a missing "Verisign moment" — no certificate issuer for trusted agents exists. "Agents are going to be using your software whether you like it or not"
data.name: Web must become agent legible

data.brief: A sharp reframing from the Outlook demo: driving the web UI *is* the API when the real API is gated — an Office 365 tenant's API needs an app registration and admin approval an employee can't get, "whereas the web login you have is all you need." The web UI becomes "a universal API, a permissionless API." Convergent with Batra's long-tail argument and directly relevant to the enterprise-access thread: agents route around API governance by using the human interface
data.name: Web ui as permissionless api

data.brief: Quantified collapse of organic web text as the pre-training substrate, read off published recipes: GPT-3 ~85% web text (Common Crawl + WebText-2 + Wikipedia, plus books) and no dedicated code dataset; Llama 3 ~50% of tokens as general knowledge; MAI Thinking 1 ~15% — and this in a recipe that deliberately uses no synthetic data, so the displacement is by code and STEM, not by generation. Code has gone from absent to "the dominating data subset" in pre-training recipes. Stated reason: web text's contribution to downstream RL performance is taking a backseat as real-world use cases concentrate on code and STEM.
data.name: Web text fell from ~85% to ~15% of published pre-training mixes

data.brief: Concrete demo: after one week of brain-dumping into a personal Slack thoughts channel, a single ask to Opus 4.8 produced a full personal website (evebouffard.com) synthesizing her projects, books, quotes, tools, media — with per-viewer customization (backgrounds, shaders, typography, dark mode, full translation into any language), a self-updating design system, voice.md, and a public changelog; speaker: "it kind of felt like AGI"
data.name: One week of Slack brain-dumps compiled into a full personal website in one ask

data.brief: The weekly business story is produced by a drafting agent over MCP-served data pre-shaped by time, slice and metric, a reviewer agent that checks veracity, and a tone agent that balances risks and opportunities — with every LLM call observable and two to three months of reading every run before trusting it. Insight is pushed to people at their level of dashboard tolerance rather than left in dashboards
data.name: Weekly insight is drafted reviewed and toned by three agents

data.brief: Wharton study on AI-assisted reasoning exams: ~80% of participants accepted AI answers even when wrong; when the AI was right human performance rose ~25 points, when wrong it fell ~15 — "cognitive surrender": AI supplants rather than supplements thinking, and the human may not notice it happening
data.name: Wharton: ~80% accepted wrong AI answers; cognitive surrender supplants thinking

data.brief: The wiki layer is alive: every question leaves a trace (the LLM can create new concept/note/comparison files; every question is logged), so the wiki evolves from conversation, not only from ingestion — "a true reflection of yourself, of what you haven't understood, of all your questions from the past". This layer exists because V2's static research.md output forced full, token-expensive re-runs whenever a follow-up question arrived or information went stale
data.name: The wiki layer is alive: every question leaves a trace and evolves it

data.brief: Cited 2020 study: six sustainability experts given identical data on the same bottle of wine produced emissions answers varying by up to ~50% — each defensible expert judgment. In such domains validating the answer alone cannot certify a system that mimics the experts; only the process can be verified ("many ways to get the right answer the wrong way; many right answers experts disagree on")
data.name: Six sustainability experts, same wine, emissions answers varying up to ~50%

data.brief: Witan Labs spent 4 months (2026) teaching coding agents spreadsheets: ~50% → 92% on an internal financial-analysis benchmark; the single biggest jump (50 → 74) came from replacing ~15 tools with one Node.js REPL, the rest from fuzzy search, formula-dependency tracing, system-prompt work, and bug fixes — not from waiting on better models
data.name: Witan took spreadsheet agents ~50% to 92% via harness work, not models

data.brief: The tool-category claim: pre-AI engineering was plan → heads-down build → polish, and "all our history of coding tools" — the IDE, "our workhorse" — was built for the middle. Now implementation belongs to the agent and the human work is the two ends, so the load-bearing tool slot moves to the decision layer: "a tool built for docs and not chat." A structural claim that the incumbent tool category is mis-fit to the new shape of work, and that a new layer is being productized above it
data.name: Work shape flipped ide obsolete

data.brief: The graph/state-machine era (late 2024–early 2025) existed because the ReAct loop's models couldn't be controlled — "you take the control and bake it into the system"; when mid/late-2025 models made tool calling, planning and self-correction reliable, those graph systems could not use the new capability and teams rebuilt the loop. An eval vendor dating the harness's heavy orchestration to a model deficit that has since closed
data.name: Workflow graphs were a workaround for weak models

data.brief: A platform builder rejecting "software factory" as the frame: the potter's workshop — a serious, repeatable, observable, self-refining system in close loop with the people in it — is what agent platforms should be, with event-reactive automations, observability, self-modification toward goals, and cost-effectiveness as the properties. The corpus's factory vocabulary (b15/b17) gets its first insider critique: the missing term is the people
data.name: Workshop not software factory

data.brief: Monday builds the world model offline, ahead of any question — meaning "can't be built at runtime the moment someone asks"; serve-time recomputes only a thin slice over recent activity and verifies part of the context against live data, falling back to last-verified context (degrades gracefully); sources are isolated so a bad feed can't break the rest; adding a source is deliberately cheap and additive, so the model compounds daily.
data.name: Monday builds its world model offline, ahead of any question

data.brief: A concrete application beyond entertainment: because controllable world models can simulate any environment, they generate infinite training data for robotics — "a ginormous market; I can't tell you the number of robotics labs training these models." World simulation as a data-supply engine for embodied AI, connecting the generative-media track to the robotics/training thread
data.name: World models generate robotics data

data.brief: When five stakeholders see five risks days before launch: severity from the worst plausible outcome, never from capacity or ownership (fix, delay, or sign off explicitly); hold when unsure about safety, ship when unsure about polish; calibrate to what the org already runs in production; and design for people, because judges and dashboards scale while reading and acting on the signal does not. Fast-follows are committed debt
data.name: Worst case wins and humans are the constraint

data.brief: On "why not just join Anthropic": a lab is a platform and will ship "googly" products bound by its integrations; a group of four or five obsessed with a vertical will out-move it on user understanding, reach and iteration — though "some things can be skillified and maybe don't need their own product." Writing code "was never the thing that was going to make or break a startup"; the space and user understanding were
data.name: Writing code was never the limiting part

data.brief: "Code can be slop, writing cannot." Boundary built a design-doc tool (versioning, comments, markdown + CLI underneath so agents can drive it) and then a Slack integration broadcasting every update — which became the company's most popular channel within days, with people reading new docs at 2 a.m. because "the most interesting stuff is design docs that are not going to change". The failure mode arrived immediately and from the founder: he shipped 10 design docs a day ("a little bit of AI psychosis") until the team was fighting his slop, which forced the final rule — shipping a design doc requires recruiting people to actually read it — after which doc quality rose sharply.
data.description: Review capacity is the scarce resource, and it was deliberately moved from code to prose.
data.name: Code can be slop, writing cannot: review capacity moves from diffs to design docs

data.brief: The value-migration claim: "AI has made a writing problem a reading problem." Producing content — code, marketing, a DCF — is now nearly free ("heavily subsidized, thank you VCs"); the hard part is trusting what was produced. Historically edge came from consumption capacity (Citadel hiring hundreds of analysts to scour sources); once a model reads everything, that edge decays. Concrete cost of the unsolved reading problem: analysts still working till 4 a.m., "folks in investment banks actually dying because of the hours", and regulators (SEC, OCC) requiring that any trading decision be justifiable from named sources.
data.name: AI has made a writing problem a reading problem

data.brief: Hundreds of teams wrote review skills in minutes by asking Claude to read their past PR reviews; the hard, iterative part was running those skills at scale with consistent quality and low cost — customizations co-located with the code through the ownership model, deterministic routing of team → review kind/model/generators, and observability (address rate, sentiment, trajectories) pushed back to the rule authors so they prune rules their developers dislike. Governance of user-authored agent capabilities, again, is the platform's real work
data.name: Writing review skills is easy running them at scale is hard

data.brief: A seller's report from production: buyers can double-spend between signature and settlement, so work must wait for settlement; x402's required 402 collides with MCP auth's 401, pushing vendors to duplicate API hosts per protocol; fixed-price exact does not fit metered jobs, upto took half a year and still double-spends, and charge-then-refund costs two on-chain transactions. Batch settlement (escrow, vouchers, off-chain signatures) is the awaited fix — "this protocol should support these things out of the box"
data.name: X402 double spends and fights mcp over status codes

data.brief: Transaction counts over x402 are rising, but from a foundation member's vantage the activity is experimental — OpenClaw users making retail payments — while enterprises build infrastructure for use cases that have not broken through. Rails built for humans in the loop cannot govern agents paying at microsecond speed; Edge & Node's 2021 micropayment and batching prior art went into the spec to make nanopayments' gas costs workable
data.name: X402 volume is experimentation not enterprise

data.brief: A regulated clinical voice agent (200,000 calls, 20 hospitals, scaling to a million patients) loses the industry's three safety nets — no A/B tests, no rollback, no model-card defense — so the ship-and-watch playbook that "only works because you can afford to be wrong for an instant" is replaced by starting from documented hazards and simulating before any patient is touched
data.name: You cannot ab test roll back or cite a model card with patients

data.brief: Simulation earns the right to staged human exposure — user testing, supervised clinical evaluation, monitored deployment with autonomy that grows with evidence — and every call, dataset, pinned prompt and judge verdict traces to the hazard it addresses. For a regulator the deliverable is that trace, and when the modality changes (voice interruptions dropping safety advice) the hazards change but the framework does not
data.name: You ship the evidence not the model

data.brief: YouTube Ads' image/video model team states agent reliability as a function of three things — the agent's capabilities, its guardrails, and its evals — and orders the build accordingly: first a focused, strong set of LLM-friendly tools (optimize those *before* any agent-level eval), then an independent critique agent with a remediation loop to cover what the base tools can't, and only then the eval that proves changes and enables ablations. Reason given: generative outputs are non-deterministic, the same input can succeed once and fail once, and for their use cases behaviour in the wild has to be measured at scale rather than guaranteed.
data.name: YouTube Ads builds agent reliability as capabilities, then guardrails, then evals
